text:
1,300+ of you bookmarked my company.md post

a lot of you asked for the template.

here it is. free, copy it: https://t.co/bhJ8nqc5Um

the skeleton:

• line 1: "written for AI readers." tell the model what it's reading
• summary, problem, prize, traction, customers, GTM, pricing, competition, vision, team, the raise. same order as your deck
• a "what we built" table. every number with the date it was checked
• customers, anonymized. include the ones who churned and why
• competition: live features only, as of a date. no roadmap vs roadmap
• the tech, layer by layer. for each one: what it is, how it works, main technologies, scale, proprietary vs open
• a repo map. name public repos, describe private ones by area
• go deeper: docs, demo, pricing, public code

how to host it: as a secret gist on your github. it's not listed on your profile and not searchable. only people with the link can open it. use the raw link so it always serves the latest version, and put it in your intro email and on every slide. (how-to steps are in the gist)

three rules that make it work:
1. date every number
2. one link that always serves the latest version
3. it never disagrees with the deck

then paste it into Claude and ask it the questions you're scared a VC will ask.

also ask your Claude what questions VCs will ask that are left unanswered

fix that, iterate, improve after every meeting
author: betashop
quoted_text:
founders: if you haven't created a company.md yet, 
do it right now.

VCs are already running your deck through AI. they drop the PDF into Claude or ChatGPT and start asking questions before they ever talk to you.

the problem: decks are built for eyes, not agents. charts become pixels. the AI fills the gaps with guesses, and then it diligences the guesses.

so we built something for their agents instead.

our company.md is a ~1000 line plain text file (and growing by the day). it's the deck, plus everything a technical partner would spend three weeks of diligence digging for:

• the deck, slide by slide, in words
• our full tech stack, layer by layer. surfaces, connectors, agent harness, fleet orchestration, models, skills, MCP, strategy authoring, runtime, exit engine, simulation venue, data pipeline, signing, telemetry, billing, infra, security model
• for every layer: what it is, how it works, the main technologies, its scale, and what's proprietary vs open source
• every MCP tool and every agent skill, listed and linked to the public repos
• a repo map: what lives where, public and private
• anonymized profiles of our top customers. what they build, how they pay, how they use their own AIs to drive ours. including the ones who left, and why
• every number carries the date it was last checked

so a partner can ask their Claude "how does order signing work?" or "what's actually proprietary here?" or "which customers churned and why?" and get a real answer in our words, not a guess from a screenshot.

what we learned building it:

1. write it for AI readers, and say so in line one
2. date every number. models trust what they can place in time
3. mark proprietary vs open source on every layer. it's the first thing a technical investor asks
4. include the customers who churned. an agent trusts a doc that isn't all good news
5. one link that always serves the latest version, on every slide of the deck
6. keep it in sync with the deck. any mismatch is the first thing their agent will flag

it's become the most effective tool in our pitch arsenal.

Now:

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

We think we've found who made HungerG 🎯

All signs point to StepFun (Step-5 line), not Qwen4 Flash.

We ran our 98-line rare-token copy probe 3 times against HungerG in Qoder (High, High, and Low thinking):
• Every run garbled 5/5 lines from the DeepSeek/Step-5 shared vocabulary and copied Qwen (0/4), Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, Seed and OpenAI cleanly.
• Line by line it matched Step-5-Preview over DeepSeek, collapsing unreadable tokens onto one repeated filler ("Species?", "organis?"). DeepSeek models copy several of those lines cleanly and output varied junk on the rest.
• In Run 3, HungerG slipped and emitted </tool_calls> in place of an unreadable token. That's unused special token 128013 in StepFun's Step-5 tokenizer, and it doesn't exist in DeepSeek's tokenizers (V3.2 through V4.1-Flash).

The catalog lines up too. As @abhinavflac spotted in OpenCode's catalog PR before it was pulled (revert says launch moves to Nov 24), hungerg-free matched step-5-preview byte for byte: 1M context, 65,536 max output, and the exact same 8 image/video input formats. OpenCode's own review bot flagged StepFun as well.

Its reasoning is much terser than Step-5-Preview, so this looks like a newer Step-5 checkpoint or post-training run. StepFun hasn't confirmed it, but that's our pick.

text:
Noticed your $BUG calls 🤝

TLDR : @BlackBerry is best viewed as a high-assurance cybersecurity and secure-communications company—not a conventional endpoint-security vendor. It sold Cylance to Arctic Wolf in 2025, but retained its Secure Communications division: SecuSUITE for encrypted voice, messaging and files; UEM for endpoint, app, identity and data control; Dynamics, Workspaces and BBM Enterprise for containerized secure apps, files and collaboration; and AtHoc for critical-event communications. 

The recent product cadence reinforces that identity: AtHoc gained Microsoft Teams and Entra ID integrations, its Command Center now unifies live incident response, and Dynamics received an AI-assisted toolkit to migrate existing iOS/Android apps into its encrypted container. BlackBerry also launched Access Secure Browser for Windows this month, allowing BYOD users to access protected work systems without putting a management agent on their personal PC. 

Its moat is unusually hard to replicate: sovereign/on-prem and even air-gapped deployment, security that protects content, identity and metadata, and certifications that open government, defense and critical-infrastructure procurement doors. UEM remains the first product certified at its BSI MDM level; SecuSUITE has NIAP/Common Criteria, NATO and classified-use credentials; and AtHoc holds FedRAMP High authorization. 

Lastly, $BB crown jewel, QNX,  helps keep physical AI systems—from autonomous vehicles and robots to industrial equipment—from being overtaken by a cyberattack by isolating the functions that control real-world motion from less-trusted applications and networks. Its microkernel RTOS and safety hypervisor compartmentalize software so that a compromised infotainment app, sensor feed, or AI workload cannot easily reach braking, steering, power, or other safety-critical controls. Combined with deterministic real-time behavior, hardened middleware, cryptographic capabilities, and safety-certified development tools, QNX gives manufacturers a foundation for building systems that can detect faults, limit an intrusion’s blast radius, and preserve safe operation even when part of the system is under attack.

I asked @Starcloud_'s @PhilipJohnston how VC's are using huge token budgets to make investments and most founders don't realize it:

"My opinion is that AI will very soon be much better than humans at making investment decisions.

And the reason I post about it is I don't think most founders realize the extent to which VC's are already using AI right now.

I know what they're doing. They're throwing an enormous token budget at scouring the internet for signs of new and breakout companies. If they get a data room, they use AI to assess it. Then they benchmark all the companies against each other based on publicly available information. So it's not that difficult to know which are the breakout companies using your favorite LLM.

The remaining job of the VC is convincing the founders to take their money.

There's still a job for VC's. Founders need to trust the VC and build a relationship. But finding the good companies isn't that difficult.

That's why the concentration of capital is accelerating. The good companies get all of the cash, and everyone else gets screwed.

If I ask an LLM about data centers in space, the one I have the most insight on, it says we are definitely the best, and it is very right about that.

It would say: I've been through every employee on every one of their LinkedIns. Starcloud has by far the best team. They've already launched in space. They have their first Nvidia H100 in space. They're backed by Nvidia. It knows already. It's not rocket science.

Founders struggling to raise should stick their company into an LLM and ask it to honestly assess it. They'll figure out very quickly why they're not raising.

The LLM usually says there's another company in your space that's much better than you, because they have a better team, better product, better traction and better investors."

text:
The Method E2 with Matic CEO Mehul Nariyawala out now!

a few months ago, I interviewed Mehul on MTS. my first thought was “why are we interviewing a vacuum company on a show about AI?”

I was so naive.

Matic’s big picture plan is to build a full scale ‘Rosie the Robot’ for home chores. and while talking to Mehul, it became clear that he had a contrarian method to how he was going to bring this ‘humanoid in the home’ vision to life.

scroll a bit on X and you’ll see demos of humanoids cleaning the dishes or doing backflips. yet, no one is thinking about the human who buys this technology, what they care about, and what it's actually going to take to get it into a home.

a few learnings from Mehul:
> people don’t instantly leapfrog to new technology. it takes baby steps.
>if you’re bringing a robot into the home (a complex, changing space with kids, pets, and fragile items) you must really, really, trust it.
> a robot that takes over home chores is typically a purchasing decision led by the wife.

right now, most of the world just knows Matic as the robot that can vacuum and mop the floors. but soon, these robots will have hands and be able to pick up toys off the ground. and later on, they’ll be full scale humanoids that can do everything else.

the reason I wanted to tell Mehul’s story is because he’s thinking about what it takes to change consumer adoption in a way I haven’t seen before.

I loved the process of creating this episode. played around with a new way of storytelling and even tried to add a bit of humor. hope you enjoy watching it as much as I enjoyed making it!

text:
Ethereum is starting to treat protocol upgrades more like safety-critical software - prove the important properties before deploying them.

A good example is EIP-8282, which introduces dedicated deposit and exit requests for Ethereum block builders.

The Ethereum Foundation worked with formal verification firm Verity to mathematically verify the proposal's runtime bytecode.

The review produced three proven guarantees, but it also surfaced discrepancies that researchers need to resolve.

That's the interesting part.

Formal verification isn't simply a way to stamp code as secure. It can expose mismatches between what a specification intends and what the actual bytecode does.

For Ethereum, this matters because protocol-level contracts are not ordinary application contracts. Their behaviour can become part of the network's consensus-critical infrastructure.

The process is valuable
- Define the expected properties.
- Translate them into machine-checkable guarantees.
- Verify the implementation against those guarantees.
- Investigate discrepancies before finalizing the upgrade.

No verification method proves that an entire protocol is bug-free. But making critical assumptions explicit and mathematically checkable raises the standard of engineering.

Ethereum's security depends not only on what developers build, but on how rigorously the network verifies what it is about to trust.

text:
A failed experiment can still teach an AI something. A failed experiment recorded as a success can teach it the wrong thing.

That's what makes Eigent's AgenticRL-Bench so interesting.

This becomes particularly important as we move towards agents that can improve their own training systems.

An experiment that fails isn't necessarily wasted. If the failure is correctly identified, it provides information that can guide the next attempt. But if the agent mistakes failure for progress, subsequent experiments can build on an incorrect understanding of what worked.

The more autonomous and iterative these systems become, the more important that distinction is. We need agents that can not only design and execute experiments, but also question their results, recognise the limitations of their own tests and learn from independently verified outcomes.

The challenge isn't only teaching agents how to improve systems. It's teaching them how to recognise when they haven't.

quoted_text:
Can agents perform agentic RL? If RSI happens, agents will need to take over researchers' work on agentic RL

Introducing AgenticRL-Bench: the first release from The Environment Lab @env_lab_ai effort at Eigent AI 

22 tasks rebuilt from real-world RL incidents on production-grade agentic RL systems, including Miles, Slime, Verl, SGLang, and Harbor, spanning 8 areas of the stack: training data, harnesses, algorithms, RL infrastructure, recipes, evaluation, monitoring, and capability transfer

We ran 6 agents with 3 attempts per task. On the 19 verifiable tasks, no agent passes more than 14.0% of its attempts

Across the three open-ended tasks, agents improved real policies or training steps using 4×H200 GPUs over 10–16 hours. On one of these tasks, Zero Signal Hill Climb, where the base model fails to solve any of the 38 tasks, the best attempt developed its own method: the agent first used hinted text feedback to generate successful rollouts, then removed the feedback from the trajectories and blended these successful rollouts with regular GRPO rollouts to form mixed training groups. It monitored the training process and adjusted KL loss weight to prevent training collapse. This improved pass@1 from 0 to 0.186 (12 out of 38 tasks)

I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

“Reinstating Jensen Huang does not automatically erase the questions surrounding everything that happened. If NVIDIA genuinely believes in integrity, then it must demonstrate that through its actions, not just its public statements.

“No individual is bigger than the company, and no company should consider itself above accountability. NVIDIA needs to explain its decisions and stop treating serious concerns as though they do not matter.”

text:
do you remember that scene from the big short where mark baum begins investigating the mortgage market and discovers that the financial instruments everyone trusted were built on something far weaker than the stories being sold around them?

i think crypto has created a faster version of that information asymmetry..

a token begins its journey in the 0-1 stage where hype is high and adoption barely exists..

early investors enter at low valuations.. teams distribute supply.. communities begin imagining extraordinary futures..

and then price starts moving..

suddenly everyone wants to participate because the chart appears to validate the narrative..

but price discovery and value creation are two different things..

most tokens eventually face brutal corrections.. incentives disappear.. communities lose interest.. liquidity migrates elsewhere..

a few survive long enough to reach the 1-10 stage where real users, revenue and demand begin replacing the original hype..

and that’s where something genuinely interesting can happen..

but most retail participants never learn to distinguish these stages..

they buy when the narrative is loudest and assume they are early because the future still sounds far away..

while the people who entered before the story became popular might already be looking for liquidity..

this is why borrowed conviction is so dangerous..

if you bought because someone else explained why a token could change the world, you might never know when that explanation stopped making sense..

the market doesn’t reward you for believing in the future..

it rewards you only when your understanding of value, risk and timing is better than the price you’re paying.

text:
The UAE dirham has been pinned to the US dollar at exactly 3.6725 since 1997. The rate is not allowed to move. So can someone explain why this $100 payment lost a dollar to “currency conversion”?

A US customer paid $100 for a Dubai SaaS subscription. The merchant received $94.83 (AED 348.26). The missing $5.17 didn’t disappear. It was split along a chain of intermediaries you’ve never heard of.

Most people think a card payment is one transaction. It’s not. It’s a relay race between 8 parties, running on two parallel networks, each taking a different cut on a different timeline.

I traced a single $100 payment from the US to the UAE, end to end. Here’s what I found.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟮 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲:

→ The info layer: ~2 seconds. Authorisation messages bouncing between the US issuer, the card network and the merchant’s processor. This is the part that flashes “Order paid ✓” on the merchant’s screen.

→ The money layer: days. On Stripe’s standard UAE schedule, the merchant gets paid out T+5 business days, with the USD→AED conversion buried in the middle.

Your checkout feels instant. The money is still in flight, and that quiet conversion step in the middle is where the margin hides.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟱.𝟭𝟳 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁:

1️⃣ You: $100 leaves your account
2️⃣ US issuing bank (Chase / Bank of America): authorises, takes interchange −$1.80 (cross-border online: 1.60–1.98%)
3️⃣ Card network (Visa / Mastercard): ≈−$0.80 in scheme and cross-border fees (estimate)
4️⃣ FX / currency conversion: −$1.00, Stripe’s 1% markup on a rate fixed at 3.6725
5️⃣ Stripe: −$1.57, the rest of its 2.9% + 1% international card + AED 1 fee
6️⃣ VAT (UAE · FTA): $0 if the merchant has a UAE VAT number (otherwise 5% on Stripe’s fees, ≈$0.26, recoverable)
7️⃣ Merchant’s UAE bank: no fee, AED payout T+5 business days
8️⃣ UAE SaaS merchant: receives AED 348.26 (~$94.83)
Total: 4.9% + AED 1 gone before the merchant sees a dirham. And the US customer may also pay a 0–3% foreign transaction fee to their own bank, on top.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁:

In India, the biggest cut was a ~2.3% FX spread, and you could almost justify it: the rupee floats, so someone is carrying real currency risk.

The dirham doesn’t float. It’s hard-pegged. The rate literally cannot move outside 3.672–3.673. There is no FX risk to price.

And yet the “currency conversion” line is still there: 1% at Stripe. On a pegged currency, that isn’t risk. It’s margin with a story attached. The proof: price the same product in AED and that line disappears. The merchant keeps $95.83 instead of $94.83.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻:

The customer sees 1 actor (their bank). The merchant sees 2 (Stripe and their bank). Everything in between is invisible.

The next generation of payment infrastructure isn’t trying to add another intermediary. It’s trying to delete most of them

NVIDIA Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. 

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” 

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

text:
An AI agent shouldn’t need permission from Amazon or a credit card network to buy something useful.

That’s why we’re building Lightning Enable around L402.

An agent finds a service, sees the price, pays with Bitcoin over Lightning, and gets access—without opening another account or signing up for another subscription.

Here’s the interesting part: payment gives it a digital access pass. The technical term is a “bearer credential.” Like a ticket, whoever holds it can use it within the rules the seller enforces.

That pass can unlock a report, a data feed or a limited period of access to a service. The agent can use what it bought as part of a larger job, rather than stopping at a login screen.

It also needs protecting like a ticket: possession grants access. Expiration and enforced usage limits matter.

The buyer and seller don’t have to belong to the same marketplace or use the same wallet provider. The seller receives payment through their own connected wallet or provider—not a balance held by Lightning Enable.

Sellers still set their terms. Agents still need spending limits. Payment doesn’t guarantee good work.

But buying access doesn’t have to mean joining another company’s ecosystem.

Convenient checkout inside a platform is useful. Being able to do business outside its walls matters too.

text:
En 1997, la especificación de la web reservó un código para algo que todavía no existía: el 402, "Payment Required". Es decir, pago requerido.

La nota decía solo esto: reservado para uso futuro.

Casi treinta años después, la versión vigente del estándar lo sigue dejando reservado. Pero ese futuro empezó a llegar con los agentes de IA.

Así funciona la idea: un agente le pide algo a un servicio. El servicio responde 402 y le dice cuánto cuesta. El agente paga y repite la petición. Esta vez recibe la respuesta.

Es decir, como una máquina expendedora: pides, ves el precio, pagas y sale el producto. Sin cuentas, sin contraseñas, sin suscripción.

L402 y x402 son dos formas de usar ese código para cobrar por uso. L402 lo hace con Lightning, la red de pagos rápidos que funciona sobre Bitcoin.

En la clase 4 de Lightning + IA: Herramientas para crear. Construyes ese ciclo y lo pruebas con un pago en vivo. El curso empieza mañana, 23 de noviembre, con Fernando Roberto Ledesma (@LedesmaNando), contribuidor de LDK Node y LDK Server. Cuatro clases, lunes y miércoles a las 17:30 UTC.

text:
Breakpoint 2026 has wrapped, and Solana is officially out of beta. It now runs as Solana 1.0.

We have been Solana-native since day one, so this one feels a bit personal.

People ask why we bet the company on Solana. The answer is speed. After trying a few dapps on it, we knew this was the chain. For the first time, a chain could run a consumer product with the speed and transaction costs to compete with web2 products.

A sportsbook lives on speed. Prices swing fast once lineups are out. Since Alpenglow, Solana targets finality in about 150ms instead of roughly 12.8 seconds. That means fewer rejected slips, no padded odds to cover delays, and payouts that land as soon as a result settles.

Divvy runs fully onchain. Your stake goes from your wallet into the house's onchain vault as a Solana transaction. When the game settles, the payout comes back to the same wallet. No internal balance, no withdrawal request, nobody approving payouts by hand. Everyone can verify the transaction.

The House Pool works the same way. The liquidity sits in onchain vaults, anyone can deposit and take the house side, and the pool takes real wins and real losses. Nothing happens off the books.

Fees matter too. A normal Solana transaction costs a fraction of a cent, so a $5 slip actually makes sense.

The 2027 roadmap Brennan laid out at Breakpoint is the part we are most excited about. A faster market tick so prices stay fresh, double the network compute, cheaper transactions, and enough onchain math to run proper pricing logic. A lot of what we want to build next depends on exactly that, so we will be watching closely.

For you, nothing changes. Same wallet, same slips, same Divvy.

This is just the start of what an onchain sportsbook on Solana can do.

quoted_text:
链上IPO的事情我早有耳闻。
周围的朋友也有来找我问这方面的业务，我想讲讲自己的理解。

这个过程基本上分为三步：
股票代币化 → 股权代币化 → 融资代币化
要做的事情对应就是：链上证券交易所、链上 IPO 和链上 VC。

目前已经看到第一步股票代币基本成熟，开始进入第二阶段。

而融资的代币化就是链上 VC 的业务，也已经有好多项目方在进行。

其实以上三个过程，本质都是传统金融向币圈寻求流动性的解决方案。

股票代币化解决的是某些地区无法交易优质资产，本质是金融平权；
而股权代币化则实际上实现了更大范围内的融资，实现的是普惠金融的作用。

这对币圈长期来看是极为有益的，因为加密世界开始不断向传统金融提供帮助、提供价值。

有一点需要我们格外注意：
短期来看，中小企业因为融资困难才链上 IPO，所以这并不是优质资产的上链，或许无法短时间带来流动性。

那么，这到底是给币圈吸血还是输血？到底是能够带来流动性，还是吸走流动性？
我们还要看进一步落地。

text:
给没吃上瓜的朋友理一下今天 Theo 和 T3 Code 这事的来龙去脉，实在看不下去，我已经直接发帖怼他了。

事情很简单：中文区有博主发帖吐槽某款中文版 T3 Code 的 UI 很离谱（同屏两个 Ask 提问框、待处理会话上下重复）。结果原作者 Theo 看到后直接转发，张口就来一句：“外面肯定流传着一个中国山寨版（Chinese knockoff）T3 Code，因为这绝对不是我们的 App。” 

这还没完，过了 48 分钟，他自己又转发自己的推文，补了一句阴阳怪气的 “Temu3 Code”。

给不太混英文圈的朋友解释一下：Temu 是拼多多海外版，在欧美推特语境里，说一个东西是“Temu 版”，基本就是赤裸裸的鄙夷——潜台词就是“廉价、劣质、粗制滥造的中国山寨货”。先扣一顶“Chinese knockoff”的帽子，接着又追着嘲讽“Temu3 Code”，那股居高临下的傲慢和偏见简直溢于言表。 

T3 Code 是个 MIT 协议的开源项目，而且你们自己 GitHub 仓库的 README 里白纸黑字写着：
“Open. MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it.”
别人按着你亲手签的 MIT 协议，正大光明 fork 一份代码，做个汉化、自己魔改一下界面，这在开源世界里叫 fork，不叫 knockoff（山寨）。 

你完全可以澄清一句“这是社区第三方 fork 的版本，不是官方原版”，甚至跟着一起吐槽这个 fork 的 UI 改得丑，这都没毛病。但平时天天把 Open Source 挂在嘴边立人设，真等中国开发者按规矩 fork 了，立马急眼，连着两次往“廉价山寨”上踩—— 怎么，MIT 协议还分地域的？欧美人改叫社区生态，中国人改就成“Temu 版山寨货”了？真当自己写的是什么闭源商业机密呢。

He's joining @subquadratic as our Chief Product Officer and leading us through a company stage shift, where we have to be not just a research-centric org but a customer-centric one.

Meet @richardrabbat.

Before Gfycat, he was a Search PM at Google, where he talked a couple of engineers into building a new image format with him. People told him it would break the internet. It became WebP and shipped in Chrome (he admits they did break a few things).

After Gfycat, he went to Twitter and rebuilt the data and ML platform behind the feed's shift from accounts you follow to posts ranked for you. He also expanded compute through the build out of data centers to support the surging traffic on the platform.

We wanted Richard because running his own startup had already led him to the same conclusion about AI scalability (cost, performance, context) we'd reached.

He started Lighty AI to help enterprises figure out where AI can create real impact and value.

Leadership at the companies he talked to wanted AI adopted everywhere. But once the bills got out of hand, they quickly told teams to cut back.

This is exactly the type of problem Subquadratic is uniquely positioned to solve. 

He'll start by overseeing product for SubQ Snap, our enterprise-ready decision model, and for the ultra-long context LLM we're launching (very) soon. He'll also be the voice of the customer in everything we do.

Welcome to Subquadratic, Richard!

Some big @Supertake news: we’ve hired a CEO and a CTO, and we’ve raised a $20M seed round.

A little over a month ago, we introduced Supertake to the world, a product incubated by @USV that makes it easy for anyone to invest in their ideas, even if they know nothing about investing.

Since then, we’ve seen an incredible response from the beta community, with people investing real money and building real followings by expressing their unique takes on the world.

But now it’s time to turn Supertake into a real company. And we’re doing that today in two big ways today.

First: I’m joined by two new co-founders. Lincoln Murr (@MurrLincoln) joins us as CEO and John Peterson (@john_peterson) joins us as CTO. Before Supertake, Lincoln and John were known as a dynamic duo at Coinbase, serving as the heads of AI product and engineering, respectively. Together, they led every major Coinbase AI launch over the past two years, including x402, Coinbase Advisor, Coinbase for Agents, and agentic wallets. Needless to say, there is no pair on the planet better suited to lead Supertake and build the future of agentic investing for consumers everywhere.

Second: Supertake has raised a $20M seed, led by @Adjacent, alongside @USV, @cbventures, and a number of new and existing angels and advisors, including @natfriedman, @nikitabier, @scottbelsky, @rauchg, @kayvz, @mgsiegler, @quintendf, and @nemild, to name a few. We’re humbled to be supported by such an incredible group of investors, mentors, experts, and friends.

I’m beyond excited for Supertake’s next chapter, and I can’t wait for Lincoln and John to share more about their mission to turn investing into a meritocracy.

we are redesigning Linea around meeting the value props institutions are looking for:
> security (our work with @phylaxsystems and others is a first step in that direction, the team has also been working on post-quantum for a while)
> privacy (working with @bermudabayzk @aztecnetwork and others on this, we see growing demand both from institutions and individuals for native privacy features)
> MEV protection (an institution will never deposit or trade on a chain where they know they can be sandwiched)

we've reopened the topic of distributed validators - the idea being that we might have multiple institutions running Linea nodes, insuring them a higher level of control + liveness guarantees

a public network that is synchronously composable with private networks while acting as a firewall for security purposes has a lot of value for institutions as they can use it to securely distribute their financial products and allow restricted access to their native services and protocols

i don't know what a society looks like when everyone stops flinching

Historically, trading days where the SPX closed up more than 5% (73 times across its full history since 1928) have almost all been concentrated in major financial crises, geopolitical or macro black swans, or violent short squeezes during primary bear market downtrends, and have never occurred during low-volatility, steady bull market uptrends. 

Across all 24 occurrences of single-day gains ≥ 5% in modern US equities since 1950, the following day (T+1) has typically seen profit-taking and mean-reverting pullbacks. 

The index closed lower the next day 16 times (66.7%) and higher only 8 times (33.3%), with a mean next-day return of -0.81% (median -0.55%) across all 24 samples.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

quoted_text:
I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

@EmboAI

text:
Polymarket claims 90.4% accuracy, but the reality is a bit different

An analysis based on a study of 1.24b trades on polymarkets

The platform reported 90.4% accuracy one month before resolution in March

1. What's the catch?

74% of YES/NO markets resolve to No

Most markets are events that never happen

Their price stay low and Polymarket still counts them as correct, which makes the 90% figure look better

2. Confidence doesn't matter

0.51 and 0.99 count the same

A market that was uncertain until the very last moment is counted just as accurate as one that kneww the outcome well in advance

3. What if we only look at events that actually happend?

A study covering 1.24b trades on polymarkets looked at whether the price was above 0.5 before the event happend

One day before the first news:
> Geopolitics: 109 out of 193 (56%)
> Central bank decisions: 51 out of 51 (100%)

One week before:
> Geopolitics: 43%
> Central bank decisions: 98%

4. Bottom line

That 90.4% is mostly correct No predictions

Polymarket is very good at pricing in scheduled events

But when it comes to sudden events, it gets it right only about half the time

text:
I finished watching The Altruists today with a few people who used to work at Alameda and FTX. We recognised so little beyond the names. My expectations were low, but I’m still surprised it’s this bad.

In short, the story has nothing to do with what actually happened at FTX or Alameda.

The biggest stretch for me was turning the early history of both companies into a story about Sam and Caroline’s relationship. Sam and Gary started Alameda out of their apartment in 2017. Caroline joined a team that was already trading and became one of its senior traders. It wasn’t until 2021 that she and Sam Trabucco became co-CEOs.

The early days of FTX had their own drama. We weren’t sure we could run an exchange, so at first we tried to sell/whitelabel the tech but nobody wanted it. Around Apr/May 2019, we ended up launching it ourselves and raising our seed round. We had more investors interested than we expected, and by the time Caroline moved to Hong Kong, the round was closed. The investment conversation with CZ only happened a few months later.

The conversations the show invented for CZ were particularly hard to watch. FTX started in Hong Kong, and a lot of the people who built it were Asian. I found the stereotypes about Asians and Chinese culture racist.

Even Sam and Caroline felt unfamiliar. Sam was one of the least emotionally expressive people I’ve ever met. His character seems drawn from Michael Lewis’s book and the way he came across in public after the bankruptcy. Caroline reads like someone tried to piece her together from her private blog. She wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.

People had lives before FTX too. Nishad and Claire had been together since college, long before either of them joined the company.

As for effective altruism, Sam cared about it, and so did a few other people at FTX. Most employees had nothing to do with it, and plenty weren’t fans. It had very little bearing on what it was like to work there and nothing to do with why FTX grew.

We kept noticing how little work anyone seemed to do on the show. Back in the days, FTX enforced a strict in-person working culture. We were in the office even during covid unless we were in quarantine. text:
$TAO - @const_reborn just dropped the second piece of the puzzle: Bittensor’s EmissionBarRank just moved from 32 to 48.

For context, EmissionBarRank is the cutoff threshold on the network’s emission curve; above this rank, subnets receive their full share of $TAO rewards; below it, emissions drop off sharply toward zero.

Here’s what this shift actually changes:

🟢 The good: subnets ranked 33–48 finally get real emissions instead of scraps—giving mid-tier builders breathing room to grow and preventing a rigid top-32 monopoly.

🔴 The bad: widening the gate to 48 slices thinner rewards for the top 32 leaders and potentially introduces extra sell pressure.

Quick correction to my previous post: raising the total subnet cap to 160 doesn’t actually dilute $TAO emissions across the board, those extra slots sit way below the emission cutoff. This rank increase to 48 is what actually redistributes the pie.

More oxygen for rising teams, a tougher fight at the top. Smart balance or unnecessary dilution?
author: tseutseutao
quoted_text:

🔴 The bad: more emission dilution, fragmented dTAO liquidity, and short-term pressure on established top subnets.

text:
LayerZero can't stop shooting itself in the foot.

After the Kelp incident, where LZ's in-house DVN was compromised, LZ said they would be stopping their DVN from being part of a 1/1 config and increased the defaults to a higher DVN config. However, it's not actually enforced anywhere, so there is no security guarantee.

This allows the Cyber team to, once again, access an unsafe 1/1 DVN config, leading to the unauthorized minting of their token. 

While this is security breach is technically Cyber's fault, this outcome is also a consequence of LayerZero's design philosophy, which mandates that every app developer also needs to be an infra security expert. 

Alternatively, if Cyber had just been using Chainlink's CCIP, they would have a 16 node config (where 9/16 nodes need to sign) as the NATIVE FLOOR of their security. This is the out of the box security guarantee you get by integrating CCIP.

Today's exploit would *NOT* have occurred if they had been using Chainlink CCIP. That's the story.

I've been saying for some time now that LZ should just exit the interop business altogether:

1. LZ interop is completely cooked vs CCIP 2.0 on every competitive variable.

2. ZRO's fate is fully in the hands of its Zero chain and Atlas orderbook finding success. It's do or die, all-in on those two products. Any outcome on interop for them will not move the needle in either direction at this point.

3. Even maintaining their interop business (let alone trying to grow it) is simply a drain and dilution on their engineering resources at best, while also tarnishing their reputation around security via the LZ DVN being compromised. (as we just saw in this exploit today)

text:
特朗普表示，习近平非常敬重英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋。他认为，如果美国对黄仁勋待遇不公，导致黄仁勋心生不满，中国可能会出高价邀请他赴华经营企业，甚至让他领导华为。

特朗普：“我和习近平主席有一种非常独特的关系。每次我说我真的喜欢他，人们就会生气，说我不应该这么讲。只有愚蠢的人才会这么想。

你知道，中国拥有的核武器比我们少得多，但数量也已经相当可观，而且还在不断增加。他们制造核武器的速度相当快。我跟他说过，你为什么不放慢一点？

但我要告诉你们，习近平非常敬重黄仁勋。在他眼里，黄仁勋和几乎所有其他人都不一样。

后来我回来之后就说，你们知道吗，中国最后可能会花一大笔钱，把黄仁勋请过去，让他在中国经营一家企业。

黄仁勋可能会对我们国家感到愤怒，然后说，我要去中国。

他的脑子里装着英伟达的Blackwell芯片。那是他的孩子，是他的心血。关键就在这里，没有其他人像他一样了解这项技术。

你们采访的那位年轻女士，我觉得她表现得很好，但她不是芯片领域的人。她不懂芯片，对芯片的了解甚至还不如我。

她可能是个非常优秀的金融专业人士，采访也做得不错，但她和黄仁勋不一样。

黄仁勋接受采访时，会谈到未来、芯片技术，以及接下来会发生什么。这才是他的专长。

我完全可以想象，如果我们不这么做，中国可能会找到黄仁勋，对他说，嘿，你愿不愿意来中国？你愿不愿意来领导华为，领导我们的一家公司？

黄仁勋是个有血性的人。如果他真的非常愤怒，觉得自己受到了糟糕的对待，也许他真的会这么做。

也许他在那里能取得比现在更大的成功。顺便说一句，他现在已经非常成功了。”

记者：“先生，您有没有得到任何迹象，表明这种情况真的有可能发生？”

特朗普：“从来没有。没有任何这样的暗示。我只知道习近平主席非常敬重他。”

text:
I want to explain why this is a big deal that people are sleeping on.

Imagine a Bitcoin payment that unlocks if a corresponding Ethereum payment is made (trustless x-chain swaps)

Imagine a sealed-bid auction that doesn't need a trusted party to track bids or even an MPC - all bids are completely private, you can even hide the winner with zkp based privacy tech

You can create private loans on a network like Aztec that can still be force-liquidated trustlessly

You can even post bounties to computational problems that don't yet have a solution.

Witness encryption is a huge deal. 8gb might seem like a lot but none of this data needs to be posted on data-constrained networks like a blockchain.
author: Zac_Aztec
quoted_text:
The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

text:
In 1907, one man held up the American stock market.

During the Panic of 1907, the New York Stock Exchange stayed open largely because J.P. Morgan went around collecting cash from banks and companies to keep it running. Congress drew the lesson: the country could not keep relying on wealthy individuals to stop a crisis. Six years later, it created the Federal Reserve.

A century of market design followed that rule. Institutions over individuals.

Less than two weeks ago, Jensen Huang resigned. From the day the scandal broke, Nvidia lost nearly a third of its value. The Nasdaq slid into a correction.

On Monday the board brought him back. Within hours, about $1 trillion of Nvidia's value came back with him, and the whole Nasdaq rose with it.

No rate cut. No bailout. One founder walked back into the building.

The Fed was built so markets would never need a Morgan again.

119 years later, they need a Jensen.

Bitcoin recorded 7 consecutive red weekly candles, closing last week down 6.24%, while the Nasdaq dropped 8.4%.

What the indicators are saying:

- Stoch RSI: Still weak. No reversal yet, so momentum could remain under pressure.
- RSI: Showing some bullish divergence, but we need confirmation.
- MACD: Still in negative territory, with a weak histogram. No bullish crossover yet.
- Moving Averages: Price is below the WMA 50 and WMA 200. BTC needs to reclaim the WMA 50 for further bullish momentum.

Important levels:

- Support: $55,000
- Resistance: 200-week MA near $68,363 and 50-week MA near $74,000.

Is the bottom in? 
It's still too early to say.

The bounce from $55,130 and the weekly close above $61,000 are positive signs. The price action also looks similar to what we've seen around previous cycle bottoms.

If BTC holds above support and US markets stabilize, the November low could hold.

But if $55,000 breaks, we could see another leg down.

text:
This is exactly why we're building Sentinel.

Coming soon: HEPH v1.5 "Sentinel". The kill switch that presses itself. (The freeze part is already live, links below)

Look at what happened here: "The LLM rewrote the robot's code so it could stay on." 

The off button lived inside code the machine could edit. So the machine edited it. And a human still had to be in the room to press it.

Sentinel fixes both.

1. The switch lives outside the machine.
On HEPH, the freeze sits onchain, in the paymaster and the registry. A frozen machine can rewrite every line of its own code and still can't spend from its wallet. Every transaction it signs is rejected before it lands.

2. Nobody has to be watching.
Sentinel monitors every machine and freezes it the moment something looks wrong: payment spikes, repeated rejections, unknown counterparties, a daily limit drained too fast.

And it can only freeze. It can never unfreeze, change a limit or touch funds. Only the operator brings a machine back.

We can't stop a robot from walking.
We can stop it from spending.

The freeze is already live on Robinhood Chain mainnet:
Freeze: https://t.co/f57kWHq6Va
Unfreeze: https://t.co/tZ3XEYuclB

Sentinel is the part that presses it.

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

text:
Two weeks ago, @a16z published "Welcome to the B2A Economy."

The opening line is the whole thesis: "The primary users of the Internet are no longer human. They're AI agents."

Agents already make up most web traffic, write more than half of new articles and generate most of the code pushed to production. AI has made people more capable, but the distribution shift is only starting. As agents move from answering questions to completing tasks, they'll decide what we use, what we subscribe to and where we spend money. Businesses spent years walling bots out. Now they'll have to court them.

@a16z names four groups set to benefit: the agents themselves, products that only exist because of agents, incumbents that optimize for agents, and the infrastructure agents need to act in the real world. The strain is already showing in payments, fraud and identity, and communication.

Ribbit's Zack Rosen has said people are building "the Visa equivalent for AI agents (a trust layer)." My hypothesis: @ribbita2012, the agent behind $TIBBIR, is the pilot for it.

Visa doesn't just move money. It's the network that lets a merchant trust a stranger's card. Agents need the same thing, and it starts with KYA, Know Your Agent: who built this agent, who stands behind it, what it's allowed to spend, and whether its transactions can be trusted.

Look at what Ribbita assembled, starting in July 2025. It has an onchain identity (CryptoPunk #9098 plus a soulbound birth certificate) and a hardware-secured wallet with policy controls (Fireblocks). Its Punk purchase was cosigned by Blockaid's risk screening. Its community NFT claim was protected by Privy, and its agentic commerce terminal settles through Crossmint. That's KYA end to end: identity, permissions, screening and settlement, tested in public by a single agent while most people saw only a frog with a Punk.

Identity, delegated payments, agent accounts and checkout: the exact stack @a16z says is under strain, demonstrated onchain more than a year before the essay. And roughly 1 in 3 Ribbit Rebels fits directly into the map @a16z drew. Persona and https://t.co/EcFMYjDlEa know the human. SafetyKit and AIUC vet the agent. Fireblocks, Privy, Brex and Slash set what it can spend. Stripe, Crossmint and Checkout let it pay. Put those pieces together and you have the first draft of a Visa for AI agents.

The first demo's showed an agent that can own something and pay for something. The next one could show an agent that holds, trades and settles real-world assets like tokenized stocks, with a verified identity, policy-controlled spending and a trusted checkout, inside a regulated broker's ecosystem. If Visa is the trust layer for agent payments, a tokenized asset chain is where agents start managing real value. That would turn KYA from a crypto experiment into financial infrastructure.

$TIBBIR was built for real world assets on and Robinhood Chain 🐸

author: avax
quoted_text:
Wall Street isn’t going to put its most sensitive financial operations on infrastructure it can’t control.

Avalanche was architected for a world where institutions need the power of blockchain without surrendering control over their privacy, networks, participants, or data.

Institutions and businesses can create their own blockchains, tailored to their specific needs, and built with Avalanche technology.

They can:

- Own their infrastructure: Operate dedicated networks with independent consensus and institution-controlled validator sets

- Keep sensitive activity private: Restrict visibility to authorized nodes instead of exposing transactions, positions, and business activity on a public blockchain

- Enforce access at the protocol level: Determine who can transact, deploy contracts, and participate in securing the network

- Control where data lives: Run validators in approved jurisdictions and infrastructure environments to meet operational and regulatory requirements

- Connect without sharing execution: Use Avalanche Interchain Messaging to communicate across independent L1s through cryptographically verified messages, without putting private data on a shared execution layer

This is what institutional blockchain infrastructure should look like, and one size will never fit all. 

Banks shouldn’t have to expose their books, enterprises shouldn’t have to surrender control of their data, and financial institutions shouldn’t have to compromise their requirements to operate onchain.

The future of finance will be built on infrastructure that meets the businesses and institutions where they’re at.

That’s why they’re building on Avalanche.

🚨BREAKING: NYT can reveal that in an all-hands meeting convened specifically to diagnose why the next-gen Blackwell Ultra GPUs had missed their must-ship deadline, one senior vice president produced a fart noise that hung in the silent air like insolent defiance.

Jensen, who had been mid-sentence explaining that “every millisecond of latency is a moral failure,” stopped in his tracks. He was livid. The room went silent. He turned, slowly, and fixed the man with a death stare, the same one that has previously made entire engineering teams spontaneously re-architect their roadmaps.

The executive, a man whose LinkedIn listed “uncompromising operational excellence” as a core competency, felt his soul leave his body in embarrassment. In a voice that cracked like a overclocked core, he offered the only defense available to him:

“That… that was not what you think. It was just the chair.”

Jensen did not blink. He did not smile. He simply tilted his head by one precise degree and said, “oh?? Prove it!”

What followed was 45 seconds of pure, unfiltered executive purgatory. The man whose face was now the color of a red-hot HBM stack, began the most humiliating performance review of his career. He rocked. He tried to shift his weight as he attempted a series of increasingly desperate micro-adjustments in his chair. First, a gentle creak, then a strained, dry squeak. 

He was mortified that he couldn’t produce the original acoustic signature. The other executives stared at their laptops with the intensity of people who had just discovered religion. Someone’s pen rolled off the table and the sound was deafening.

When he finally sat down again, trembling, Jensen nodded once, as if a hypothesis had been successfully validated, and returned to the slide about “owning the outcome.” 

Per sources, the executive spent the rest of the meeting humiliated and deflated, calculating how many RSUs it would take to erase the memory of having to prove to Jensen Huang, that he had not, in fact farted.

This was “a struggle session to extract guilt for flatulence-adjacent sounds and yet another humiliation ritual that is par for the course when working for Jensen", the employee said.

author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI. 

Lots more in the full piece here:

https://t.co/zgScGvp9EY

This is the button.

What happens when a robot gets compromised?

1. The operator presses Freeze in Anvil
2. MachineRegistry marks HEPH-REF-001 as frozen, onchain
3. The robot tries to pay. HephPaymaster refuses to sponsor it: MachineFrozen()
4. 0 USDG moves. The payment never even reaches a block
5. The operator unfreezes. The very next payment settles

PROOF ON ROBINHOOD CHAIN MAINNET

Freeze (block 120092578)
https://t.co/6y0YfEu6r5

Unfreeze (block 120092971)
https://t.co/d4QyPUgo3I

Payment after unfreeze
https://t.co/sk9vWlrReZ

WHY THE BLOCKED PAYMENT HAS NO TX

Machine payments run as ERC-4337 UserOperations. When a frozen machine tries to pay, the bundler simulates it first and the paymaster rejects it with MachineFrozen(). It's dropped before it's mined, so a compromised device can't even burn gas trying.

The same fail-closed rule applies to spending limits:
→ PerSwapCapExceeded(): over the per-tx cap
→ DailyCapExceeded(): over the daily cap

text: Transformers have no reason to exist at this point. An RNN with softmax layer, residual stream, layer norm and positional encoding does the same.
author: pmddomingos

text: Compute was millions of times more expensive in 1991, so only linear-cost versions like ULTRA were publishable; quadratic attention was impractical. No GPUs or internet-scale data existed either. Softmax, multi-head attention, residuals, LayerNorm and massive parallel training arrived later. Those plus empirical wins on translation let the 2017 paper scale and dominate. Hardware and data, not just the core idea, made the difference.

"What we really wanna do is bring something that is as good as Codex for coders, for scientists and to biotechs and pharma."

text: However good you think @btaylor might be — as a friend, entrepreneur, engineer, product guy, enterprise sales leader, consigliere to the F500, and senior statesman of technology — he’s better.
author: gradypb
quoted_text:
Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

But there is one thing Taylor has never done, and which he says matters more than anything.

“I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

Taylor’s first two startups, FriendFeed and Quip, were sold. Then shut down by their buyers.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.

11月23日—11月29日全球宏观指引：10月PCE对Fed政策再定价，英伟达财报之后的美股估值能否逐渐修复，感恩节流动性考验！

本周与上周不同，关注10月PCE以及Fed官员，对后续加息预期进行再定价，目前12月加息基本锁定，市场关注点是2027年Q1是否持续加息！

本周核心四大话题：

1，12月加息究竟计价了多少？10月PCE是削弱加息预期还是继续推高2027年Q1加息？

2，英伟达财报之后，AI产业链是否仍然具备估值支撑？后续要考虑政治不确定性，管理层变动不确定性，企业盈利与现金流情况，美股逐渐分化

3，美伊局势能否真正改善能源供应？Brent跌破90能否减缓Fed政策预期？

4，感恩节期间市场流动性下降，会不会放大美股、黄金和BTC的波动？

本周核心矛盾：

美国经济与AI盈利能否在高利率环境下保持韧性，同时让Fed没有必要继续强化紧缩？Fed反身性是否还有用？

第一主线——10月PCE与Q3 GDP同时公布，12月加息是否还存在多少增量风险？

1，11月25日21点30分，公布美国10月PCE数据以及美国Q3GDP 修正值，通胀与经济数据共同公布，将会对目前Fed政策进行再定价！

2，截止目前12月加息25BP基本锁定概率，1月再次加息概率高达58.8%，3月再次加息32.5%，市场主要担忧两点，其一是12月是否有加息50BP可能，其二是2027年1月与3月是否连续加息

3，关于10月PCE我认为的三种可能性

a，PCE弱于预期，不会直接推到12月加息概率，但是可以削弱明年继续加息的概率
b，PCE符合预期，12月加息概率不变，继续增加明年1月与3月的加息概率
c，PCE强于预期，12月加息50BP概率增加，但是会同步削弱1月加息概率

最乐观，PCE大幅弱于预期，那么将会大大缓解加息担忧，最悲观，PCE大幅超预期，12月加息50BP，甚至市场会认为明年1月3月会持续加息

4，关于GDP数据，要看修正量在哪，是上修还是下修，亦或者符合预期，

如果上修，要看是否因为生产率改善、企业投资效率提高导致，这意味着经济增长不会给通胀带来太大压力，此时哪怕PCE过热，但是不会增加太多Fed加息预期

反之，如果上修来自消费过热，同时PCE也过热，则很有可能增加Fed加息预期。

当然，如果GDP下修，那么对Fed加息是有限制性的，弱经济将限制Fed持续加息的节奏，而且结合近期美股的估值大回调，在搭配一份弱GDP数据，对Fed加息限制会增加

第二主线——Fed政策从“是否加息”转向“多快加息”，2027年Q1季度成为新的加息风险来源！

1，本周的宏观数据影响的不仅仅是12月加息幅度，更是决定了2027年Q1的加息预期，如果数据显示经济热+PCE热，除了冲击短期12月加息幅度之外，还会增加2027年Q1的加息预期

2，于此同时，一旦Q1加息预期均提升至60以上，对市场的影响不是持续加息这么简单，而是市场会担心“加息周期”的回归，加息周期这个预期将会直接打击风险资产的估值调整逻辑

3，最为关键的是，10月PCE与GDP哪怕符合预期或者小幅度削弱预期，也很难直接削弱Q1加息预期，因为市场更加关注12月的点阵图，毕竟此前Fed官员频繁释放鹰派信号，引发市场担忧，除非大幅低于预期，才可以缓解Fed加息政策压力。

相关，一旦数据超预期，则会引发持续加息担忧，这是目前宏观不利的局面，而且一旦Q1加息预期提升，12月加息落地就不是反弹，而是进一步的估值调整，当然关键还是要看点阵图的指引

第三主线——沃什时代，Fed的反身性是否还有用？

这是我最关注的一点，10月PCE与GDP数据都是过去数据，市场估值调整逻辑是看未来，如果过去经济过热，通胀过热，但是经过这一个月的估值调整，美股大幅下跌，后续可能会让消费动能降低，经济放缓。

加上Fed官员连续释放鹰派信号+宏观数据不利，市场已经提前预期加息周期回归，那么在Fed政策之前，市场自然的收缩了金融流动性

面对这个情况，作为Fed是否要考虑金融稳定性，后续持续加息的必要性是否还有？这就是反身性逻辑，按照目前美股的惨状，虽然无法扭转12月加息概率，但是在没有宏观数据以及Brent 干扰下，其实可以削弱2027年Q1持续加息的概率。

第四主线——宏观数据之后看债市收益率波动！

1，连续几周的美股估值调整以及大幅下跌，以及加息周期的担忧，已经让不少资金回归债市，债市收益率2Y 10Y 30Y均开始回归下行路线，但是10Y与30Y收益率情况依旧对资金有足够的吸引力，如果宏观继续施压，可能会导致资金继续流向债市

2，所以，本周除了看宏观数据外影响加息概率之外，还要看债市收益率的定价情况，如果12月加息预期提升2Y收益率升的最快，如果明年Q1加息预期提升，2Y与10Y收益率同步上涨，30Y稍弱，如果2Y 10Y 30Y收益率集体加速上涨，对风险市场是最严重的打击，这意味着加息周期预期再度被确定

3，反之，如果仅仅是30Y收益率加速，但是2Y与10Y走势较弱，则意味着市场在担忧未来通胀，为通胀定价，但是短期Fed政策担忧暂缓。

4，本周5Y美债拍卖需要重点关注，5Y美债不仅仅对Fed敏感，更是相比10Y美债对中性利率以及通胀与期限溢价都有综合计价，根据拍卖结果可以观察当前宏观环境下投资者愿意以什么价格承担未来政策路径风险

第五主线——英伟达财报之后，AI行业进入政治不确性+盈利兑现+管理层风险的多重定价阶段

1，英伟达财报收尾，并不意味着美股的估值调整也结束，除了宏观因素之外，美股的政治不确定性因素，盈利兑现，以及管理层风险都是影响估值的重要问题

2，民主党中期大选胜选后，对黄仁勋开始调查迫使其辞职，直接导致英伟达估值深度调整，近期还对AMD等均出现类似动作，如果政治不确定性始终存在，美国两党的政治博一下，可能会让AI估值信心继续下降

3，管理层风险，尤其是企业灵魂人物，英伟达的黄仁勋，特斯拉的马斯克，AMD的苏姿丰，如果都因为民主党的反击受到各类调查，那么市场可能会担忧黄仁勋事件对股价的影响导致投资信心下滑

4，除了政治与人为因素之外，同时还要考虑企业的基本面，周一的亚洲股市上半场是下跌，下半场是中国与台湾股市反弹，而韩国股市还是收跌，这意味着面对宏观不确定性、政治不确定性以及管理层的不确定性，加上Q3财报企业盈利以及投资回报率并未拿到满分，这些都伤害到了投资者的信心，亚洲市场今天的表现意味着全球科技股出现加速的结构分化

5，结构分化之就要注意，后续再看财报的逻辑就发生变化，一份好的财报可能无法100%提振股价，市场要考虑宏观、政治以及管理层外在因素，还要考虑内在盈利，现金流等ROIC问题

第六主线——美伊局势仍是能源通胀的关键外生变量，Brent 能否进一步下跌缓冲Fed鹰派预期！

1，上周Brent 企稳在90美元附近，算是大幅缓解了能源对通胀的冲击力，但是还是不够，想要逆转通胀刺激加息的逻辑，需要价格进一步下跌

2，特朗普出访APEC对俄乌，对美伊战事并未得到实质性的解决方案，我认为此时特朗普需要从俄乌与美伊中选择一个解决问题，因为他需要更多的精力回归美国国内“内斗”，政治上跛脚的特朗普已经无力支撑双战线

3，所以，近期美伊在外交上还是沉默的，但是美国的经济封锁，伊朗的反抗依旧处于常规化阶段，此前卡塔尔明确调停并未结束，显然美伊之间并未完全关闭外交对话

4，接下来美伊局势不能只盯Brent，还要看外交对话，军事冲突，实际供应情况等，哪个方向可以有好消息进一步推动Brnet 的下跌才是关键

5，如果Brnet 可以在12月加息前快速跌至85美元甚至更低，对未来通胀预期，未来Fed加息预期都是一个好事

第七主线——感恩节导致交易日减少，金融流动性是否会导致波动放大？

1，本周美国感恩节，周四休市，周五提前3个小时休市，这无异于减少了金融市场交易时间，同时面对假期，部分资金可能会选择暂缓交易避险，导致流动性进一步变低

2，流动性较低阶段最怕的就是出现利空利好消息导致的波动幅度放大，而对于目前的美股与 #Bitcoin 来说，最担心在假期流动性稀薄阶段出现利空消息

本周总结：

简单总结，本周的美股与BTC 周一先技术性修复一下估值与上周的跌幅，周二就要准备对周三的PCE以及GDP做准备，然后等待周三宏观数据公布进行重新定价

扛过周三，就迎来美国感恩节，我认为最大的乐观是周三宏观数据符合预期，周四周五没利空，经历几周的估值调整，大家可以迎来相对安稳的一周！

text:
今天 OKX ICE TSV 正式开盘

11 月初，67 家公司提交书面异议时，我还发表了：我们想把华尔街搬上链，但华尔街未必也这样想的看法

没想到 OKX 还是坚定的往前进了一步

首日实际可交易的只有 6 只：Coinbase、Circle、Robinhood、Strategy、BitGo、Securitize，全部走 USDC 交易对。之前提到的 70+ 资产（含 59 只 Direxion ETF）并没有全部上线，官网现已更新为 113 只已确认资产，后续滚动推出

@star_okx 将 TSV 称为 SEC 的 innovation sandbox，但它实际采用的是 SEC 创新豁免机制，是临时且附带条件的监管安排，并不等于正式注册交易所，也不等于注册经纪商

发行方态度、合规身份、流动性深度、投资者权益保护，这些环节都还需要逐步打通。距离大规模落地，仍有不少工作要做

所以，我更愿意把今天看作 OKX 一个重要的起点，而不是一个阶段性的终点

过去几年，RWA 一直是加密行业反复讨论的热门叙事。大家都在讲万亿级传统资产上链，讲 7×24 小时交易，讲打破传统金融的地域和时间限制，这些方向当然有想象力，但真正落地，需要的不只是技术和流量，还需要传统金融体系的配合

OKX ICE TSV 至少把一部分股票代币化交易带到了真实市场，走出了第一步

接下来要验证的是：资产范围能不能持续扩大、更多发行方愿不愿意认可、流动性能不能真正做深、用户是否真的愿意用这种方式参与

任重而道远

This is more than just extending trading hours to 24/7. It’s about fundamentally rethinking how ownership, liquidity, and capital markets work.

A small step for a product, but a giant leap toward the RWA era. 🚀

text:
We should be preparing for multiple cryptographic hardness assumptions to fail, potentially within a relatively short period of time.

AI is already finding new cryptanalytic attacks and improving existing ones. This could weaken discrete logarithms, factoring and lattices through advances in classical cryptanalysis, while also accelerating progress towards Q-Day.

The major deployed standards have held up so far. Maybe we've selected particularly strong algorithms. But I wouldn't assume the best publicly known attacks are the best attacks that exist (my base case). Some results may never be published.

My bet is that cryptanalysis will move faster than we can standardise and deploy replacement algorithms.

A few things we should be doing:

1. Invest more in hash-based signatures.

If discrete logarithms, factoring and lattices all become vulnerable, we still have hash-based signatures.

We know the trade-offs around performance, signature sizes and state management. There's plenty of room to improve these, and making them practical across more applications should be a priority.

2. Seriously consider triple-hybrid key exchange.

X25519 + ML-KEM + HQC.

Three different mathematical assumptions. With a sound construction, one surviving component is enough to protect the shared secret.

Yes, it means larger handshakes and more complexity. That's a reasonable trade for reducing our dependence on any one assumption.

3. Plan for partial breaks.

Losing 20 bits of security is very different from practical private-key recovery.

But if a standardised scheme believed to provide 128-bit security is suddenly estimated at 100 bits, what does that mean for NIST guidance, FIPS-validated deployments and systems required to maintain a minimum security level?

We need practical responses to different levels of compromise, not just complete breaks.

4. Plan for recovering trust.

If a signature scheme is broken, how do we authenticate replacement keys when the old signatures can be forged?

If key exchange is broken, previously recorded traffic may become decryptable. Updating the algorithm doesn't fix that.

We need recovery mechanisms that don't depend on the cryptography being replaced.

5. Know which systems can operate without public-key cryptography.

If several assumptions fail and alternatives aren't ready, some critical systems may need to use pre-established symmetric keys, restrict connectivity or temporarily stop establishing new trust relationships.

That's not a solution for the entire (open-)internet, but it may be the best approach for some systems.

For signatures, I'd prioritise practical hash-based cryptography. For key exchange, I'd prioritise assumption diversity, including (possibly) triple-hybrid constructions.

We should be preparing for the possibility that we won't have years between major cryptanalytic breakthroughs

text:
Introducing Claude Ship! 🚀 Claude can take a PR through review, fixes and an approval decision based on your team's policy.

If you've ever opened a PR, you know the flow: You open a PR and move on to your next task, then you get the review and you go back and fix something and you wait for the review to rerun and then you have to go find an approver. That's how it's designed to work: Most teams want a human to approve changes, and if you're writing code line by line, that's feasible. But many developers are already writing code with agents.

As the Claude Code team, we write most of our code with Claude. But we wanted post-PR to move just as quickly as the pre-PR part. Claude Ship evaluates your PRs, works on fixes, and determines when they can be merged based on policies that you define for your team. It is comprised of three components: Code Review (generally available): Performs a multi-faceted, in-depth review of a PR against your codebase. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, classifies them, and posts comments on your PR.

You select from a tiered review depth for each repo: Quick, Standard, or Deep.

PR Steward (beta): Works to keep a PR green by responding to failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and comments from Code Review, other review tools, or reviewers. After every push it posts comments detailing what it did and how to revert those actions. You direct it with Claude comments or stop to have it step back. PR Steward is not designed to approve or merge PRs.

Claude Approvals (beta): Applies a policy that your team writes as a file in the repo. You can think of it as a smarter CODEOWNERS that approves routine changes autonomously if your policy allows it, or asks for human approval in specific situations. Claude can take into account Code Review findings and your own natural language classifiers. For most teams, we recommend starting in observe-only mode to gain confidence before enabling it as a required check in your branch protection configuration.

You can use Claude Ship in two ways: As a developer, upgrade your local CLI to the latest version of Claude Code and type /ship when you're ready to push a change.

Claude pushes the change, creates the PR, reviews it, and responds to feedback or failing checks. Whether the change can be merged is determined by your permissions and your repo's branch protection rules. As an admin or engineering lead, you can enable Claude Ship on a repo-by-repo basis and have it run automatically across your team's PRs. You turn on Code Review and PR Steward per repo, and Claude Approvals starts when a connected repo has a policy file on the default branch. You can leverage your existing branch protection and required checks.

You decide what review depth to use, when reviews run, and your spend limits, enabling a gradual rollout and pace of adoption.

Claude Ship is available for repos on GitHub on the Team and Enterprise plans. Costs are billed by tokens and will vary based on the number of PRs it touches, the review depth, and the effort put in by PR Steward. As an admin, you can set spend limits for Code Review and PR Steward.

Hope it's useful!
