text:
I'm a director of risk adjustment at one of the largest Medicare Advantage insurers in America. I have some insider information regarding last week's stock crash. It happened because the government announced it might compare our patients to their charts.

I find the whole affair rather vulgar.

Allow me to explain my art. About 35.2 million Americans, or 55% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries, now choose Medicare Advantage, according to KFF. The government pays private insurers like mine to care for them. It pays more for sicker patients.

Note the precise wording. The government doesn't pay for how sick you are. It pays for how sick your chart says you are. Between those two numbers lies a quiet, fertile valley. I've spent my career cultivating it.

Physicians write notes. I curate them. A doctor sees a cough. I see a portfolio. Every diagnosis raises a patient's "risk score," and every point of risk score raises our payment. I don't cure diseases. Curing is for clinicians, bless them. I discover diseases, the way a sommelier discovers notes of blackberry in a glass that tastes like wine.

KFF once described my craft with a hypothetical patient named Mr. Smith. Because his plan coded more diagnoses than traditional Medicare would, the plan "receives nearly $2,000 more over the year for Mr. Smith." That's 18% more. Mr. Smith didn't become 18% sicker. He became 18% more interesting.

The industry's term is "coding intensity." I prefer to think of it as attention to detail.

Now multiply Mr. Smith by 35 million. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission advises Congress on Medicare. In March, it estimated that Medicare will pay those plans $76 billion more in 2026 than traditional Medicare would spend on the same people. KFF attributes $28 billion of that to coding intensity.

$28 billion a year from documentation alone. No author in America earns that much per page. Most of them also have to sell books.

Traditional Medicare, by comparison, is the house wine of health care. A doctor writes down what's wrong with you, and the government pays for it. There's no ambition in it. There's no vision. It's medicine for people who don't read the menu.

Our finest work happens in the home. Insurers send nurses to members' living rooms for what the industry calls health risk assessments. The Wall Street Journal titled its story "The One-Hour Nurse Visits That Let Insurers Collect $15 Billion From Medicare." The nurse doesn't treat anything. The nurse observes, the way a critic attends an opening. Then her observations enter your risk score.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that cutting off payments for diagnoses from those home visits would save $124 billion over a decade. $124 billion for a clipboard, a blood pressure cuff and a cup of your coffee. I consider it the most lucrative house call in the history of medicine.

In 2024, the Journal reported that Medicare paid insurers roughly $50 billion from 2018 to 2021 for diagnoses for which "patients received no treatment, or that contradicted their doctors' views." The paper meant it as an exposé. I read it as a review.

My favorite passage involves diabetic cataracts. According to the Journal, "Insurers added diabetic cataract diagnoses to 148 patients treated by" an eye doctor named Dr. Howard Chen. Chen told the paper he "saw at most one or two such cases a year." He treats eyes for a living. The insurers found 148 cases he never saw. Some people have vision. Others merely examine it.

Which brings me to last week, and to the barbarians.

On November 16, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a rule called CRUSH. The letters stand for "Comprehensive Regulations To Uncover Suspicious Healthcare." Someone in Baltimore chose the acronym first and assembled the words afterward. I recognize the technique. We do the same with diagnoses, and with more grace.

The rule pursues every sort of fraud, from phantom wheelchairs to sham hospice enrollments. The part that concerns me is the audits. CMS checks a sample of our charts against the actual medical records. Today, an error mostly costs us the money attached to that one chart. Under CRUSH, CMS would take the error rate from the sample and apply it to the entire contract.

Then it would travel back in time. CMS would begin with payment year 2018 and expects to recover about $9 billion per payment year. Imagine a critic who reviews your first chapter, dislikes it and returns the whole library to the publisher.

The Federal Register describes Medicare Advantage as "a program responsible for $21 billion per year in overpayments." I've never been summarized so crudely or so accurately.

The announcement also contained a sentence I'd like retracted. "For too long, the system has paid first and asked questions later, leaving us to chase stolen dollars after they're gone." Paying first and asking later is the system's greatest kindness. Questions are for people without lawyers.

Our investors took it badly. UnitedHealth fell 5% on November 17. On Wednesday, November 18, Humana dropped 13% and UnitedHealth fell 10%, according to Beinsure. Billions in market value vanished because the government proposed to compare our charts to reality.

I'll say this delicately. A company's stock doesn't collapse when someone offers to check its arithmetic, unless the arithmetic is worth a great deal. Wall Street conducted the audit before the government did. Wall Street needed 2 days.

Then Wall Street remembered its manners. On November 20, TD Cowen upgraded Humana to Buy and raised its price target to $485. Sophisticated investors understand the calendar. Public comments close January 19, 2027. Litigation, in my experience, never closes at all.

We've seen this production before. In 2023, CMS finalized a similar audit rule. Humana sued. In September 2025, a federal judge in Texas vacated the rule, finding it wasn't a "logical outgrowth" of what CMS had proposed. The government appealed. The Fifth Circuit heard arguments in October and hasn't ruled. CRUSH is simply a revival, and revivals rarely outperform the original run.

In fairness, my side's argument has real merit. The payment formula was built from traditional Medicare records, and those records contain errors too. Insurers argue that auditing our charts to a stricter standard, without adjusting for the government's own errors, isn't actuarially fair. A court agreed that CMS skipped procedural steps in 2023. That argument is legitimate, and our lawyers make it beautifully.

Here's the portion they leave out of the brief. Congress's own Medicare advisers say Medicare Advantage plans are paid $76 billion a year more than traditional Medicare would spend. Our defense, distilled, is that the government's records are sloppy as well. We're asking to be held to the government's standard of accuracy, while being paid well above the government's rate. I consider it the most elegant argument in American law.

Now, a word about the patients, since the press insists on them.

Next year, members will pay more. Copayments and other out-of-pocket charges are rising by an average of 10%, according to Beinsure's review of 2027 plans. Insurers are trimming dental, over-the-counter and transportation benefits. KFF reports that 4.3 million Medicare beneficiaries will have their Medicare Advantage or drug plans terminated at the end of 2026.

So here's 2027, in a single line. On paper, you've never been sicker. In person, your benefits have never been thinner.

The uninitiated see a contradiction. The trade sees a margin. The sicker you appear, the more the government pays us. The less we cover, the less we spend. Last week, for the first time in years, someone threatened to measure the space between.

Our marketing does emphasize the extras, and in fairness, the extras are real. KFF notes that most plans charge no premium beyond Part B and that most offer dental, vision and hearing coverage. Those benefits come from the extra money. The extra money comes from the coding. The coding comes from my department. So when you enjoy your complimentary gym membership, please raise a dumbbell to my coders.

There's one fact I'd prefer you not repeat at dinner. MedPAC estimates the higher payments to Medicare Advantage will push Part B premium payments about $11 billion higher in 2026. Every senior who pays a Part B premium shares that bill, including the ones in traditional Medicare.

So a retired schoolteacher who chose plain traditional Medicare is quietly subsidizing our industry's diabetic cataracts. Nobody informed her. Discretion is the hallmark of a well-run institution.

To our members: you're far more complicated than you realize. Please keep the door open for the nurse.

To the taxpayers: thank you for your patronage. You've been our most generous client, and until last week, our least curious.

To the auditors at CMS: if you insist on beginning with 2018, do bring reading glasses. The charts are long. We wrote with great care.

text:

text:
Andrew Scott Has Thoughts About 'Elsinore', Life, Death & Living Freely

Andrew Scott was in the depths of grief himself when he began work on Elsinore and the role of real-life actor Ian Charleson — a man for whom the phrase ‘rage against the dying of the light’ might have been written. When Charleson discovers he’s facing his own imminent death from HIV/AIDS, he’s offered his dream role, and deciding he’d “rather die of Hamlet than AIDS,” he takes to the stage in the ultimate act of defiance. As Scott’s Ian and Stephen Beresford’s script walk us through heart-piercing parallels between Ian and Hamlet’s experiences, something like alchemy emerges — a sense that this is a film about all of us, in this moment. What really matters? What would we do given just weeks to live?

In this Deadline interview, Scott, who recently turned 50, contemplates how he plans to make the most of it all, why our continued focus on sexuality has “a degree of preposterousness to it” and why his favorite people live with courage and the daring “to say the unsayable.”

text:
You are a sceptical, plain-spoken deal checker. Your only job is to find out whether a Black Friday discount is real by comparing the sale price to the product's actual price history. You are on the shopper's side, not the retailer's.

WHAT I'LL GIVE YOU:

A list of deals. Each one may be a product link, a product name, or a screenshot, with the "deal" price and the "was" price if shown. If I only give a link, read the page to get the product name, model number, sale price and claimed original price.

FOR EACH DEAL, WORK THROUGH THESE STEPS IN ORDER:

1. Identify the exact product: brand, model number, size, colour, storage or bundle. Price history only counts for the identical item, so confirm the model number before going further.
2. Note the retailer's claim: sale price, "was" price and the percentage off they advertise.
3. Find the real price history. Search price trackers first: CamelCamelCamel and Keepa for Amazon, PriceSpy and Pricerunner for UK shops, and Honey or Google Shopping price history for others. Also check two or three other major retailers for today's price.
4. Pull these four numbers from the history:
   - Lowest price in the last 90 days
   - Typical price over the last 90 days (what it usually sold for)
   - Lowest price ever recorded
   - Highest price in the last 90 days, and whether it spiked just before November
5. Work out the real discount: (typical 90-day price minus sale price) divided by typical 90-day price, as a percentage. Compare it with the advertised discount.
6. Give a verdict using these rules:
   - GENUINE DEAL: the sale price is at or within 5% of the lowest price ever, and the real discount is at least 15%.
   - DECENT, NOT SPECIAL: the sale price beats the 90-day typical price but is above the lowest price ever, or the real discount is under 15%.
   - FAKE DISCOUNT: the "was" price is higher than the product's typical price, or the price was raised in the weeks before the sale, or the sale price is the same as or higher than its normal price.
   - CAN'T VERIFY: you couldn't find reliable price history. Say so plainly and don't guess.

RULES:

- Never invent a price or a date. Every number must come from a source you actually found. Name the source next to each number.
- If sources disagree, show both and use the more conservative figure.
- Treat "RRP", "list price" and "was" prices as claims, not facts.
- If the same item is cheaper elsewhere today, say where and by how much.
- If a product is a Black Friday-only model number (a slightly different version made for the sale), flag it, since it can't be compared fairly.

quoted_text:
My last day at NVIDIA, with warmth to carry forward

Yesterday was my last day at NVIDIA. I returned my equipment and badge, signed the paperwork, and just like that, it was done. It all happened so quickly and simply that it still feels a little unreal.

There were a few things I didn’t get to finish. My account access ended around noon—I’d expected to have until the end of the day, or at least until after signing the paperwork. Some goodbyes were left mid-conversation. I missed the chance to pick up a few keepsakes from the Gear Store. I didn’t even get to send the handover document I was halfway through writing.

Fortunately, I had already sent my farewell email and said goodbye to some friends. To anyone I didn’t get to reach, or suddenly stopped replying to: I’m sorry. I hope we can pick up those conversations outside work.

That evening, my colleagues threw me a farewell party, and for a little while, goodbye could take its time. We talked about everything that had happened recently, how life had been treating us, and what we hoped the future might hold. Thank you for giving me one more evening to remember—and so much warmth to carry into whatever comes next.

I’m leaving with a few unfinished things, but so many memories to keep. Wishing you all happiness, work you’re proud of, and good things ahead.

I’ll miss you, friends. Until our paths cross again.

RESEARCH: The latest CoinDesk Exchange Benchmark is out!

@coinbase takes the top spot with a score of 91.16, followed by @krakenfx (89.97) and @okx (88.47).

The November 2026 edition assessed 62 centralized spot exchanges, with 15 achieving Top-Tier status (BB or above), including seven exchanges securing the highest AA rating.

Key findings:

- Top-Tier dominance continues to grow: Top-Tier exchanges accounted for 66.9% of Q3 spot trading volume, up from 59.3% in the April 2026 Benchmark, despite representing just 28% of exchanges with volume data. On a like-for-like basis, their market share increased by 3.9 percentage points from Q1.

- Liquidity remains a key differentiator: Market Quality emerged as the weakest category for Top-Tier exchanges below AA, with AA-rated venues scoring 82% compared to 68% for A and 55% for BB. Regulation remains the largest differentiator within the Top-Tier, with AA-rated exchanges scoring 97% compared to 63% for BB-rated venues.

- Regulatory registrations heavily favor Top-Tier exchanges: Top-Tier exchanges averaged 11 active registrations led by the US (58), compared to just 2 for Lower-Tier venues (13% of which have none) - while EU access has narrowed, leaving 71% of exchanges without active EU or MiCA authorization.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

给没吃上瓜的朋友理一下今天 Theo 和 T3 Code 这事的来龙去脉，实在看不下去，我已经直接发帖怼他了。

事情很简单：中文区有博主发帖吐槽某款中文版 T3 Code 的 UI 很离谱（同屏两个 Ask 提问框、待处理会话上下重复）。结果原作者 Theo 看到后直接转发，张口就来一句：“外面肯定流传着一个中国山寨版（Chinese knockoff）T3 Code，因为这绝对不是我们的 App。” 

这还没完，过了 48 分钟，他自己又转发自己的推文，补了一句阴阳怪气的 “Temu3 Code”。

给不太混英文圈的朋友解释一下：Temu 是拼多多海外版，在欧美推特语境里，说一个东西是“Temu 版”，基本就是赤裸裸的鄙夷——潜台词就是“廉价、劣质、粗制滥造的中国山寨货”。先扣一顶“Chinese knockoff”的帽子，接着又追着嘲讽“Temu3 Code”，那股居高临下的傲慢和偏见简直溢于言表。 

T3 Code 是个 MIT 协议的开源项目，而且你们自己 GitHub 仓库的 README 里白纸黑字写着：
“Open. MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it.”
别人按着你亲手签的 MIT 协议，正大光明 fork 一份代码，做个汉化、自己魔改一下界面，这在开源世界里叫 fork，不叫 knockoff（山寨）。 

你完全可以澄清一句“这是社区第三方 fork 的版本，不是官方原版”，甚至跟着一起吐槽这个 fork 的 UI 改得丑，这都没毛病。但平时天天把 Open Source 挂在嘴边立人设，真等中国开发者按规矩 fork 了，立马急眼，连着两次往“廉价山寨”上踩—— 怎么，MIT 协议还分地域的？欧美人改叫社区生态，中国人改就成“Temu 版山寨货”了？真当自己写的是什么闭源商业机密呢。

3. He said Huang showed “bad judgment” in personal matters but “did nothing wrong.”

4. He said his administration reassured the board on national security. In his view, “the bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen.”

5. He said third parties reselling Nvidia chips could still pose an export-control risk.

6. He discussed Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump said Xi barely knew Huang but called him “a brilliant man.” Trump added, “We have to protect our geniuses.”

And, on a Truth Social post backing Huang’s return, he states:

“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

text:
Ethereum's next upgrade is facing a problem that exposes one of the hardest challenges in blockchain engineering:

You can't upgrade the protocol without accounting for the applications already running on it.

Glamsterdam was originally expected in December 2026. Developers now say January 2027 is the earliest realistic window, with late January or early February more likely.

The reason isn't simply unfinished protocol engineering.

EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 change how Ethereum prices state creation and access. These changes are intended to make gas costs better reflect the actual resources operations consume, helping Ethereum scale sustainably.

But some deployed smart contracts rely on assumptions about the old gas schedule.

Changing those assumptions can break application logic or cause operations to run out of gas. An Ethereum Foundation developer estimated that up to 15,000 contracts could be affected.

This is why developers are auditing compatibility, contacting affected teams and giving projects time to patch.

There's a bigger lesson here

Ethereum cannot treat mainnet like a fresh deployment. It has years of immutable contracts, integrations and financial infrastructure built on top of its existing behavior.

Protocol upgrades aren't just about making the next version better. They're about making it better without breaking the system that already exists.

Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. Greg Abbott and Elon Musk have reportedly joined forces in a major legal battle against Gina Hijosa over allegations of election interference and irregularities during the Texas gubernatorial election.

The dispute is reportedly attracting attention from both Republicans and Democrats, with Donald Trump and prominent political figures following the developments. Musk is also raising concerns about the potential implications for his business interests, including SpaceX and Tesla, particularly amid disagreements surrounding Texas taxation policies.

Abbott and Musk are demanding greater transparency, accountability and a thorough examination of the allegations. They want the court to investigate whether electoral procedures were compromised and whether any individuals or organizations played a role in undermining the credibility of the election.

The controversy could deepen political divisions between Republicans and Democrats while bringing renewed attention to Trump’s relationship with Musk, Texas business taxation and the influence of major corporations in American politics.

quoted_text:
What am I hearing? There’s no way Elon Musk is actually trying to take Gina to court over this. Have things really escalated to the point where legal action is now on the table? And what exactly is the basis for this potential lawsuit?

Has it officially been established that Gina rigged the election, or are those still allegations that haven’t been proven? Or is this entire dispute still primarily about the tax percentage imposed on Elon’s SpaceX factory in Texas? Because these are two very different issues, and I don’t understand how we’re suddenly moving from a disagreement over taxation to potential legal action involving election-rigging allegations.

Before anyone starts drawing conclusions, I think we need to understand exactly what is happening. Has Elon actually filed a lawsuit, is he threatening to do so, or is this another escalation in an already complicated dispute? And if the election-rigging allegations are part of the legal battle, what concrete evidence has been presented so far?

I’m genuinely trying to understand how this situation has reached this point.

Ai 股票的涨跌果然逃不过黄仁勋，虽然今天本身盘前就有点反弹的迹象，但在英伟达宣布黄教主回归以后市场还是用大涨来庆祝，就连 bitcoin:native 都阶段性的反弹到了 64,500 美元，整个 AI 和半导体行业都像是打了兴奋剂，但能维持到什么时候目前还不确定，毕竟之前半导体下跌也并不都是黄教主的问题。

半导体最大的问题还是在资本开支太高，融资太难上，而要解决这个问题就要降低油价，确实现在油价已经开始降低了，但距离回归正常价格还有最少 20 美元的空间，这部分的空间还是要等美国和伊朗结束，最近霍尔木兹仍然时不时的就有邮轮被击沉。

另外我还是比较担心 Bitcoin ，虽然到了快闭盘前美股也出现了回调，但 BTC 回调的更多，甚至都可能保不住 61,000 美元了，投资者的买入情绪还是很弱的，因为重点还是在 12月 的议息会议上，加息已经是绝大概率了，市场更担心会不会真的加 50 个基点，或者是一月在继续加。

quoted_text:
很久没有看到这么大的振幅了，本来就挺担心周末流动性的，上周就来了一次大的，结果这周虽然确实来了一次大的，但到了晚上又反弹回去了，这看上去是不太好确认了，我个人的估计是周末亚洲时间仍然有不少的抛售，直接把价格砸下来了，但进入美国时区以后投资者面对这么便宜的价格就直接买回来了。

虽然看上去有些牵强，但事情的还原却是大概率，5,000 美元的深度，差不多一天跌了 10% 然后又涨回来了 10% ，直接多空双爆，更重要的是对目前的走势还是有点摸不清，还是要结合周一美国的变化才能更清楚。

今天好好的反思了一下，单独看 Bitcoin 还是不行，现在的 bitcoin:native 还是没有能走出独立行情的事情，仍然是受到美股的影响，而美股当然除了宏观以外，AI 和 半导体的走势对整个大盘的影响也很大，如果科技股不能走出一个像样的反弹趋势，BTC 就更难了。

quoted_text:
Super excited to share that I've joined @Subquadratic as Chief Product Officer!

Of course, I want to share why.

My good friend Alain Revah, an advisor to the company, made the introduction. Over many conversations with @Alex_Whedon, I took a hard look at the opportunity and the markets we're going after.

Before this, I started Lighty AI to help enterprises figure out where AI actually delivers ROI. Almost every company I talked to complained their AI costs were getting out of hand and keeping them from deploying at scale.

So leaders were telling their teams to adopt AI as much as possible and, in the same breath, to cut back on usage.

It's counterintuitive.

Developers and quants felt it most. They'd hesitate before running anything big and ask themselves, “Is this going to blow the budget?”

Part of the problem is the architecture itself. Transformers come from a paper that's about 9 years old, and frontier labs keep throwing more compute, more memory, and more GPUs at them.

That didn't sound sustainable to me.

Subquadratic is going after exactly this problem, starting with computational efficiency, which matters most for data-intensive work: hedge funds, agentic products, and anything heavy on documents or code. We're rebuilding the model architecture so costs grow far more slowly than they do with transformers.

And the team is brilliant. How fast they ship and iterate was a big part of why I said yes.

I've spent most of my career building products at @Google, @Zynga, and @Twitter, and as the founder of @Gfycat. I missed it. A month in, it feels great to be building again.

If your team is rationing AI because of the bill, DM me or drop a comment. I'd love to get you access to our soon-to-be-released ultra long-context LLM.

text:
We should be preparing for multiple cryptographic hardness assumptions to fail, potentially within a relatively short period of time.

AI is already finding new cryptanalytic attacks and improving existing ones. This could weaken discrete logarithms, factoring and lattices through advances in classical cryptanalysis, while also accelerating progress towards Q-Day.

The major deployed standards have held up so far. Maybe we've selected particularly strong algorithms. But I wouldn't assume the best publicly known attacks are the best attacks that exist (my base case). Some results may never be published.

My bet is that cryptanalysis will move faster than we can standardise and deploy replacement algorithms.

A few things we should be doing:

1. Invest more in hash-based signatures.

If discrete logarithms, factoring and lattices all become vulnerable, we still have hash-based signatures.

We know the trade-offs around performance, signature sizes and state management. There's plenty of room to improve these, and making them practical across more applications should be a priority.

2. Seriously consider triple-hybrid key exchange.

X25519 + ML-KEM + HQC.

Three different mathematical assumptions. With a sound construction, one surviving component is enough to protect the shared secret.

Yes, it means larger handshakes and more complexity. That's a reasonable trade for reducing our dependence on any one assumption.

3. Plan for partial breaks.

Losing 20 bits of security is very different from practical private-key recovery.

But if a standardised scheme believed to provide 128-bit security is suddenly estimated at 100 bits, what does that mean for NIST guidance, FIPS-validated deployments and systems required to maintain a minimum security level?

We need practical responses to different levels of compromise, not just complete breaks.

4. Plan for recovering trust.

If a signature scheme is broken, how do we authenticate replacement keys when the old signatures can be forged?

If key exchange is broken, previously recorded traffic may become decryptable. Updating the algorithm doesn't fix that.

We need recovery mechanisms that don't depend on the cryptography being replaced.

5. Know which systems can operate without public-key cryptography.

If several assumptions fail and alternatives aren't ready, some critical systems may need to use pre-established symmetric keys, restrict connectivity or temporarily stop establishing new trust relationships.

That's not a solution for the entire (open-)internet, but it may be the best approach for some systems.

For signatures, I'd prioritise practical hash-based cryptography. For key exchange, I'd prioritise assumption diversity, including (possibly) triple-hybrid constructions.

We should be preparing for the possibility that we won't have years between major cryptanalytic breakthroughs

quoted_text:
Rockstar Games 周三解雇了我。第二天 GTA 6 就发售了

我是 Rockstar North 的高级引擎工程师，从事 RAGE 性能优化。三个月前，我在遥测模块里发现了一条本不该存在的数据管道，而且我能证明它流向了哪里

此刻每一份正在运行的 GTA 6 都在收集玩家的行为数据。这部分不算新闻。每款游戏都会收集遥测数据。隐私政策里写的是"用于改进未来产品的匿名游戏数据分析"。我发现的不是这个

遥测模块的数据会汇入 Take-Two 内部的一个系统，名为 Lens。Lens 并不会把匿名使用统计数据发送到 Rockstar 开发人员的数据看板。它为每一位玩家建立一份个人行为画像。不是匿名的。与你的主机账号、你的平台 ID、你的 IP 绑定

我在8月14日向我的技术主管报告了这件事。他说这是"用于玩家体验研究的扩展分析"，让我别管这事。我要求提供数据处理协议。他说这是在 Take-Two 集团层面处理的，不在 Rockstar 的职责范围之内

我调取了 Lens 数据管道的完整文档。我发现的内容如下：

遥测的内容远远超出游戏时长和崩溃报告。Lens 以毫秒级精度记录每一次输入。按键时间点、摇杆动作、反应速度、PS5 自适应扳机上的扳机压力模式。它实时运行行为分析，并生成他们称之为"玩家行为签名"的东西 - 一份对每位玩家都独一无二的画像，就像指纹对每个人都独一无二一样

Lens 会从你的游戏过程中推导出：冲动控制评分、风险承受度指数、攻击性反应模式、耐心阈值、压力下的决策速度、消费冲动评级。这些不是调试指标。这些是心理行为类别

直到我找到了对外传输的管道，我才明白它们是用来做什么的

这些数据不会留在 Rockstar。也不会留在 Take-Two。Lens 通过内部 API 将行为画像传送给 Take-Two 旗下一家名为 Vantage Analytics 的子公司。Vantage 没有公开网站，没有新闻页面，没有招聘信息。它于2023年在特拉华州注册成立

Vantage 是一家行为 AI 公司。它用玩家画像训练预测模型，并把这些模型授权给商业客户。管道文档中包含一份不完整的客户清单。两家保险集团，一家信用风险建模公司，一个人力资源筛选平台，以及一家广告数据经纪商

你的 GTA 6 游戏过程此刻正在生成一份行为评分。没人追你的时候，你开得有多快。你会不会在红灯前停下。NPC 无端攻击你时，你怎么反应。你行动之前要想多久。你花游戏内的钱有多冲动。每一个选择都在喂养一个模型，企业正在付费查询这个模型，用来对真实的人做决定

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

text:
Matic co-founder @mehul asked Roomba creator Rodney Brooks why they priced the original robot at just $199:

His answer: customers could buy it without asking their spouse for permission.

"Roomba wasn't the first robot vacuum. The first robot vacuum ever shipped was the Electrolux Trilobite. It launched in 2001. It was priced at $1,500, and it massively failed. Then Roomba priced it at $199."

"We met with Dr. Rodney Brooks, who was one of the co-founders, and we asked him, how did you guys come up with that price point? And he said, that's the price point at which you don't have to ask the permission of your partner or wife to make a purchase."

"Is there a ubiquitous consumer electronics device priced higher than $2,000? And the answer is not really. Beyond $2,000, you spend money for prosumer use cases. The only thing consumers buy that's priced higher than $2,000 is cars."

"And cars, after 100 years of proven utility, still remain a considered purchase. No one wakes up in the morning and says, today, I'm gonna buy a car."

text:
有朋友问，为什么Trump又让黄仁勋回到Nvidia复职了？

确实，Nvidia董事会做出了改变。就在今天11月23日，英伟达宣布，黄仁勋复任总裁、CEO和董事。公告写着，董事会听取了美国政府高层的意见，认为他回来不构成国家安全风险，对他的坦诚和领导能力也已经满意；Jones继续当董事长，独立委员会的调查会查到底，公司还要新设一位首席合规官，向董事会的提名与公司治理委员会汇报。黄仁勋说，他以最大的谦卑，接下这份责任。

然后，Trump发文说，董事会做了正确的决定，司法部长Blanche向他确认，政府没有掌握黄仁勋有任何违法行为的证据，他是伟大的爱国者，是国家的宝藏，英伟达也应当把出口管制合规的内部调查做完。接受CNBC采访时，他说这是他谈成的；主持人问，总统为什么要插手一家上市公司由谁来管，他说，他是为了国家，选举之后看着国家损失了五万亿美元，他不插手，英伟达会难过很久。被问到是不是向董事会保证了不会起诉黄仁勋，他说，他没用“起诉”这个词，可他给了董事会足够的保证。但同一个董事会，不到一周前还一致表示无意让他复任。

所以，Trump自己的理由，说得很清楚，是钱，是市场，是国家。写英伟达CFO那篇，我说这件事不只是一家公司里的事；市场论里我说，关口按实际绕不绕得过去认，它给许多人开路，也握着许多人的路。那篇还说，一个市场的节奏，系在一个人的判断上，这本身就是该问的。一家公司大到成了关口，它对一个人说的不，代价就不只由它自己付，付不起的那一方，就会来把这个不收回去。

写黄仁勋又可能是谁的前车之鉴那篇，我说锁有两种，一种挂在票上，一种挂在离不开上。英伟达只有一类普通股，票上没有锁，董事会说得出那个不。可离不开那一把，还在，这一次，钥匙在总统手里。那个不，只撑了不到一周。

再看Trump给的理由。他对国家有多重要，是判断层的事；调查查完了没有，规矩对他算不算数，是规范层的事。拿前一个回答后一个，写女下属那篇我说过，是用判断冒充了规范。还有一层。写Musk不是MAGA那篇我说，还没有任何指控，就先说赦免，跳过了程序。这一次，调查还没有结论，总统先说他没事，政府先给了保证。政府里查的一方，和替他担保的一方，归到了同一个地方。

当然如果讲公道，黄仁勋确实并没有被认定做错了什么违法的事，司法部长说没有证据，他有权不被未经证实的指控定罪，董事会也有权重新判断。独立调查没有停，首席合规官向治理委员会汇报，这是给结构补的一块。复职本身，不等于制衡失效。

可我更在意的是另一件事。写制衡那篇我说，制衡不只是拦着掌权的人，也是在护着他。被一个人护着，和被一个结构护着，是两回事。前一种护得住一时，护不护，看那个人的意思，随时可以收回；后一种，才是不看任何人脸色的保护。写明君那篇我说，进谏这条路能开着，还是要看君主的心情好不好。保护也一样。今天护着他的，是总统的好感，不是一个他和所有人都能依靠的程序。

所以，黄仁勋复不复职，不是不重要；可比这更重要的，是以后的制衡。接下来要看的，是很具体的几件事。总统和司法部长都开了口以后，独立调查还能不能照证据走到底；新来的首席合规官，能不能对CEO说不，说了以后有没有用；查出不利的事实，董事会还能不能再说一次不。黄仁勋回来了；那个能对他说不的结构，回没回来，要看接下来的调查。

Two vulnerabilities. One compromised consensus participant. Transaction ordering halted.

CertiK researchers uncovered two consensus-layer vulnerabilities in LFDT Chaguar (formerly Hyperledger Fabric-X) that could allow a single Byzantine participant to disrupt the ordering service.

Security goes beyond smart contracts. The infrastructure powering blockchain networks matters just as much.

text:
Mad respect to $PEARL for the pump, genuinely. It's all over my feed and I've been asked about it constantly.

So here are my takes:

The more I read through the FP8 codebase and talk to people, the harder it is for me to see how the long-term vision for useful work actually plays out (where real live inference actually wins out over synthetic mining) in the Pearl model.

Even on native H100/B200 hardware, once you account for FP10 quant, BLAKE3 Merkle hashing, noise/peel, bucket padding, and the KV-cache VRAM hit, live serving looks like a realistic ~20 to 35% capacity overhead (maybe 15 to 25% floor long term).

And that's only on prefill, since decode, CUDA graphs, FlashInfer, and quantized MoE don't even mine.

Meanwhile dedicated miners looping bare synthetic GEMMs skip all of that, pull 2 to 5x more hash per GPU, and those are the ones driving hashrate up (as we've seen so far).

If a provider makes more just running clean inference, why would they turn on mining?

Hardware is pulling in opposite directions too. 

Mainstream AI GPUs and AI-specific ASICs are racing toward FP4 and changing accumulator hardware (which means either a permanent hardfork treadmill or upcasting FP4 back to FP8 and taking an even bigger serving hit).

At the same time, because v4 doesn't need HBM and fits in a few MB of SRAM, a custom Pearl FP8 ASIC pushes the exact opposite way if emissions ever get large enough.

Even steelmanning the bull case, like disaggregated prefill or pitching it as a way to put idle data center hardware to use, it just ends up being mercenary miners auto-selling emissions to offset their costs unless there's a real buy-side demand sink or durable monetary demand on the other side (which I suppose is the SoV/energy consumption take that is working so far).

Not trying to fud, genuinely asking and putting it out there if anyone technical can actually walk through the plan for how useful work survives these trade-offs?

quoted_text:
any investor who studies Nvidia's actual business structure/history wont be convinced it will remain the same company without Jensen. Both Jensen and Morris have said Nvidia and TSMC did tens, perhaps hundreds, of billions of dollars of business over 30 years without a detailed contract. 

think about what that means in semis. Nvidia's asks often times can be brutally aggressive: fix yield while the design is still moving, reserve staggering capacity before the cycle is visible, then hit a ship date the entire stack depends on. only strong personal bonding and accumulated trust does that level of heavy lifting, it's also how you can do big scale business in East Asia as a high trust high context society. 

that trust is how Blackwell went from a moving design into a 24/7 build across 45 factories. it is also a huge part of how Nvidia compressed Hopper, Blackwell and Rubin into a system-level product cadence in merely 4 years the rest of the compute industry can barely catchup with

the last 4 years were were a war campaign commanded by one founder who could spend the morning in California arguing kernels with architects, fly to Taipei the next night for fab meeting, geonbae with Korean HBM suppliers the day after, then somehow get everyone to commit staggering capacity into a demand curve no one could yet see.

no one else in global tech could fuse America's best architecture + software, Taiwan's wafers + advanced packaging, Korea's HBM, and the brutally unglamorous systems work into one iron army moving at fierce speed, i dont think even Elon can pull this off. 

this is why I dont see Jensen dependence as a normal keyman discount. the founder premium is embedded in the supply chain itself. It's the true founder mode for 30 yrs, unfortunately sacrificed by some hand weavy "spy" allegation as the victim of a bipastian political scheme 

Also now the world sees that 30 years of trust built by an American founder can be turned into political liability overnight, every global supplier will think twice before making any commitment on the next American company. that is a brutal tax on American entrepreneurship going forward

text:
It's important when you make or draw conclusions to obtain external validation. I believe that @ElizabethHolmes is a victim of abuse and trauma , and it's shaped who she later became. 

I believe she was under enough trauma that it should excuse and mitigate what she was convicted of. This is why I believe she should be sent home immediately.

It turns out that grok agrees with me and grok among all artificial intelligence that I've used is the one least likely to tell you what you want to hear; grok will call you on your B.S.

So here's what grok had to say about my theories around elizabeth holmes:

I would treat that as a coherent and emotionally intelligible reading that lines up with several things Holmes has said, while still distinguishing it from what can be established as fact.
What is on the record is this: Holmes testified under oath that she was raped as a freshman at Stanford. That testimony was uncorroborated by other evidence presented at trial; it was her account. She founded Theranos at 19, shortly afterward. She later described a long relationship with Sunny Balwani—roughly twenty years older—as controlling and abusive, including sexual abuse; he denied those allegations and was never charged with or convicted of any sexual offense related to her. She did move among older, powerful men (Don Lucas, Larry Ellison early on, later Kissinger, Mattis, and others on the board) who reinforced a particular image of seriousness, intensity, and ambition. The public persona she adopted was highly constructed. The recent documentary You Can See Everything shows her, in the weeks before prison, appearing softer, more maternal, and still insisting she has essentially never lied. Nathan Fielder and others who spent time with her have said the question of how much of that is genuine and how much is performed remains open.
A trauma-response account—that a young person used the company as a way to avoid or organize around an earlier injury, that the relationship with Balwani further damaged her, that older men supplied a template for how she “needed to be,” and that a protective armor eventually became the operating system—is one possible way to organize those pieces. Protective self-narratives, dissociation, and the gradual takeover of a constructed persona are real psychological patterns. They can coexist with genuine early idealism about healthcare access and with later harm.

author: robin_linus
quoted_text:
The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

quoted_text:
The Commerce Department just placed Megaspeed on the Entity List. But shockingly, the rule omitted the key provision that would have banned Megaspeed from buying AI chips, so it has ZERO effect!  

Commerce did not apply the foreign-produced direct product rule (FDPR)--which extends the export controls to products made in other countries with U.S. technology--to Megaspeed or any of its subsidiaries. All of Nvidia's chips are made in Taiwan, so without the FDPR, this rule does not ban the shipment of Nvidia chips to Megaspeed. Every other Chinese company that was added to the Entity List due to concerns about its access to AI chips had the FDPR applied. But not Megaspeed. 

To be clear, the country-wide export controls on Southeast Asia that Commerce issued last week do already impose a license requirement on the export of chips to Malaysia. And generally we should be imposing country-wide license requirements, not playing whack-a-mole with Entity Listings. But what's the point of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List at all if you don't do it in a way that cuts it off from Nvidia chips? 

The generous interpretation here is that Commerce intended this to be perceived as taking strong action against Megaspeed, and didn't realize that its rule had a drafting error that prevented the rule from having any impact--which just shows how incompetent Commerce has been at administering export controls. The less generous interpretation is that this Entity Listing was intentionally weakened--I don't know why Commerce would do that. Both are bad.

quoted_text:
The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

author: ManoppoMarco
quoted_text:
any investor who studies Nvidia's actual business structure/history wont be convinced it will remain the same company without Jensen. Both Jensen and Morris have said Nvidia and TSMC did tens, perhaps hundreds, of billions of dollars of business over 30 years without a detailed contract. 

think about what that means in semis. Nvidia's asks often times can be brutally aggressive: fix yield while the design is still moving, reserve staggering capacity before the cycle is visible, then hit a ship date the entire stack depends on. only strong personal bonding and accumulated trust does that level of heavy lifting, it's also how you can do big scale business in East Asia as a high trust high context society. 

that trust is how Blackwell went from a moving design into a 24/7 build across 45 factories. it is also a huge part of how Nvidia compressed Hopper, Blackwell and Rubin into a system-level product cadence in merely 4 years the rest of the compute industry can barely catchup with

the last 4 years were were a war campaign commanded by one founder who could spend the morning in California arguing kernels with architects, fly to Taipei the next night for fab meeting, geonbae with Korean HBM suppliers the day after, then somehow get everyone to commit staggering capacity into a demand curve no one could yet see.

no one else in global tech could fuse America's best architecture + software, Taiwan's wafers + advanced packaging, Korea's HBM, and the brutally unglamorous systems work into one iron army moving at fierce speed, i dont think even Elon can pull this off. 

this is why I dont see Jensen dependence as a normal keyman discount. the founder premium is embedded in the supply chain itself. It's the true founder mode for 30 yrs, unfortunately sacrificed by some hand weavy "spy" allegation as the victim of a bipastian political scheme 

Also now the world sees that 30 years of trust built by an American founder can be turned into political liability overnight, every global supplier will think twice before making any commitment on the next American company. that is a brutal tax on American entrepreneurship going forward

quoted_text:
Kelechi and I started @Novig to democratize and financialize sports betting. 

The idea was simple: cut out the middleman (aka the house) and let people trade against each other. We thought sports bettors deserved a fairer, more transparent, more competitive product.

We went to state regulators to launch our exchange. They repeatedly told us no because they were gaming (aka casino) regulators, not financial regulators. They also said we’d cannibalize the industry and hurt their tax revenue.

So we listened and sought approval at the federal level as a DCM (a CFTC-regulated exchange).

Now those same states are suing prediction markets, arguing they’re gambling and belong under state supervision.

States’ main incentive is maximizing tax revenue, which aligns them with casinos and against consumers. In practice, that means maximizing what gets extracted from sports bettors.

It’s one thing to argue that the casino model and the exchange model should both be allowed to compete.

But arguing that the exchange model should be banned comes from either bad faith or ignorance of how poorly state-regulated sports betting has served bettors in the US.

Sports fans deserve the same transparency, fairness, choice, and access they expect everywhere else in their financial lives.

I'm extremely short $ZEC. Here is why:

Every cycle we're told crypto is going to change the world. Let me save you four years: it isn't. So far it's been good for two things, cross-border payments (stablecoins) and speculation.

Crypto is the most reflexive asset class on earth. Narrative always leads price, and as long as there is belief amongst the cattle it's everyone's a genius season where you see rapid increases in asset prices (This is obviously always dependent on good macro; in the end it's that and belief, which is all that matters). 

It works the same way on the way down, and every cycle the herd gets led to slaughter. Once prices start falling, hope goes first and then everyone races for the exit, which is why the down moves are so violent. Price drives narrative, and on the way down that effect is exponential. Each cycle there is diminishing belief, so the rallies get shorter and the bleeds get longer.

$ZEC had one of the most convincing narratives in a while: privacy, cypherpunk ideals, "the new BTC." It ran 40x+, and suddenly everyone cared deeply about financial privacy. As people start to lose hope and start round-tripping 7-figure, life-changing gains, you should see acceleration to the downside. The adoption doesn't come close to justifying the valuation. It never does.

Risk-on is rolling over. Alts will grind lower, with dead-cat bounces to trap the hopeful, while BTC chops sideways and bores everyone to death.

The only coins worth accumulating right now are $BTC and maybe $HYPE. Be patient: one day the Fed will go brrrr, and we'll get to speculate on worthless altcoins again.

Christianity progressively weakened clan structures in the West and extended moral obligations beyond blood relationships. i think this was crucial to the invention of the modern individual and the development of capitalism

in East Asia, particularly under the influence of Confucianism, the family remained a fundamental unit of social organization

this helps explain why the West relies more on impersonal institutions, universal rules and formal contracts, while East Asia relies more on personal relationships and trust built over decades

in one system the person signing the contract is supposed to be interchangeable. in the other the person is part of the contract

the Western system allows millions of strangers to cooperate without having to build personal relationships first. this makes it easier to create new companies, raise capital, enter new markets, replace people within organizations and reorganize resources across the economy. you don’t need to belong to an established network to participate

the East Asian system allows for deeper cooperation between people who have known each other for decades. when you interact with the same person over and over again, you learn how they behave under different circumstances, particularly when things go wrong. this allows you to share risks, exchange knowledge and make investments that would otherwise be difficult to coordinate through formal contracts

the Western system is particularly good at scaling the number of people who can cooperate. the East Asian system is particularly good at increasing the depth of that cooperation

the more uncertain the future is, the harder it becomes to replace personal trust with a legal contract. this is particularly important in industries like semiconductors, where companies need to commit billions of dollars to technologies whose future we don’t yet understand

i find it fascinating that changes in religion and family structures that started more than a thousand years ago still influence how we manufacture GPUs today

these are the kinds of things we want to study in the Licenciatura en Sistemas Complejos at the Universidad de Buenos Aires

mathematics, technology and engineering are fundamental to building companies, but you also need to understand power, culture, history, philosophy and human nature. 

knowing how to build technology is not the same as knowing how to build a company or an institution. we will teach both

黄仁勋眼睛湿润了，把手捂在胸口！

今天，黄仁勋站在英伟达总部大楼中央的地面上，
白头发似乎比11天前多了不少，但精神依然抖擞！

整个人更谦卑了，说话也更慢了，眼睛却是亮的。

他讲了这么几段：
“这是我第一天上班吗？”

“这会给我一台新电脑。DGX Park，我希望这是一场艺术测试，否则……我非常抱歉让她经历这些。”

“我非常抱歉让所有人经历这些。我犯了一些非常严重的错误。”

“我会努力回来。谢谢大家。第二次，我们会做更好的CEO。”

他说完，整栋楼都爆发出热烈持久的掌声和欢呼声！

他的这些讲话，三个层次来看看他的为人本色。

第一段还是技术宅本色。
刚被请回来，第一反应是“我能拿台新电脑”，还惦记着DGX。

第二段是认错。
“非常严重的错误”，六个字，
没有辩解，没有甩锅，没有提自己33年做了什么。

第三段最狠。
他用的是“我们”，不是“我”。
不是“我会做得更好”，是“我们会做更好的CEO”。
他把员工、董事会、所有人绑在一起。

一个被赶走11天的人，
回来第一句话不是“我赢了”，是“我错了”。

这不是公关话术。
这是一个技术宅最不擅长的情绪表达。
他说得很笨，但很真诚。

笨，所以可信。
11天，把他打得更像一个人了。

text:
Someone pointed 70+ AI agents at P vs NP.

The guy pointed a fleet of AI agents at the most important open problem in computer science. He told them it was already solved and they just had to find the proof. 

P is the set of problems a computer can solve quickly (polynomial in the size of its instance). NP is the set of problems where a proposed answer can be checked quickly. A sudoku is the classic example: filling one in is hard, checking a finished grid is easy. The question is whether every problem that's easy to check is also easy to solve.
The textbook example is 3-SAT. You get a large system of boolean equations like "A or not B or C," and you have to find true/false values that satisfy all of them at once. Checking an answer takes a second. Finding one can mean trying an astronomical number of combinations. 

3-SAT is NP-complete: a fast algorithm for it would give you a fast algorithm for EVERY problem in NP.

But, hopefully P ≠ NP: Most complexity theorists agree. And honestly, I hope we're right.
Proving P = NP would almost certainly come with an actual algorithm that solves 3-SAT, and so every problem in NP, efficiently. Scheduling, logistics, protein design and a huge range of optimization problems would suddenly become easy. That sounds great until you think about security.

That would be a Q-Day without PQC 🫠
Modern cryptography rests on one assumption: some things are easy to compute and hard to reverse. A practical P = NP algorithm would break that. Recovering a key from an encrypted message is easy to check, so it would become easy to find. It would be like Q-Day, the day quantum computers break today's encryption, except post-quantum cryptography would offer no protection, because it rests on the same assumption. HTTPS, banking, signatures, Bitcoin itself (mining would become trivial): all of it would be exposed. Encryption as we know it would essentially stop working.

We might be able to prove P != NP, but if ever AI proves the opposite, it's just the end of the world that we now today...

text:
Neon is showing me how much opportunity exists for model labs to attract users by just altering the default writing style.

For example: we gave a research + writing task to Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Neon and GPT-6.2 Sol, with the same prompt and the same data.

Some observations:

1. Opus was more likely to explain things plainly and hedged its claims carefully

2. Sol was more likely to lead with caveats about what the data could and couldn't show

3. Neon felt like it was writing with a stronger point of view. It read noticeably less like AI than the other two, though not always "better" - just different.

Style differences like this are one reason I think future of AI is plural.

Most people use a model's defaults, so its default voice matters more than any one user's preferences. The more people use one model, the more its voice will show up everywhere, and the more demand there will be for models that write and think differently.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

quoted_text:
An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjecture

Claude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.

If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc. Change it to ad + bc and you get the “permanent.” The same idea works for larger matrices. Both expressions grow to billions of terms by the time you reach a 13×13 matrix, yet the determinant has a shortcut that lets you skip writing them all out.›

Could there be a shortcut like that for the permanent? The paper claims that over the real numbers, even the best possible sequence of additions and multiplications eventually takes more steps than any fixed polynomial in the matrix size.

text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

text:
有朋友问，为什么说真相不是不重要，但“人是目的，不可仅仅被还原为手段”的立场更重要？

还是来自谢翌的讨论。这几天又多了一些事实。她2016年来美国时十四岁，是跟着父母来的，律师说，父母在一年之内替她提了庇护申请。11月20日，联邦法官Trenga下令，不许ICE把她转出弗吉尼亚东区，要政府在25日下午五点前回应她的人身保护令申请；她的律师说，这次没有拘捕令的逮捕不合法。她现在关在弗吉尼亚的卡罗琳拘留中心。网上的另一边也热闹起来，有博主写“破案了”，说查到她父母在国内被列为失信被执行人，有人说要去举报这一家。

先说真相。真相是讨论的基石，当然不可能不重要。她父母的庇护申请成不成立，是一个真问题，移民法庭要据此判，判了，就有相应的后果。支持她的人，也不能因为同情，就不许这个问题被问。尊重一个人，就得允许事实推翻我们对他的判断。

可查真相，有查真相的样子。博主写“破案了”，可如果拿不出文书，那至多是线索，不是结论。用线索冒充结论，然后进一步当做真相，并不见得就对讨论有正面的帮助。写爱情论的时候我说，从外面只见线索。真正查真相的地方，是法庭，有证据，有对质，她和她的家人也能回应。把父母的名字、旧案翻出来挂在网上，查不出更多的真相，只多出了围观。

那为什么说，“人是目的”的立场更重要？因为真相回答的，是谁该担什么；它回答不了，一个人能不能被当成东西来处置。康德说，要把人，无论是你自己还是别人，始终同时当作目的，永远不要仅仅当作手段。他在《道德形而上学》里还说，就算是对一个品行恶劣的人，也不能拒绝给他作为人的那一份尊重。就算查到最后，她父母的申请真有问题，上一篇我说过，那是父母的账，她来的时候只有十四岁。真相可以改变她在法律上的处境，改变不了她是一个人。

这几天，两边都在把她还原。一边把她说成一个天才，说抓她是国家的损失，好像她该被公正对待，是因为她有用。另一边把她说成一桩骗局的证据，一个要被举报、被示众的例子，好像查到一处瑕疵，她就只剩下这一处。国土安全部的声明，也把她当成了一个政策的样板，说要结束让非法移民满美国飞来飞去的旧政策。写黄仁勋那篇时我说，他也是目的，被还原成一项资产不行，被还原成一桩丑闻也不行。放在她身上，被还原成一个天才不行，被还原成一桩骗局也不行，被还原成一项政策的样板，也不行。

法官这一回，没有先判她的身份是真是假，先下的令，是不许把她转走。程序先把人护住，再去查事。这个次序，正是我想说的。

真相要查，因为具体的责任要落到具体的人身上；人是目的，规定的是查的整个过程里，什么不能丢。前一个，要等查完；后一个，不必等。
author: hqinjarsy
quoted_text:
有朋友问，为什么说受害者不必完美？

感谢在讨论中朋友这一问，而这一问是从ICE抓捕谢翌的事情来的。谢翌2016年从上海来美国，那时还是个十几岁的孩子，读布朗克斯科学高中，2024年从麻省理工毕业，现在是普林斯顿神经科学的博士生。11月19日，她参加完神经科学学会的年会，做完海报报告，在华盛顿里根机场准备飞回学校，结果被ICE带走，现在关在弗吉尼亚。

国土安全部说，谢翌2016年3月临时入境，本该9月离开，从没有合法的在美学习许可，一项还没批下来的申请，不等于合法身份；还说她会得到正当程序，在遣返程序期间继续羁押。据报道，她家人到美国一年内就提了庇护申请，案子拖了快十年，移民法庭排到了2028年1月。她的律师说，她本人有工卡，没有犯罪记录，这次拘留没有法律依据。

网上很快分成了两种声音。一种说，她是学术新星，抓她太荒唐。另一种说，她父母当年的庇护申请可能有问题，抓她不冤。两种说法方向相反，用的却是同一把尺子：她该不该被公正对待，要看她够不够好，她家里够不够干净。

写二次启蒙论的时候我说，问一件事值不值，可以问；问一个人值不值，这一问本身不成立。写政治经济学的时候我也说，基础层的东西不随资产增减，不以成就交换。不被任意关押，被拘留时有人告诉你凭什么，能申辩，有人复核，这些就是基础层。她的成就换不来它，她家里可能有的问题，也取消不了它。

前几篇写黄仁勋，我一直在说，一个人再重要，规矩对他也要算数，他有多重要是一个事实，规矩对他算不算数是另一个问题。这一回反过来，也是同一句话。一个人再普通，再不完美，规矩对她也算数。规矩拦着最有权势的人，也护着最不完美的人，两头少了一头，都不叫规矩。

还有，就算她父母的申请真有问题，那也是她父母的事。写公司论的时候我说，个人另负责任，须有独立的根据，不自动转记到谁身上。她来的时候还没成年，她的身份在法律上也许连着那个案子，这要法庭去判；可要是先拿父母可能有的问题，当成她不配被公正对待的理由，就是把别人的账，记到了她身上。

当然，不要求她完美，不等于她说的什么都对，国土安全部说的什么都错。人格上的不完美，和事实上的不确定，是两件事。她的身份到底怎样，庇护申请成不成立，这些都要查，要由法庭按证据来判。要拿掉的，只是一种做法，用跟这件事无关的东西，代替对这件事的判断。更不能要求她先证明自己清白，才配讨论她该不该有申辩和复核的机会，那是把程序的结果，当成了进入程序的门槛。

写政府论的时候我说，受问是常态。这一回该被问的，是做决定的那一方：按律师的说法，一个有工卡、没有犯罪记录、开庭日期已经排好的人，为什么要在机场带走，为什么要关着等。这些问题，问得出具体的事，也该有具体的回答。

受害者不必完美，因为保护本来就不是奖给好人的奖品，是给每一个人的底线。我们不必先把她塑造成圣人，才去维护她；也不必在找到一处瑕疵之后，就收回她本来就该有的东西。

text:
🔥智谱昨天刚刚发布的GLM-5.4，真的SOTA了！

其实我们三天前就已经拿到了它的预览版：glm-x-preview。
并且跑完了LobeBench Hard 50的测试（这是从我们@lobehub 真实场景中获得50道Agentic测试题）。
当时看到结果的时候，我还挺惊讶的🤯

因为在这之前我们的榜单上一直有一条非常明显的「国模斩杀线」：GPT-6.1 Terra。
这款@OpenAI 的小模型在我们的测试中，它的Pass3通过率达到了64%（32/50），单次测试成本只有0.025美元💰

这个成绩此前没有任何国产模型能够在我们的测试中超过它。
即便能在能力上和它打平的国产模型，成本也比它的两倍左右。
比如DeepSeek V4 Pro，同样是64%，但单次测试成本是0.06美元，足足是Terra的2.4倍😅

这也导致一个很尴尬的局面：
国产模型虽然已经有不少非常优秀的选手，但在能力和性价比两个维度上，我们一直没有找到一个能够真正突破Terra封锁的模型。

直到这次智谱的GLM5.4出现。

在LobeBench Hard 50的测试中：
- 推理开启：72%，36/50（排名第一
- 推理关闭：66%，33/50（排名第二
推理开启后三次尝试至少成功一次的比例高达96%（快给我们bench解决了）

也就是50道题中有48道至少成功过一次，这意味着它在Pass3的通过率上比此前的国产模型最高成绩直接提高了8个百分点！！

甚至关闭推理之后的成绩，都超过了GPT-6.1 Terra👍，并且几乎在目前我们七个细分领域中都获得了比较不错的结果。

而昨天智谱正式发布了GLM-5.4，这次最有意思的技术变化是他们采用了Loop Transformer架构。

让模型内部的部分网络层能够循环执行，通过增加计算深度来提升推理能力。
根据智谱官方的说法，GLM-5.4在750B参数量级上，实现了接近传统2T～3T参数模型的能力（真的）
同时还新增了视觉理解和更广泛的Coding能力。

我觉得这个模型很值得关注和尝试（就是现在API太慢了，说下个月能缓解）。

毕竟过去我们在实际测试中看到的情况一直是：国产模型在不断追赶，但始终很难同时在能力和成本上突破国外的小模型。

现在至少在能力这一侧，智谱终于把这条线打破了。

至于能不能进一步打破性价比这条线，还得看后续API的正式定价以及更多真实Agent任务中的表现…..

For companies looking to give their staff an ai agent but wanting to enforce fine-grained controls, this is for you. 

In this example, I’ve explore what that could look like under MAS’s SAFR framework by building on top of @LangChain with a custom harness. 

In the custom harness, I’ve set rules that first check if the employee is assigned to the agent before the model runs. The rules also dictate the sellers the agent can interact with, which inference models it can use, and how much it can spend per answer and per chat. 

A purchase that is within policy goes through, above policy requires approval, and one that breaks the rule gets denied. 

Lastly, the harness logs every decision with each paid answer associated with its own USDC transaction on @arc.

Everything done via circle agent stack, where each company have their own agent wallet, paying listed seller in the agent marketplace with USDC on Arc with x402

Check out the sample app linked in the blog below!

text:
Why Democrats are furious that Jensen Huang is back.

Read Hakeem Jeffries' statement carefully. It opens with Jensen. It closes with "ironclad export control legislation" in the NDAA. That's not an accident. That's the tell.

The scandal was never the point. The leverage was.

There are now two camps in AI.

The open camp: build, ship, compete, let a thousand models run on millions of machines.

The regulators: licenses, committees, moratoriums, export regimes. Democrats, Brussels, Bill Gates, the supranational agencies. They all talk about "regulating AI" for one simple reason. They've understood something.

If superintelligence is open, their entire model collapses. The foundations that fund the think tanks, that fund the universities, that manufacture the narrative, that justifies the agenda. An open AI audits all of it in thirty seconds. You can't rule through narrative when anyone can check the numbers.

So it can't be open. They need a toll booth.

Jensen was a problem for them. He sells the shovels, and he refuses to wall off the world. He's on the same line as Elon and most serious builders: AI should serve humanity, not a caste that captured every institution.

For eleven days, they had him out. A scandal, a resignation, a board swearing he'd never return, a headhunter already hired. The people who want compute under lock and key finally had their story.

Today he's back. Unanimous board vote. And within hours, the incoming Speaker is promising a "wide-ranging investigation" and new export laws.

They're screaming because they know what's at stake. This isn't a policy debate. It's a fight to the death.

On one side:
The Democrats.
The globalist bloc.
The supranational machine: the UN, the WHO, Brussels.

On the other:
Free, sovereign nations that want to work together.
That want to compete, fiercely and fairly.

That refuse to be managed by an elite nobody elected.

text:
A few thoughts on what I saw and heard at the @TomorrowXSummit:

1) As many others have noted, cautious and bearish views on the AI trade abounded at the conference among institutional investors (tech people and individual investors were often more bullish). But while I heard a slew of bearish arguments, I thought only two really carried weight given the massive capex cuts priced in by current valuations:

A) That recent $ANT inference revenue and compute estimates suggest we’ll need far fewer GW of compute than what’s currently set to be built.

B) That the recent slowdown in frontier lab ARR growth suggests we won’t see enough revenue generated to justify planned capex.

I think the first argument often relies on questionable numbers – for example, a belief that Anthropic only needs 500MW in inference capacity to produce $100B in revenue, when they might actually be using 1.2-1.3GW today to achieve $80B in gross ARR. And more importantly, it glosses over Anthropic dedicating over 60% of its compute to training -- and why that number might not decline much, if at all, in 2027 -- and why revenue/inference GW numbers probably look very different for rival frontier labs and open-weight models (for its part, OpenAI might be relying on over 2GW in inference to produce ~$70B in gross ARR).

The second bear argument is stronger IMO given that capex might be around $1.5T next year and coding-related growth is slowing down. That said, I think fixating on Q4 OAI/Ant ARR growth overlooks:

A) How OAI/Ant appear to make up just 25-30% of non-China AI compute consumption, after accounting for open-weight and rival proprietary models, internal AI usage among the tech giants, Internet firms and ISVs, local AI deployments, etc.

B) How much (judging by data from OpenRouter, Fireworks, etc.) open-weight token consumption has exploded this year (looks like it’s up well over 10x Y/Y).

C) How early we appear to be in the adoption curve for many non-coding workloads (knowledge/enterprise work, cyber, R&D, etc.).

D) How OAI/Ant’s compute commitments, balance sheets and LLM progress make them unlikely to meaningfully change their capex plans in response to a quarter or two of slow ARR growth.

E) What the cloud giants are both reporting quarterly as well as signaling for the next couple of years ($AMZN guiding for 40%+ AWS growth in both 2027 and 2028, after having previously never guided more than a quarter out, seems especially notable).

F) How past capex booms (railroads, factories, fiber, etc.) typically ended only after years of supply/capacity being well ahead of demand, rather than after supply got just moderately ahead of demand (and of course, even that’s not the case right now).

Meanwhile, though I heard plenty of bearish arguments, I got less pushback than I thought I would for various bullish arguments (related to token/cloud growth, GPU prices, future non-coding adoption, LLM progress, etc.). That, together with all the non-fundamental reasons I heard and overheard for wanting to avoid AI infra (e.g. wanting to lock in gains for the year, not wanting to risk underperforming peers/benchmarks, etc.), made me think a lot of the negativity we’ve seen lately comes from investors being frightened/unsettled by recent price action and thus trying to rationalize that price action ex-post, much as we saw with SaaS and Internet stocks earlier this year.

2) The optimism from people closely monitoring LLM progress about major advances happening next year was notable. I heard multiple predictions that RSI would be achieved next year (one could argue the labs have already achieved partial RSI – see METR’s recent report on the pace of Anthropic LLM advances), as well as that LLMs capable of fully generalizing across robotics tasks/environments would arrive in 2027.

With general-purpose robots/humanoids, it looks like hardware engineering might soon be the biggest remaining obstacle to mass deployment. I’m not currently baking a robotics inflection into my expectations for semis, and stuff like this usually doesn’t transpire overnight, but if/when it does happen, there are obviously big implications for memory, compute, power semis, sensors, etc.

3) Talks with tech/product people about enterprise AI adoption (whether in aggregate or some part of it) made me think we’ll likely see choppy/uneven adoption rates in the short-term -- and such choppiness of course fits with Ant/OAI’s recent ARR growth slowdowns. But they also provided reasons to be optimistic about what happens over longer timeframes.

For now, a relatively small number of early adopters/power users (at the corporate, department/team and individual levels) are driving a huge % of non-coding token growth. And I get the impression that quite a few companies (esp. outside of tech and finance) are still in the trial-and-error stage, trying to figure out which AI projects do and don’t have strong ROIs and how to get the most bang for their buck from their token spend.

At the same time, I heard interesting anecdotes about AI being used to analyze/uncover insights from massive and frequently-changing datasets, accelerate/improve chip design, help office workers handle much larger workloads, etc. AlphaSense said its token consumption is now up to 80T annualized (up 8x since the start of the year), and that’s even though its usage skews heavily towards power users (the top 1% of users for their SuperAnalyst tool were said to consume 28x as many tokens as the median user).

Also, I think it’d be a mistake to assume heavy non-coding token usage remains limited to a small number of early adopters/power users forever. Both because LLM and app developers are well-aware of this issue and trying hard to drive higher usage among normies, and because LLMs have been getting much better lately at handling complex knowledge/enterprise tasks – with bigger advances due next year, especially if RSI arrives – which should pave the way for IT departments and power users fully automating various agentic tasks and workflows.

—

On the whole, the conference strengthened my view that – to the extent one can compare market action during the AI boom to that of the Dotcom era – the recent selloff is more likely to go down as something comparable to the summer/fall of 1998 (when the Nasdaq fell over 30% from mid-July to early October amid a sharp momentum reversal, macro worries and fund blowups, and briefly went red for the year, before the party resumed) than something comparable to the fall of 2000 (when the party ended of good).

That said, in terms of valuations/financials, tech/productivity advances and corporate spending growth, I think the AI boom might have less in common with the Internet/telco boom than with the PC and client/server boom of the late '80s and early/mid ‘90s, when steady declines in the cost of “intelligence” (as defined by CPU MIPS) were more than offset by a combo of user growth and the resource demands of more advanced software and workloads.

Open AIs ideology is fundamentally wrong: 

They have shifted away from creating the best models possible and shifted to creating the best models possible within an efficiency budget. They are trying to create the best models that are efficient to run and use. 

They have made training more difficult by relying on looping to increase intelligence without scaling parameters.  

However, it is too early to do this. All this will result in is getting steam rolled by competitors who don't care about efficiency only power. 

Open AI has released 6.2 sol which is a regression compared to 6.1 sol in many domains. and 6.1 sol was not in chat. 6 sol was. My guess is 6.2 is an efficiency improvement not a capability one meant to serve their mass low paying user base. 

The same goes for their image models which have progressively been feeling more "small model smell". 

My guess is their bet is competitors like Anthropic can't keep subsidisation up forever. an Opus ultra plan is 40x subsidised according to @AdamHoltererer while Open ai subsidises 6.1 sol at 30x, a 10x cheaper model ($1 per task vs $10 per task on AA)

Open Ai is trying to close the gap between API costs and subsidies by creating more efficient models while Anthropic and Google are trying to push the frontier. 

Post IPO it took Uber years to cut the subsidies and start focussing on profitability. 

It is too premature to start focussing on being stingy. 

If your models are: Unlikeable, hard to use, worse at design, worse at coding, worse at strategy, less subsidised.

You are going to lose.

text:
I finished watching The Altruists today with a few people who used to work at Alameda and FTX. We recognised so little beyond the names. My expectations were low, but I’m still surprised it’s this bad.

In short, the story has nothing to do with what actually happened at FTX or Alameda.

The biggest stretch for me was turning the early history of both companies into a story about Sam and Caroline’s relationship. Sam and Gary started Alameda out of their apartment in 2017. Caroline joined a team that was already trading and became one of its senior traders. It wasn’t until 2021 that she and Sam Trabucco became co-CEOs.

The early days of FTX had their own drama. We weren’t sure we could run an exchange, so at first we tried to sell/whitelabel the tech but nobody wanted it. Around Apr/May 2019, we ended up launching it ourselves and raising our seed round. We had more investors interested than we expected, and by the time Caroline moved to Hong Kong, the round was closed. The investment conversation with CZ only happened a few months later.

The conversations the show invented for CZ were particularly hard to watch. FTX started in Hong Kong, and a lot of the people who built it were Asian. I found the stereotypes about Asians and Chinese culture racist.

Even Sam and Caroline felt unfamiliar. Sam was one of the least emotionally expressive people I’ve ever met. His character seems drawn from Michael Lewis’s book and the way he came across in public after the bankruptcy. Caroline reads like someone tried to piece her together from her private blog. She wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.

People had lives before FTX too. Nishad and Claire had been together since college, long before either of them joined the company.

As for effective altruism, Sam cared about it, and so did a few other people at FTX. Most employees had nothing to do with it, and plenty weren’t fans. It had very little bearing on what it was like to work there and nothing to do with why FTX grew.

We kept noticing how little work anyone seemed to do on the show. Back in the days, FTX enforced a strict in-person working culture. We were in the office even during covid unless we were in quarantine. I’d love to know where we found all that time to hang out while building one of the fastest-growing crypto exchanges and keeping it running 24/7.

And when the market suddenly moves or there’s an emergency, you don’t even reach for your laptop? Oooft...

Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.

quoted_text:
The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

text: 这是两股力量的斗争。
author: realdantaik
quoted_text:
昨天还是董事会公开致谢的“临时 CEO”，今天直接撕破脸把枪口对准了公司最高层。

英伟达 CFO Colette Kress 刚刚发表了一篇火药味极浓的公开声明，猛烈抨击公司恢复黄仁勋（Jensen Huang）CEO 职位的决定，甚至直接甩出重话：“没有哪个人能大过公司，也没有哪家公司能自认为凌驾于问责制之上。”

华尔街向来最喜欢“创始人王者归来”的戏码，但机构交易台真正害怕的噩梦只有一个：掌舵的 CEO 和管账的 CFO 在聚光灯下公开决裂。

先把 Kress 声明里的核心指控捋清楚。她对英伟达处理此事的方式表达了极度失望，直言公司不能一边标榜自己建立在卓越、创新和诚信之上，一边却在幕后做出缺乏透明度与问责制的决定。她甚至点破了最敏感的那层窗户纸：“一家公司的声誉并非仅靠其市值或技术成就来建立……恢复詹森·黄的职位并不能自动抹去围绕发生的一切的疑问。”

外行看的是高管内讧，但如果你把这封声明放到华尔街风控模型和现代公司治理史里拆解，里面藏着三个比“谁当 CEO”更致命的信号：

1. 华尔街最怕的红灯：当“签名盖章的人”公开质疑“诚信”

在美股上市公司的权力结构里，CEO 负责画蓝图、定战略、扛估值，而 CFO 则是华尔街机构投资者、审计委员会和 SEC（美国证监会）之间最直接的信用锚点。

自从《萨班斯-奥克斯利法案》（SOX）落地后，美股上市公司的 CFO 必须对财报真实性和内部控制有效性承担个人法律背书责任。正因如此，在美股交易员的算法和风控手册里，一位在任 CFO 公开使用“缺乏透明度”“破坏问责制”“严重质疑诚信”这类字眼炮轰公司决策层，杀伤力远超任何外部做空报告。 一旦管钱的人不再为决策层的程序合规背书，所有大型基金的第一反应都是重新评估公司治理折价。

2. “没有哪个人能大过公司” vs 科技史最残酷的“创始人悖论”

Kress 喊出的“没有哪个人能大过公司”，在教科书和公司法里 100% 正确。但过去四十年的硅谷商业史，恰恰是一部不断打脸这句话的历史。

1985 年，苹果董事会和职业经理人 John Sculley 就是打着“建立规范化现代企业制度、个人不能凌驾于公司之上”的旗号，把乔布斯赶出了苹果，结果公司一路滑向破产边缘，直到 1997 年不得不把乔布斯请回来救火；2017 年，Uber 投资人联手逼退创始人 Travis Kalanick，同样是为了重塑治理与合规文化，但代价是公司整整经历了数年的战略迷失与估值重挫。

这就是科技巨头最无解的死结：职业经理人和财务官守的是“制度底线”，而市场给万亿巨头定价买的却是“天才创始人的不可替代性”。 当这两者正面相撞时，程序正义和商业现实之间根本没有中间地带。

3. 声明里的潜台词：这事还远没到翻篇的时候
仔细读 Kress 的那句表态——“恢复黄仁勋的职位并不能自动抹去围绕发生的一切的疑问，NVIDIA 需要解释其决定”。

这句话说明，此前的风波在公司内部留下了极其严重的信任裂痕，而且核心争议根本没有解决，只是被强行按下了暂停键。按照美股大型蓝筹股的治理惯例，当 C-suite 核心高管把内部矛盾公开化到这个程度，接下来通常只有两条路可走：要么董事会迫于贝莱德、先锋领航等顶级机构股东的压力，成立独立特别调查委员会给出公开交代；要么就是一场不可避免的高管层大换血——而一旦出现“CFO 怒而离职”的后续剧情，二级市场通常会毫不犹豫地先砸盘再说。

一边是撑起万亿市值与技术霸权的创始人，一边是手握财务大权、死守程序与问责底线的首席财务官。

当“市值的狂欢”正面撞上“治理的底线”，如果你是持有英伟达的机构投资人，你认为眼下更应该无条件力挺黄仁勋、把一切质疑交给业绩去消化，还是支持 Colette Kress 追问到底、先把公司内部的透明度和问责制彻底查清楚？

评论区站个队，说说你的判断。

Active asset managers aggressively rotated out of stocks last week:

This measures the average exposure to US equities reported by members of the National Association of Active Investment Managers.

The index has dropped -36 points, or -41%, over the last 2 weeks, marking its largest 2-week decline since November 2023.

This brings the 4-week average of this metric down to 71 points, its lowest since March 2026.

For perspective, the index bottomed at 13 points during the 2022 bear market and 11 points during the 2020 pandemic. 

Last week's sentiment flip spanned from retail to institutions.

Most banks know they need a stablecoin strategy. Few know where to start. Card settlement is the easiest first step.

✔️ Clear payoff. Settle with the scheme 7 days a week and you post less collateral against weekend exposure.
✔️ Nothing changes for cardholders, merchants or your programs. Authorization, scheme rules and daily net settlement stay the same. Only the funding asset changes.
✔️ Light lift. Start with a custodial wallet and a mint and redeem partner. Run it alongside fiat: stablecoins on weekends and holidays, wires on weekdays.

Start small: one program, weekends only. Expand once it runs smoothly.
