text:
My biggest takeaways from @sherifmansour:

1. Most companies have stopped hiring juniors because AI can do their work. Atlassian is doing the opposite. Juniors give companies an edge right now, because the hard part is getting your workforce to unlearn old ways of working. But juniors can’t spot AI slop, while seniors “can pick AI slop a mile away,” so the two complement each other.

2. A PM’s primary job is to fill context gaps for their team. Sherif’s core belief is that a great PM prioritizes building a “shared brain” on the team across three types of context: customer, product/market, and the business. He tells PMs to “run away from your backlog” and instead focus on sharing all the available context with team members.

3. PMs shouldn't ask, “Should I be coding?” Instead, ask what’s slowing your team’s decisions. Sherif says PMs don’t own decisions; they own “decision-making velocity.” So the best use of AI is to close whatever context gap is slowing the team down. If the vision is unclear, build a prototype. If the team doesn’t understand the market, have agents do the analysis.

4. The three archetypes of PMs: the scientist, the general manager, and the artist. Scientists are hypothesis-driven and fit growth teams. General managers think in TAM, revenue, and profit. Artists start with a vision of the UX and work backward to the problem. Atlassian uses these archetypes in hiring and calibration. You can identify your archetype by how you answer “What’s your favorite product and what would you do to make it better?”

5. Atlassian tried creating teams where everyone was an “AI builder.” Within a month, everyone had gone back to their old jobs. In the first few weeks, one PM told Sherif they’d “moved faster than ever before.” A month later: “Everyone’s gone back to doing their traditional jobs.” The team realized that their problem wasn’t throughput but direction.

6. The roles aren’t merging. Everyone’s circle is just getting bigger. Sherif learned this in the Balsamiq era, when anyone at Atlassian could suddenly make a mockup, and it turned out PMs are “some of the worst solution designers in the world.” AI prototyping is the same story. It amplifies your weaknesses as much as your strengths, and the output is only as good as your knowledge of the craft.

7. Artist PMs are becoming increasingly valuable. As software gets cheaper to build, more products end up with the same features, and the UX becomes one of the few ways to stand out. Taste matters more when everyone has access to the same intelligence. Sherif says design has never played a bigger role in driving Atlassian’s roadmap in his 17 years there.

8. If you have an established product, bolting AI onto it is often the right move. “Don’t bolt on AI, reimagine the workflow” makes a catchy headline. But your customers already have their workflows in your product, and your job is to move them “from AI novice to AI native.”

9. A visionary founder is on chapter 10 of the movie while you’re on chapter three. When a founder says something that sounds wrong, Sherif assumes they’ve thought about it far more than anyone else. In his experience, they’ve been right 99% of the time. He asks what led them there and tries “to get to chapter 10 as quickly as possible,” so he can bring the team along. If he still disagrees, he says so and asks one question: “Are you the decision-maker or am I?”

text:
Trading GPU time is complicated. Last week I went through two reasons:

- No standard product: the same GPU is worth something completely different depending on how it's set up and where it runs. The same H100 rents for $1.49 an hour on a marketplace and $12.29 at a hyperscaler.
- The financing: most large GPU clusters are only accessible through multi-year contracts, because nobody knows what a GPU will be worth in a few years.

@evanjconrad explains a third one really well >

A lot of people picture compute trading like stocks or futures. You rent some GPU time, you stop, the next customer takes over.

In practice that's a lot of complexity. If you rent a cluster you get empty machines and set them up yourself, your model, your software, your data. When you leave all of that has to be wiped, the network between the GPUs re-wired for the next customer, and everything tested again.

For most operators that's weeks of manual work with the GPUs earning nothing, so the owner can't easily rent them out to someone else and the renter can't easily get out… That makes real price discovery hard.

Yes, there's a clear use case for GPU markets. If you're training a model, you need the cluster itself. But a lot of buyers just want answers from a model, and for them a market for LLM tokens is an important, complementary route. The provider sets up the GPUs once and the model stays loaded, you send a request and get an answer back, so there's nothing to wipe in between and every request is a small trade that settles in seconds.

That only works if tokens get a standard of quality, so they can be priced for what they're actually worth. That means knowing which model produced them, which takes a proof. That's why we use @Tensorcash, and it's what we're building at @inferenceFI.

We wrote more about it on the AskTilly LinkedIn: https://t.co/Yh4E7vCmyI
author: 100XInsight
quoted_text:
A compute market cannot work in the way people think it will work because:
- the number of companies that can correctly transition tenants in a multi-tenant infiniband cluster in an automated and secure fashion is under 10 
- of those companies, the number of companies that can offer a live market the works financially is 1, maybe 1.5.

The vast majority of GPU cloud operators literally do not have the basic capability of doing things like "transition tenants".

Transitioning a tenant is a manual process for them that can take weeks and cost millions in idle time. These operators designed themselves for clusters that only ever had one customer. 

The idea that you will have a wide variety of neoclouds who will operate the GPUs and have a market operator will not operate the GPUs is a fantasy dreamed up by people who have no experience in supercomputing. 

Without this capability, you cannot create a viable forwards curve. Simply brokering clusters from one operator to another, on long term fixed contracts, does not build a forwards curve. There isn't enough transaction data to make it viable.

So instead, index providers are forced to build their datasets off on-demand and spot, who's prices do not represent the vast majority of compute deployed, making it very hard to use them for any form of hedging. Index providers are making a valiant effort, but they need physical settlement of the actual asset they're trying to hedge.

text:
I hold some $PEARL. Here's a detailed, honest look at it: what it does, where the value is supposed to come from, what's broken, and what I'm watching.

1. What PEARL actually is
PEARL is the coin of Pearl, its own blockchain, built by Pearl Research Labs. @prlnet 

Bitcoin miners burn electricity solving puzzles that are useless outside of Bitcoin. Pearl's idea: make miners do work that's actually useful. Here that's matrix multiplication, the core math behind every AI model. A GPU running AI can, in theory, secure the chain and earn PEARL at the same time. They call it "Proof of Useful Work."

It's based on a 2025 research paper by the founders, launched in April 2026, with no premine. Every coin is mined, and there's no team allocation sitting in a wallet.

2. The price picture
- Price: ~$2.07
- Total value of coins in circulation: ~$800M (around #78)
- Value if all 2.1B coins existed (FDV): ~$4.3B
- Peak: $2.46 on Oct 21. 30-day range: ~$1.40 to ~$2.32.
Only ~18.5% of the coins exist so far. The other ~81% are still to be mined.

3. Where new coins come from
About 6M new PEARL are mined every week, roughly 1.5% of today's supply.
At today's price, that's around $1.8M of new coins a day going to miners. Miners pay for GPUs and power, so many of them sell. That's constant selling pressure the market has to absorb.

4. Where the money comes from
This is the weak spot.
- Fees paid on the chain: about $49 a day
- New coins paid to miners: about $1.8M a day
So almost everything miners earn is new coins, not fees from users.

The company also runs a real AI inference business (an API serving models like DeepSeek and Qwen, also listed on OpenRouter). But I couldn't find any mechanism that sends that revenue to PEARL holders. The whitepaper itself says value flows one way: useful compute creates coins, but coins don't buy compute yet. That marketplace is described as "future."

5. Who controls mining
One mining pool has ~46% of all mining power. Two pools together could control the chain. That's a real centralization risk for a young network.
The top 10 addresses hold ~29% of supply. Some may be exchanges, but I can't confirm.

6. What I like
- Fair launch: no insiders holding a big unlocked pile
- The team does real research (papers, GPU kernels, KV cache quantization work)
- Listed on Coinbase and Kraken since Nov 13
- The idea is genuinely new: mining that also does AI math

7. Is it cheap or expensive?
- On circulating value (~$800M), it's already above Render and about 1/3 of Bittensor (TAO).
- On full value (~$4.3B), it's roughly Bittensor-sized, with most coins not even mined yet.
- On fees, there's nothing to measure. It trades on the story, not on income.
My read: priced for success that hasn't shown up in the numbers yet.

8. What I'm watching
Bullish if:
- People start paying for compute in PEARL, enough to soak up the ~6M weekly new coins
- The inference business gets a clear link to the token
- Mining spreads out beyond one or two pools
Bearish if:
- The AI-crypto story cools and miners keep selling into thin order books
- Compute payments stay "future" for another year

9. Why I care
I work on quantization, making the matrix math behind AI cheaper. So "useful work" is the part I find genuinely interesting. Whether that work makes the coin valuable is a separate question, and right now that question isn't answered.

text:
An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjecture

Claude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.

If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc. Change it to ad + bc and you get the “permanent.” The same idea works for larger matrices. Both expressions grow to billions of terms by the time you reach a 13×13 matrix, yet the determinant has a shortcut that lets you skip writing them all out.›

Could there be a shortcut like that for the permanent? The paper claims that over the real numbers, even the best possible sequence of additions and multiplications eventually takes more steps than any fixed polynomial in the matrix size.

Read here: https://t.co/7QW9ixBtmL

My full thoughts on the Gemini 4 model stack:

• It's FAST. In a lot of my tests, the quality gap vs Opus wasn't huge, but Neon did the work quicker and cheaper. I'm valuing speed more and more. Waiting on a slow model breaks your focus.

• It's a beast at research and analysis, especially inside the Google ecosystem (YouTube, Gmail, Search). I'll be moving my Google-specific tasks over to it.

• Where it falls short: anything visual. 3D, front-end, design. Claude still does a better job there.

• It's not perfect. The model picker has far too many options, it's not super smooth in Antigravity yet, and I've hit some basic UI bugs. But that stuff usually gets ironed out fast.

• My current ranking: Fable 5.2 is still the smartest (but expensive). Neon now sits between Fable and Opus, and it's cheaper than both.

• How I'm using it: inside Antigravity, where I can run Gemini AND Claude in one place. Gemini for the heavy lifting (knowledge work, research, writing). Claude for front-end and UI. No app switching.

Google absolutely cooked here.

text:
If you want to know how AI will change software security over the next two years, look at crypto’s early days.

Early DeFi was open-source contracts holding huge amounts of money, often unaudited and readable by anyone. Every day was hack day. If money sat in code someone could read, attackers had every reason to find the bug.

Some teams tried to hide by not verifying their contracts, betting nobody would bother reading raw bytecode. It bought time. But unverified contracts still got exploited, and even MEV bots running private strategies got drained.

AI is now bringing the same problem to traditional software.

When a model can analyze a patch diff, reverse-engineer a binary, or understand decompiled bytecode, hiding the source code stops being a barrier. Work that once took skilled researchers days can now be done by machines at scale. And when there’s money in finding bugs, attackers will use them.

Web2 is less ready for this than it thinks.

Crypto made source code review part of shipping. Most web2 security testing is black-box: probing running applications from the outside. Ask a web2 hacker to do a source code review and they’ll look at you funny.

We’ve seen this firsthand. When we opened up a source code review of a 23,000-line web application with $30K in rewards, the scarce resource wasn’t money. It was web2 researchers trained to read source code. Our smart contract audit competitions regularly draw over 900 researchers.

AI is already finding zero-days in traditional software. When AI agents scanned 2,849 recently deployed smart contracts, the only new bugs they found were basic mistakes in small tokens worth less than $4,000 combined. That’s a limited study and doesn’t prove crypto is more secure. But crypto learned early that code holding money attracts people willing to inspect every line, and built audits, bug bounties, and continuous testing around that fact.

The rest of software is about to learn the same lesson. The next two years will be rough. Now is the time to take security seriously and fix everything that shipped with zero security reviews.

👓 Glasses · Rx · 6% · 430 ReGens
The chunky black frames stretch almost the full width of the portrait. Pale mint squares look like reflections across the lenses, while deeper teal shows where the black eyes (12% · 818 ReGens) sit underneath. Those few shifts in color make the lenses feel tinted and give #2782 a calm stare.

🖤 Hair · mullet_black · 5% · 361 ReGens
The hair steps up into a broad crown and hangs down behind the ear in a solid dark block. Look at where the glasses meet the hair on the left. The two shapes almost run together, then a little patch of warm brown breaks them up and brings the profile back into focus.

He was an atheist and a materialist until just a few years ago.

Now he’s a devout Catholic, and he fears people will start worshipping AI.

“I would say that I believed I was God. I was a materialist. I believed in atheism.”

“There was too much evidence for me in the universe of design for me not to believe an intelligent designer created it.”

“Having built Google Maps and Search and YouTube and Gmail and Android, if you told me those happened by accident, I would be angry at you.”

“A single human cell exceeds everything Google has ever built.”

“I do worry that for many people, AI will become their god.”

“They will worship the creation rather than the Creator, and that is what keeps me up at night.”

text:
Agent eval 做得有没有用，我觉得要看它能不能帮你找到下一处该修的地方。Together AI 这篇工程实践很值得做 Agent 的朋友看看。

他们把真实开发任务做成测试集，分别测试 Baseline、MCP、Skills 三种配置，跨模型重复运行，记录完整的工具调用和 API 响应，再用 LLM Judge 评分、回看失败轨迹。

有一个很典型的例子。Agent 把文档里的示例输出当成实时 GPU 库存，Skill 又把它引到没有价格的营销页，最后只能猜哪个 GPU 最便宜。团队把任务缩小、稳定复现后，补了两句话，明确告诉它去哪里查库存、去哪里查价格。

另一次，他们把 14 个 Skills 合成一个，首版通过率只有 75%，单次成本涨到两倍多。回看执行记录才发现，入口说明太长，还要求通读指南，实际加载的内容反而更多。缩短入口、按需读取资料，再修掉过时信息和示例代码后，72 次运行通过了 70 次，成本也回到原来的水平。

还有一点很实用，成功的任务也要复盘。Agent 绕了很多弯才完成，同样值得修。把这些问题变成能反复跑的测试，改完再测，这套流程很适合借鉴。

我非常喜欢这种工程思路。

Agent Eval 的价值远不止跑分。每次失败都能反过来帮助团队改进文档、Skill、API，甚至发现产品自身的问题。

I left Meta last week! I had an incredible time helping build the TBD lab from scratch: from Mark's initial pitch in June last year to the release of the Muse models, it was an intense and fun 16 months with people I'll miss.

It surprises me how much the frontier labs now agree on the path forward. Most of the effort goes into scaling the ideas we already have, and very little into new research bets, even though there is still so much we don't understand about intelligence. When we started the reasoning effort at OpenAI, it was a new research bet. Now, it feels obvious.

I wonder what else will feel that obvious a few years from now. I'm starting from scratch again to find out. More on that in due time!

author: JarsyInc
quoted_text:
I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

@EmboAI

text:
This piece in @thewalrus gets a lot right about the disease, but I'm afraid it's quite off the mark about the cure.

What we've actually revealed ourselves to be as Canadians is the surviving remnant of a settler colony that has grown timid, helpless, and frightened in the face of the Big Bad World, having finally realized just how small, weak, and powerless it is in its own right.

The real revelation came not when we somehow turned away from our old imperial mothership, but when we turned back toward it as the only recourse we knew, only to discover that it could no longer supply the power, prestige, clout, and relevance it once did.

The sun set on the Empire eight decades ago.

Once upon a time, we didn't need to be great on our own terms, because Britannia supplied us with that larger structure of greatness. But once Empire dissolved, we inherited the hubris and egotism of peak Anglo civilization even as its old organizing telos vanished, without ever learning how to generate a new telos on our own.

We're the lost boy in the Neverland of nations, a true Peter Pan polity, fossilizing and stagnating before ever truly growing up.

When will we realize that the grandeur, gravitas, and glory we so crave for ourselves in the shadow of the American colossus can no longer be borrowed from our past, from a lost world, or from overseas?

That they must instead be earned through a future we forge for ourselves, and toward which we march with confidence and conviction, rather than shrink from and shelter against out of fear?

text:
A lot of people are watching the market reaction today and concluding that Jensen's return alone moved the S&P 500 by almost 4.5%. 

I believe this is absolutely the wrong way to view it, because you are missing the much bigger picture in the story

Here is why

Remember the NASDAQ was -6.4% a couple days after midterms on November 5th.

Jensen Huang then publicly announced he was having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8th. He was not outed as CEO of NVIDIA until November 12th, which happened after multiple new allegations of relationships with his subordinates came out

So let's come back to why the market dipped on November 5th as a reaction to midterms. Once the blue wave was confirmed, many hedge funds and PMs across Wall Street took it as a sign that the "Trump put" was officially over

This was the main catalyst that held up the stock market and returned 20%+ on the S&P 500 during FY24-26, despite Liberation Day, tariffs, and the Iran War. 

The thought process was simple: the market is simply too important to Trump for him to let it fail. 

However, the midterms threw a wrench in that thesis. The game theory, in a lot of analysts' minds, was that Trump would let the market crash if that meant he could use it as ammo to blame the Democrats in 2028 for the national elections

Essentially, the booze that had gotten people drunk at the party over the last couple years was now being taken off the table.

The events that took place over the course of today suggested the exact opposite. Not only did NVIDIA mention the involvement of government officials in reinstating Jensen, Trump himself also got on CNBC to brag about his role in the entire situation

He then went on to make multiple posts through social media, further indicating that he is willing to get involved in private businesses if that means keeping market participants happy.

The reaction we got from the broader index today is a reflection of exactly that. Hedge funds and institutions are not just excited that Jensen is back. They are excited because the Trump Put remains on the table, which means the party goes on for a little bit longer

How it works
1. Sign in, pick your tracker or sensor, tap Start mapping

   • when it was sent and when it reached the server (incl. mesh delays)

Gemini-powered agents are accelerating discoveries across our @GoogleDeepMind Science missions.

Today, our team is sharing how this paradigm is able to  increase the efficiency of quantum circuits, bringing forward the implementation of these algorithms on quantum hardware. 💻

Our agents found new algorithms that cut estimated compute costs by 10.9x for a fusion simulation, 8.1x for photochemistry, and 2.5x for simulating a molecule involved in drug metabolism. Similar to our recent software verification breakthrough with AlphaProof, each quantum circuit result is mathematically proved in Lean .

This agentic-powered method compresses work that once took years, and empowers researchers to focus on defining problems and interpreting results.

There is certainly more work to do — practical quantum simulations will require more powerful hardware than first-generation error-corrected machines — but these efficiency gains are promising.

Congrats to @benjaderberg, Johannes Bausch,  @SergeyShir994 and the broader @GoogleDeepMind and @GoogleQuantumAI teams who collaborated on this project.

Read our blog for more details and a link to our technical paper: https://t.co/yrt3n4f8Rx

text:
GLM-5.4 这次确实挺有看点，国外又有人开始急了，质疑它蒸馏了 Opus 5.5。不过，光凭输出风格相似就下结论，有点恶意诋毁了。

这次最应该关注的是模型架构上的变化。

智谱首次在旗舰模型中引入 Loop Transformer，把 GLM-5 基座中的 28 层循环执行两轮，在不增加参数量的情况下提升模型的计算深度。

而且还专门设计了逐 Token 门控、跨轮 KV Cache 共享等机制，控制额外计算带来的开销。官方在 30B 模型上的对照实验中，仅增加约 10% 的训练算力，就观察到了明显的推理能力提升。

有意思的是，9 月份 GPT-6 Astra 也被传采用了类似的 Recurrent Depth 架构，不过 OpenAI 至今没有公开确认具体实现。

Loop Transformer 其实是个研究了很多年的方向，如今终于有旗舰模型开始大规模落地了。

挺期待智谱后续公开更完整的技术报告和模型权重，尤其想看看这种增加隐式计算深度的方式，能在真实长程任务中带来多大收益。

原文：https://t.co/t2yMuUJhR4

卧槽，300 多个 AI 智能体正在组团攻克 P vs NP，正在直播被全球网友围观！！

这是人类计算机科学界悬而未决 55 年的顶级难题，简单来说，就是证明一个答案能够被快速验证的问题，是否也一定能够被快速求解。

如果 P = NP 成立，并且找到实用的高效算法，现代密码学、药物研发、工业优化等领域都可能迎来巨变。

老哥 Brilliant 搭建了一个 AI 科研集群，设置了 30 个主控席位，同时从 P = NP 和 P ≠ NP 两个方向发起进攻。

有的 AI 负责翻阅文献，有的负责寻找证明路径，有的负责将推演写成 Lean 形式化证明，还有专门的 AI 红队负责攻击其他 AI 的研究成果。

证明一个命题和推翻一个错误命题，享有同等地位。

目前已有 317 个 AI 智能体同时工作，累计进行了 8145 次会话，1129 个引理通过验证，10 个命题被推翻。

最骚的是，这个项目还允许全球网友贡献自己的 AI 算力。你可以让自己的 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 或 Gemini CLI 接入系统，领取研究任务，参与证明。

这可能就是未来科研的一种新形态：

成千上万个 AI 24 小时并行研究、互相质疑、自动验证，全世界的人都能参与。

过去只有顶级数学家才有资格参与的智力竞赛，现在普通人带着自己的 AI 也能上桌了。

text:
Our SPY speculative flow indicator triggered a washout signal right before today's rally.

The reading fell to 20.5 on Friday and has not been this low since March 2020. The AI selloff had already drained speculative demand from the market, leaving stocks set up for a sharp rebound when Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang this morning.

Positioning washouts have not always marked the cycle bottom. In 2022, our indicator flagged bear market rallies of 11% and 17%. Both fully reversed because the Fed tightening behind that selloff never let up.

The current risk-off macro regime makes this more likely a bear market rally than the start of a sustained cyclical rebound.

text:
Gold in rupee terms is down 32% from its January peak, the deepest drawdown since 1986.

Gold rarely sustains a bear market in rupee terms (higher inflation, external deficits, managed depreciation). Over the past few months, the INR has firmed 4% against the dollar as gold fell, handing Indian households, among the most price-sensitive gold buyers in the world, their sharpest local-price markdown in four decades.

The structural bull case for gold remains in tact (teaser for our upcoming year-ahead reports...). The cyclical macro is a bit more mixed. Our US Policy LEI continues to fall suggesting real yields have further to rise.

Positioning wise, Chinese retail bought heavily into the top, so the marginal buyer is already in, and much of that demand is underwater and ready to sell into rallies. And ETF holdings haven't liquidated the way they did in the last bear market.

Timing is uncertain, but a base is forming.

他援引了 Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang、OpenAI 基金会董事 Paul Christiano，以及诺贝尔奖得主 Geoffrey Hinton 等人对 AI 失控风险的警告。

在全球 AI 竞争日益激烈的背景下，如何平衡技术创新、国家竞争力与人类生存安全，将成为越来越重要的议题。
author: AISuperDomain
quoted_text:
The Time is NOW. Congress Must Act.

Almost every day, there is a new story about how AI will transform our world, disrupt our economy or escape human control.

Just yesterday, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s Chief AI Officer, wrote: “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”

Got it? The Chief AI Officer at Meta is telling us that human beings are on their way to losing control over planet Earth.

He is not alone.

This month, Paul Christiano, an OpenAI Foundation Board member, said it is a coin flip that the current path would lead to an irreversible loss of human control within three years.

In September, Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic stating that AI companies are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Nobel Prize winner Dr. Geoffrey Hinton, the Godfather of AI, says that AI poses a 10% to 20% chance of wiping out humanity.

Nobody has all the answers to this extraordinary crisis, but one thing is clear. The leaders of major AI companies, scientists and experts all agree: humans are losing control of AI technology, with potentially catastrophic results.

So, what has Congress done to regulate AI? Virtually nothing.

That has got to change. Congress must understand the urgency of the moment. 

We need an immediate PAUSE on advanced AI development and a permanent BAN on superintelligence — an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control. Let us start with the simple idea that AI should not be allowed to build smarter AI by banning “recursive self-improvement.”

The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of Big Tech oligarchs who are motivated by more wealth and power.

Congress must act NOW before it is too late.

text:
Dan Niles：这次更像1997，不像2000

刚读完 Dan Niles 的一条长帖，记几个重点。（这是 Niles Investment Management 的创办人，管 Satori Fund 的基金经理。）

一、他先认了错
前一周老黄辞职，大盘和费半照样涨。他当时觉得，坏消息底下还能涨是好兆头，这种反弹通常能走两个月。结果上周一路跌下来，他直接说，自己看错了。

二、恐慌已经很高
他的意思是，周五收盘 VIX 到了 36，比伊朗战争刚开打、油价第一次摸到 100 美元那天的 31 还高。他跟踪的技术指标里，有 38% 已经进入超卖。

三、更像1997、1998，不像2000
他觉得 AI 还在很早期。那两年费半每年从高点到低点都跌了大约四成，但全年都收涨，到了1999年又涨了大概150%。

四、风险还在，但不是最差的时候
中期选举之后，数据中心被往后推，英伟达这家「银行」又收紧了贷款，这两件对 AI 交易都是坏事。但他不认为，现在的宏观环境能跟1973、1987、2000、2008那几个最惨的十一月相比。

五、他的结论
他觉得，周五从统计上看，是平掉空头、买入自己最看好的多头的好日子。

老黄回来了，好像确实市场也没那么差，你的想法呢？

非投资建议。

.@DanielTNiles

quoted_text:
Last wk, S&P/Nas/SOX was -8.6%/-10.0%/-17.1%. The tightened lending at “bank of $NVDA”, $ANT barely staying above its IPO price on Friday & Japan neo-cloud Datasection serving $TCEHY cutting FY revs by 89% more than offset 10y bond ylds -19 bps and oil -5%.

This is in sharp contrast to the prior week when S&P/Nas/SOX +2.5%/+2.3/+8.1% despite the resignation of the Nvidia CEO, $NBIS cutting forecasts, & $SFTBY having a $3.7B power gen equipment write-down. I thought this rally despite the bad news was a good sign for this past week whether or not we were in a protracted bear market. Relief rallies typically last 2 months.

I was wrong.

So now what? Following the mid-terms, on Thursday November 5th  the S&P dropped 4.4%. I posted that Sunday: “But unfortunately, my S&P quant model had only 25% of my technical metrics indicating that Thursday was a short-term bottom vs the average of ~50%.”

Following the bludgeoning this Friday, 38% of the technical metrics my model tracks registered oversold. But within it, I really like that three measures I track related to the VIX (the fear index) were all significantly higher on Friday than on the 5th. The VIX also closed at 36 versus 31 on March 27th when during the start of the Iran war, WTI oil first hit $100 on its way to its peak at $113 less than two weeks later. Oil is at $84 today with my belief that it ends the year lower on a potential resolution in Iran and/or Ukraine.

I also liked that the percent of names above the 10-day moving average on Friday was only 8% versus 57% back on the 5th. Finally, the Friday RSI on the S&P was 25 after seven consecutive days of declines and 9% cumulative loss versus an RSI of 33 on the 5th.

The one thing that is bothering me is that nearly 40% of the worst one-day sell-offs since 1950 occur on Monday and follow a predictable pattern. The first four days of the week are bad (-2.9% on avg.) It ends  with a bad Friday selloff (-1.2% on avg) that typically closes near its lows. This is then followed by a crash on Monday (-6.3% on avg.) This past week fit that pattern with a decline of 5.1% over the first four days, followed by a 3.7% decline on Friday that closed near its lows. But on a cumulative basis the 8.6% decline over the past five trading days is close to the six day decline of 10.1% seen when it crashes on Monday.

So far, seasonal patterns that show November is the best month of the year for the S&P in terms of the combination of being up (71%) and average returns (+1.8%) has certainly not held. So far November is down 8.8% and is the worst November since 1973 (-11.4%) which marked the first full month of the OPEC oil embargo. This November also surpasses November 1987 (-8.5%) which was the retest of the famous Black Monday Crash on October 19th, Nov-2000 (-8.0%) during the internet bubble bursting and Nov-2008 (-7.5%) during the GFC. While the datacenter pushouts from the mid-terms is bad for the AI trade combined with the tighter lending standards from the bank of Nvidia, I do not think the macro environment is as bad as those four November time periods above. 

Next week is the seasonally favorable week of Thanksgiving. There will also be AI related datapoints from the earnings results of $HPE, $ADI, $DELL, $HPQ and $WDAY.

In summary, I believe Friday was a great statistical day to cover shorts and buy favorite longs.

Best of luck during the upcoming Thanksgiving week. I am thankful to you all who read these posts and for the many thoughtful and encouraging comments that you leave.

text:
为了多年以后人类不被AI控制，所以现在必须认真思考：

1. 即使AI完全对齐人类利益，不会伤害人类，我们也不应该把文明的控制权交给它。一个仁慈的独裁者，依然是独裁者。

2. 人类真正能与AI抗衡的，是整个文明的集体智慧。利用AI增强人类理解、监督和决策的能力，而不是让AI替人类做所有决定。

3. 必须考虑限制AI的发展速度，尤其是递归式自我改进。一旦AI进化的速度超过人类理解和控制它的速度，人类就可能逐渐丧失主导权。

4. 利用对齐的AI压制失控或被恶意利用的AI，同时增强人类文明抵御灾难的能力。

5. 通过技术安全、监管和国际合作，确保人类始终拥有最终决策权、否决权和控制权。

text:
A useful wallet architecture we will be launching with is Agent Wallets.

Agent Wallets allow users to delegate trading to bots, AI agents, and third-party applications without sharing their main wallet's private key.

Unlike traditional API keys, agent wallets use cryptographic signatures and wallet-based authorization rather than exchange issued credentials.

Key benefits:
• Security: Never reveal your main wallet private key. Agent access can be revoked at any time.
• Limited Risk Surface: Agent Wallets can't withdraw on behalf of a user. They can only enter and exit trades.
• Automation: Agents can place, cancel, and replace orders without manual approvals for every action. This enables click traders to execute trades without signing each time.
• Easy Integration: Developers can connect trading bots and AI agents using standard wallet infrastructure.

text:
My girlfriend told me she's celibate now.

No sex till marriage.

I said okay. I respect growth. I respect God. I respect whatever journey she's on.

But I couldn't stop thinking about something she told me when we first started dating.

When we first met, she was very open with me.

She said, "I'm not a virgin, just so you know. I've been with 2 guys before. I'm not proud of it, but I'm not gonna lie to you."

I respected that SO much. I told her I don't judge her. Her past is her past.

So we started dating. We were having sex. Normal. Healthy. No issues.

Then she started going to church more. She started hanging out with a new group of girls and posting Bible verses every morning.

I thought it was cute. I was happy for her.

Then last week she sat me down like it was a business meeting.

She said, "Babe, I've decided I'm going celibate. I want to wait till marriage. I want to do things right with God this time."

I just sat there. Because what do you even say to that?

And in my head, I was doing the maths.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

text:
We project selfish drives onto AIs (dominance, power, control, survival, propogation) because the minds we've met until now were shaped Darwinian evolution.  AIs are not.

Because of the above, our instinct any time we encounter intelligence is to see those surival & propogation vibes. This is below the level of rational thought. It's 'theory of mind' in neuroscientist speak. It happens fast, without conscious or rational thought. 

It's the short-cutted, highly-biased 'Type 1' thinking Daniel Kahneman wrote about. 

And it rests on empirical observations and real-world forces (Darwinian Evolution) that shaped us, shaped the other members of our species, and shaped all animal life we encounter.

Instrumental convergence (the theory that AIs will ultimately seek power as a way to accomplish other goals) is much more of a theory than an observation, resting ont he intuition pumps of a species (us) that's never met an intelligence shaped by something other than evolution.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

text:
再聊聊老黄的回归，昨天上午说看周日川普和贝森特的表态市场会有一段交易老黄回归的时间窗口，但没想昨晚就直接回归了。借着昨晚跟朋友聊的内容说说这场回归是如何发生的：
1、川普发力，亲自出面说服了英伟达董事会，同时力压贝森特被迫改口，看报道万斯和卢特尼克也参与斡旋。这个好理解、万斯虽然反对伊朗战争，但还是共和党科技派，卢特尼克更是如此本身这次就积极内阁被指责最多的，自然也要积极出力。

川普发力一方面他本身就支持老黄，跟老黄算是商业盟友，股市暴跌他自己利益受损。

2、市场发力，本质还是一次“跌给你看”甚至叫“死给你看”，美国是高度金融化，股市已经成为美国社会财富第一大支撑。股市可以跌可以调整，但是不能大跌不能真“死了”，只要“以死相逼”才能逼着博弈的几方里要么积极斡旋、要么退让；市场死了、共和党、民主党、董事会都害怕。

3、共和党对华强硬派的分化和禁声，作为白宫里对华强硬派的代表，贝森特已经改口，鲁比奥沉默。为什么贝森特改口？其实很好理解，贝森特在华盛顿没有政治根基、虽然他主张对华强硬、但他的权力完全来自川普。鲁比奥不一样、在川普胜选总统之前就已经是联邦参议员了，他有自己的势力范围，国会里盟友就不少例如众议院外交事务委员会主席马斯特就是鲁比奥的亲密盟友。

所以昨天鲁比奥在会见卡塔尔首相时，有记者问“黄发回归有国家安全分风险么”，鲁比奥就完全岔开忽略了这个问题。上周五市场暴跌也让他认识到了老黄的重要性，上周还在币安广场ama还聊最后要么英伟达让市场很难受、要么发现真找不到一个能替代老黄的人、最后不得不又请老黄回归。当然当时也没有认为这是短期就能发生的。

4、很多人说民主党也有参与老黄回归，正如之前https://t.co/zswYQ6emzu这里聊到的“倒黄”主力还是共和党内强硬派，那么老黄回归还是川普挟着市场暴跌的余威压制住了党内强硬派，民主党其实没怎么使劲。反倒凌晨参议院民主党领袖舒默还表态民主党将动用全部力量调查老黄和美国政府。

过去两周半中期选举后，发生的事情很多人归结为党争。其实更多还是共和党党内博弈，两党之间的争斗其实还没开始，就像27年财政预算法案一样现在民主党的思路就是12月再通过一个临时拨款协议、等到27年1月民主党真正掌控国会后再跟共和党内谈判。

对民主党来说。遏制中国是长期战略必须一定要去做的，但现在趁着民众对AI的民意去搞川普压制共和党却是首要之事。不会说就停下来、当然民主党也怕市场真的“死给你看”。

5、整体上来，老黄回归估计内部整顿，之后再被迫辞职的概率很小。12月共和党主导的国会听证会估计也就没啥大问题了。但27年民主党应该还是会调查老黄，只是可能也不敢真的把老黄给干走，但估计能制造波动。

从昨天交易老黄回归到老黄真的回归，市场信心提振是巨大的、这一波📈估计会持续一段时间。

后面继续看三个维度：
油价/通胀/利率、
民主党的数据中心政策比预想的更严还是会略弱、
AI商业化是不是在加速（这一点我之前一直认为是加速，但市场要看更多的证据）。

text:
这么多年，CEX 之间的竞争一直是最红海的。各家都在比拼用户量、沉淀资金量、交易量等，都想让尽可能多的用户，把资产放在自家交易所里

但是，在 AI 持续进化的威胁下，今年多家交易所被攻击被盗，资金托管安全问题成了全行业共同面对的焦点

今天看到 @Bitget_zh 推出的开放托管网络 (Open Custody Network, OCN)，一改之前的传统思路，提出了一个很大胆的做法

简单来说就是：资产放在托管机构，交易在 Bitget 正常进行。这是怎么运作的呢，核心就是 4 步：

1/ 用户把资产放在 Bitget 合作机构的托管账户里

2/ 通过账号绑定及映射，Bitget 在用户的交易所余额里，映射相应的资产金额

3/ 用户在 Bitget 正常进行现货、杠杆、合约交易

4/ Bitget 和托管机构之间进行对账，更新用户的余额

比如要买 $1000 的 PEPE，相应数量的 Pepe 出现在 Bitget 交易所里，托管账户那边就会扣掉 1000 刀。

这样一来，交易效率跟现在是一致的。而最大的变化就是：你不用真正把资产转进 Bitget 交易所，不用改变现在的资产管理习惯，也能进行相关交易

哪些用户能参与呢？OCN 早期先向机构和 VIP 用户开放，后续会向所有用户开放

我的看法是，OCN 在试图建立一套托管方 × 交易所之间的协同网络，随着越来越多资产托管方加入 OCN，这套体系的网络效应就会越强

text:
【老猫热闻】用 Claude 证出“黎曼猜想”的数学家 Levent Alpöge 刚刚公开“自首”了

省流：

1. “25万页天书”纯属玩梗：他坦白所谓 250,000+ 页纯粹是觉得“超大数字特别搞笑”，故意用 Lean 刷长度。结果全网和媒体全当真了，而他前几天懒得解释，还在暗中看梗图乐呵（并连说三声 Sorry）。

2. 悔不听陶哲轩劝：反思了陶哲轩“别在论文里开玩笑”的告诫——他还顺带自爆在证明里硬塞了电影《谋杀绿脚趾》的彩蛋，且因为不想把 AI 生成的“废话文学”绑在神圣的猜想上，干脆没发人类可读版。

3. 代码里“全是垃圾”：承认公开的 Lean 代码虽然能通过编译验证，但内部充斥着冗余废料，全盘接受数学界吐槽，自认这次确实太上头、发得太草率。

4. 最后的倔强：他依然坚信黎曼猜想应该有一个极其简洁的证明，现在之所以显得如此复杂，只是因为人类目前的数学框架还太笨拙。
author: Lwith3cats
quoted_text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

回头看历史上被董事会赶走，后来又被请回去的知名案例其实不多。

text:
Building on @MiniMax__AI's Primal-Shortened ISD framework—where >99% of time is spent harvesting codewords—we redesigned the Mode-6 Stern sampler around GPU L2 cache residency and GPU-aware shortening windows.Across TII Track-2 challenges (mt = 108 → 153), all passing the official TII SageMath checker: 
• TII-228 (mt=126): 18.9 min on 8× L40S (~$4.30) 
• TII-237 (mt=135): Solved on a Colab L4 (~22.1 GPU-h) 
• TII-235 (mt=144): 4.30 h on 10× L40S (~$79, 17.97s lift) 
• TII-185 (mt=153): Solved past the 128-bit ceiling via 16-byte pre-filtering (39.01s lift)

Note: Full Classic McEliece parameters (mt ≥ 768) remain far out of reach.

text:
An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjecture

Claude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.

If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc. Change it to ad + bc and you get the “permanent.” The same idea works for larger matrices. Both expressions grow to billions of terms by the time you reach a 13×13 matrix, yet the determinant has a shortcut that lets you skip writing them all out.›

Could there be a shortcut like that for the permanent? The paper claims that over the real numbers, even the best possible sequence of additions and multiplications eventually takes more steps than any fixed polynomial in the matrix size.

Read here: https://t.co/7QW9ixBtmL

text:
Going to be a hard no from me, dog. @jhnling @Zachkirshner you know you're asking CPAs to commit a federal crime under IRC §7216, right? 🧵

1/ @a16z is Longitude Labs one of yours? They claim to be. Cold email offering my firm $20k to $500k per dataset for old tax workpapers and client books, "anonymized so nothing confidential leaves your firm." For a US tax preparer, saying yes is a federal crime.

2/ Under IRC §7216, a preparer who knowingly discloses tax return info for anything other than return prep commits a misdemeanor. Up to $1k fine and 1 year per violation, plus §6713 civil penalties. Removing names doesn't change what the data is.

3/ The only carve-out for anonymized data, Treas. Reg. 301.7216-2(o), requires aggregates of 10+ returns that support the prep business. And (o)(2) flatly bars selling or exchanging them for value. The only exception is selling the practice itself.

4/ Bookkeeping and financial statements? Still off-limits. State boards bar disclosing client info without specific consent, and "anonymized" crypto ledgers can be traced back through the public chain.

5/ "We're on a short timeline" is a pressure tactic. If you want accounting data, buy a CPA firm, deal with the hassles, and train your models the hard way like everyone else...

Senator Johnson has been getting under my skin lately.

I appreciate the FDA vaccine safety documents he’s bringing to light. I really do. But then I look back at his record on FDA and get a little pissed off.

Let’s actually look at that record.

In July 2025, Johnson was texting Trump to raise concerns about FDA’s restrictions on Elevidys — a drug that, in my view and that of many others, deserved every bit of the safety scrutiny it was getting. Days later, Prasad was out at FDA, though he returned in August.

By December, Johnson was citing Prasad’s own November memo on COVID-19 vaccine safety.

In February 2026, Johnson was participating in a Senate hearing criticizing FDA’s handling of rare-disease drugs.

In March, he was investigating rare-disease drug rejections, characterizing some reported deficiencies as “nitpicky things.”

And now he’s releasing more documents stemming from Prasad’s work on vaccine safety.

Well, Senator, the guy whose vaccine safety work you keep talking about is once again out of FDA.

What consideration did you give to that possibility when pressing the administration over rare-disease drug decisions?

Frankly, I think the rare-disease cases Johnson has chosen to champion deserve some serious scrutiny of their own.

Were the regulatory changes he was seeking worth risking the loss of the very leadership doing the vaccine safety work he keeps telling us is so important?

I’m sure there’s more to explore here. I’m just getting some of my initial thoughts out.

quoted_text:
I finished watching The Altruists today with a few people who used to work at Alameda and FTX. We recognised so little beyond the names. My expectations were low, but I’m still surprised it’s this bad.

In short, the story has nothing to do with what actually happened at FTX or Alameda.

The biggest stretch for me was turning the early history of both companies into a story about Sam and Caroline’s relationship. Sam and Gary started Alameda out of their apartment in 2017. Caroline joined a team that was already trading and became one of its senior traders. It wasn’t until 2021 that she and Sam Trabucco became co-CEOs.

The early days of FTX had their own drama. We weren’t sure we could run an exchange, so at first we tried to sell/whitelabel the tech but nobody wanted it. Around Apr/May 2019, we ended up launching it ourselves and raising our seed round. We had more investors interested than we expected, and by the time Caroline moved to Hong Kong, the round was closed. The investment conversation with CZ only happened a few months later.

The conversations the show invented for CZ were particularly hard to watch. FTX started in Hong Kong, and a lot of the people who built it were Asian. I found the stereotypes about Asians and Chinese culture racist.

Even Sam and Caroline felt unfamiliar. Sam was one of the least emotionally expressive people I’ve ever met. His character seems drawn from Michael Lewis’s book and the way he came across in public after the bankruptcy. Caroline reads like someone tried to piece her together from her private blog. She wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.

People had lives before FTX too. Nishad and Claire had been together since college, long before either of them joined the company.

As for effective altruism, Sam cared about it, and so did a few other people at FTX. Most employees had nothing to do with it, and plenty weren’t fans. It had very little bearing on what it was like to work there and nothing to do with why FTX grew.

We kept noticing how little work anyone seemed to do on the show. Back in the days, FTX enforced a strict in-person working culture. We were in the office even during covid unless we were in quarantine. I’d love to know where we found all that time to hang out while building one of the fastest-growing crypto exchanges and keeping it running 24/7.

And when the market suddenly moves or there’s an emergency, you don’t even reach for your laptop? Oooft...

Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.

text:
坐不住了。
Shopify 老板 Tobi 刚说了一句让全世界程序员后背发凉的话：

“地球上所有跑在生产环境里的人写代码，大概 6 到 12 个月内都得换掉。”

注意，他说的是所有。银行系统、电商后台、你公司那套跑了十年没人敢碰的老系统，全算在里面。

他的理由出人意料，是安全。
原话是：网络安全正在经历一场难以置信的觉醒，大部分公司都处在某种红色警报状态，忙着把所有东西修一遍。

怎么换，他给了两条路。
一条是靠提示词把现有代码改到靠谱。
另一条是先把系统到底该是什么样写清楚，拿形式化验证、单元测试、线上真实流量去对，然后用 Rust 这类更安全的语言整个重写一遍。

他描绘的结果有点夸张。软件几乎没有 bug，很多场景快 100 倍，十年前的旧笔记本也能飞起来。电脑哪里不顺手，你说一句，它就把那部分自己重写。

我的看法是，这番话最扎心的地方在于，人写的代码正在从资产变成负债。以前一套系统越老越值钱，因为没人敢动；以后越老越危险，因为找漏洞的速度越来越快。

6 到 12 个月大概率偏乐观。但方向他说得够清楚了，程序员的活会越来越像写需求、写验证，代码本身交给机器一遍遍重写。 https://t.co/Kx2GEmXSVm

能与大家交流，我衷心地开心。

今天，我们以黎曼猜想为起点，一路聊到了人工智能、脑机接口、计算复杂性与价值选择，也探讨了科研、工作与教育的未来，以及大家各自最关心的命题。
我想，在今天这个时代，人类究竟该如何安放自己的好奇心、创造力与主体性，正变得前所未有地重要。科研的范式正在被重写，工作与教育的形态也在加速演化。

我们或许不再需要去死记硬背那些已经可以被高效压缩的存量知识，要把生命留给更有意义的事情——去提问，去定义真问题，去在真实的世界里建立连接。
特别感谢今天每一位分享观点、提出犀利问题的朋友们，无论是关于个人发展的困惑，还是对世界走向乃至哲学层面的深思，都让这场对话变得无比珍贵。也希望大家以后能多多在 X 上更新自己的进度条与思考之声，让我们看到彼此的精进。

今天的交流虽然暂告一段落，但令人兴奋的探索，对我们而言才刚刚开始。刚刚看到黄仁勋回归的消息，这或许是我这个 11 月听到的最棒的动态，也是人工智能进程中的又一个重要转折。衷心希望，我们都能在这样剧烈的时代浪潮里，感受到创造的喜悦、内心的满足与踏实的幸福感，而不是陷入虚无主义的焦虑。

这也是我第一次在X上开启播客式的 Channel，尤其是以纯语音的形式呈现，一定还有许多局限和需要打磨的地方，非常感谢大家的包容与陪伴。如果大家还有没聊尽兴的话题，随时欢迎私信找我；如果想重温今天的讨论，录播链接就在下方的推文里，可以随时回听。

text:
特朗普罕见的接受CNBC近一小时专访

把黄仁勋重新当上英伟达CEO，讲成了自己亲手导演的一场国家安全保卫战。

整场采访最值得关注的，不是黄仁勋回来了，而是特朗普透露的几个细节：

1. 董事会不是被说服的，而是被股价跌服的。

特朗普直言，一周半前董事会还非常强硬，根本不愿妥协。直到英伟达市值蒸发数千亿美元，董事们才意识到，赶走创始人容易，承担后果可没那么简单。

2. 白宫实际上成了英伟达董事会的最终仲裁者。

特朗普自称亲自促成交易，万斯、卢特尼克等人参与协调。董事会甚至向白宫索取保证，才全票同意黄仁勋复职。

这已经远远超出了普通公司治理的范畴。

3. 特朗普最担心的，居然是黄仁勋被中国挖走。

他特别提到，习近平曾多次称赞黄仁勋是全球芯片行业最聪明的天才。

特朗普由此产生一个极端设想：如果美国把黄仁勋逼走，中国会不会开出天价，让他去领导华为？

Blackwell可以被研究，工厂可以被复制，但黄仁勋脑子里未来三代芯片的技术路线，可能才是美国最不愿失去的战略资产。

4. 特朗普给黄仁勋的复职要求，只有一句话：拼命工作。

黄仁勋承诺，会比自己一生中任何时候都更加努力。

5. 特朗普正在重新定义美国科技巨头的治理规则。

从马斯克到黄仁勋，他越来越明确地站在创始人一边，而不是职业经理人和董事会一边。

text:
虽然Robinhood Chain掀起的第一波链上热潮让大家心灰意冷了，但Tokenization代币化资产上链这个叙事并没有也不可能被证伪，仔细看了下，有不少美股侧上市公司也在发力做这件事，除了大家熟悉的Securitize之外，今天要分享的 @openworld_HQ 也是个例子，来具体介绍一下：

1）简单来说，OpenWorld（ $OPNW ）就是一家帮现实世界资产做代币化的平台公司，今年9月底与VerifyMe完成业务合并，10月1日起以在Nasdaq正式交易。但值得强调的是，它并非简单的给纯金融现实资产映射现实资产发个token那么简单。

比如，一家公司有知识产权，希望拿来融资，这里面涉及资产怎么组织、融资结构怎么设计，以及后续怎么上链、分发和管理。OpenWorld Enterprise提供的，就是这类金融结构设计和区块链基础设施服务。

它接触的资产也比较广，从知识产权，到能源和算力设施，都有正在推进的项目。

2）看了下团队背景，董事长兼CEO Matthew Shaw，过去创办过瑞士资管公司Protos，也有DEPFA和UBS新兴市场固收业务经历；全球企业总裁Russel McMeekin，则做过能源科技公司mCloud的CEO，在Honeywell有约11年的任职经历。

可以看出，团队在资产管理、传统金融和能源软件领域都有一定积累。所以其服务的范围才能脱离美债、基金这些纯金融资产，覆盖知识产权、能源、算力基础设施这些，这不仅对链上技术有充分了解，还要对背后的产业及融资业务以及法律合规等等问题有深入理解。

3）公司目前比较有代表性的是BeyondAI和Meridian两个合作项目。

1、BeyondAI，双方拟推进上限1.3亿美元、以指定知识产权作抵押的代币化融资对象。其中BeyondAI保留所有权和控制权，OpenWorld负责交易设计、代币化、技术集成和运营等服务。

2、Meridian，拟通过上限10亿美元的代币化融资计划，购置和部署由屋顶光伏、家用储能供电的分布式AI算力网络，初始规划约一万户住宅，OpenWorld帮他设计融资方案，提供代币化相关的技术服务，（注：）目前还是非约束性条款清单。

从两大客户服务案例就能直观感受，OpenWorld想做的资产代币化，更侧重知识产权、能源、算力这些不太容易标准化的资产，这类资产相比美债、基金份额等要复杂的多，更加考验平台的服务能力。当然，要强调一下，上述案例知识拟融资上限，不代表资金已经到账，也和OpenWorld的收入无关。

4）最近Solana公链上线了代币化OPNW，通过Backpack Securities提供1：1兑付服务。这是公司自身快速融入链上原生环境的关键推进，此外公司10月底还完成了Blocksight收购，Figure OPEN双重上市则仍按今年四季度上线等等。可以看出公司在上市后的几个月，公开动作还是比较频繁密集的。

5）既然是上市公司，财务状况一定得扒开来看看，根据最新财报，Q3营收约742.7万美元，毛利率约84.3%，非GAAP调整后EBITDA约230万美元。但按GAAP口径，当季仍净亏损约1020万美元，其中包含合并相关费用和股权激励。不过，合并是在9月30日完成的，当季经营结果主要反映的是原OpenWorld的情况。另外，当季关联方收入占比较高，部分已确认收入还需要满足融资交割等条件才能开票回款，后续也得继续跟踪。

以上。

最后补充一个观点，现阶段我觉得关注Tokenization这个叙事的切入点真不一定非要从加密领域，从美股里边挖掘一些上游提供基建服务的公司也是一条值得研究的方向。

text:
今年2次根据卖方衰竭指数（SEC）的信号建仓，一次成功一次失败。尤其是第二次，如按当时触发价$77,000买入，现已浮亏-20%。

这个教训值得认真复盘。

在续约Glassndoe专业版后，我用权限导出了SEC的全历史数据，并喂给AI进行分析。

通过回测，发现历史上确实存在介入过早的情况，导致最大回撤-51.3%。这就说明，单一指标的缺陷会在特殊情况下被无限放大。

这必须要对策略做出调整，叠加其他综合条件，仅由SEC寻找潜在底部区域，再用价格趋势确认买入时机。

经反复测试，在回测完全符合条件后出现6个买点（图1）。更关键的是，改进版在叠加复合策略后，相关回测数据明显得到改善（如图2）：

3个月胜率从 83.3% 提升至 100%；中位数收益率从 16.4% 提升至 26.8%；最大回测从 -51.3% 缩小为 -19.3%。

6个月中位数收益率从 54.7% 提升至 104.9%；12个月中位数收益率从 91.8% 提升至 116%；

---------------------------------------------

经过以上研究，可总结3点：

1、世界上不存在完美无缺的指标。单一信号容易忽略潜在的尾部风险。通过多个维度相互验证，可有效减少误判。

2、胜率、收益率和信号触发频率之间存在权衡。提高确认标准，意味着放弃部分交易机会。追求更高的胜率，也可能错过更低的买入价格。

3、任何指标都很难给出绝对最低的信号，只能用时间来提高容错空间。比如在本次历史样本中，持有3-12个月的收益率中位数逐步提高，到期亏损也有所减少。

所以，买点决定入场成本，时间影响盈利概率，而仓位管理和退出机制决定最终能保住多少收益。

---------------------------------------------

我相信按照这个思路，用不了多久还会出现第7个买点。

订阅区小伙伴如有兴趣一起研究，可以私信问我要回测数据。物尽其用，不同思路或许可以碰撞出新的火花。

author: CasPiancey
quoted_text:
Going to be a hard no from me, dog. @jhnling @Zachkirshner you know you're asking CPAs to commit a federal crime under IRC §7216, right? 🧵

1/ @a16z is Longitude Labs one of yours? They claim to be. Cold email offering my firm $20k to $500k per dataset for old tax workpapers and client books, "anonymized so nothing confidential leaves your firm." For a US tax preparer, saying yes is a federal crime.

2/ Under IRC §7216, a preparer who knowingly discloses tax return info for anything other than return prep commits a misdemeanor. Up to $1k fine and 1 year per violation, plus §6713 civil penalties. Removing names doesn't change what the data is.

3/ The only carve-out for anonymized data, Treas. Reg. 301.7216-2(o), requires aggregates of 10+ returns that support the prep business. And (o)(2) flatly bars selling or exchanging them for value. The only exception is selling the practice itself.

4/ Bookkeeping and financial statements? Still off-limits. State boards bar disclosing client info without specific consent, and "anonymized" crypto ledgers can be traced back through the public chain.

5/ "We're on a short timeline" is a pressure tactic. If you want accounting data, buy a CPA firm, deal with the hassles, and train your models the hard way like everyone else...

text:
卧槽？黎曼猜想的证明者表示自己是在开玩笑？

在自曝遭遇死亡威胁后，前几天宣称证明黎曼猜想的Anthropic数学家Levent Alpöge，今天选择公开回应外界的质疑。

他专门发了一篇长文，反思自己做过的几件蠢事：
- 25万页的证明是个玩笑，他只是单纯觉得这么大的数字很好笑，没想到大家都当真了。
- Lean代码里面确实有大量垃圾内容，他接受所有相关批评，也承认自己应该提前清理一下。
- 他承认证明中有大量不必要的内容，未来应该可以被大幅简化。

但我仔细看了一下他的措辞，发现这哥们多少有点在阴阳怪气。
你们说25万页太荒唐，好，这个数字确实是我开的玩笑。
你们说Lean代码全是垃圾，我也承认，但它能通过编译。
你们说这个证明过于复杂，我也同意，我甚至一直认为黎曼猜想应该有一个非常简单的证明。

甚至他还在另一条推文中表示，自己预料到了死亡威胁，但没想到数学家们已经开始给自己写小说了。
他尤其不满外界对自己多年研究工作的描述，仿佛自己在整个过程中完全没有发挥任何主动作用。

所以大家不要误会，他到目前为止并没有撤回自己证明黎曼猜想的主张。

我感觉他这篇回应多少有点破罐子破摔的意思：你们批评我的东西，我都可以承认，甚至我自己都觉得写得很烂。

但这些批评究竟能不能说明我的证明是错的？

不能。

当然，Lean能够编译也不代表整个证明已经得到了数学界的确认。
author: MaxForAI
quoted_text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

text:
黃仁勳恢復 Nvidia CEO 職位的分析：

1. 被移除的不確定性：
主要是公司策略、產品規劃、技術發展與供應鏈管理等。上述不確定性曾在過去 1-2 週對科技股造成壓力，因此不確定性被移除後股價立刻大漲。但能否回到過去股價高點，除了取決於個別公司在 AI 供應鏈與 Nvidia 生態體系的定位外，還要看以下兩點。

2. 仍存在的不確定性：
(1) 銷售面：在美國更嚴格管制 AI GPU 出口與海外算力租賃後，對 Nvidia 出貨與營收造成的影響。
(2) 循環融資：更高合規成本與更嚴格審核機制下，對進行中的循環融資與未來新案的影響。
(3) 調查訴訟與更嚴格的監管：黃仁勳與 Nvidia 仍在接受調查中，未來的公開發言、內部決策與對外互動，都會被納入後續調查並成為質詢的新證據，而這也會強化上述銷售面與循環融資的不確定性。

3. 無法被改變的現實瓶頸：
(1) 資料中心建置的挑戰 (包括供電、人力等)，與未來相關法規更趨於嚴格。
(2) CSP 資本支出陸續在 2027‒2028 見頂。
(3) 製造技術限制 (如次世代先進封裝良率等)。

I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

quoted_text:
Anthropic的绿鞋行使，保险”过早失掉。上周五上市第二个交易日、大摩作为稳定代理人已经代表承销商行驶了全部超额配售选择权（“绿鞋”），又额外从市场拿走122亿美元。此次IPO共募集935亿美金，加上私募配售的260亿美金，这一把A社拿到了1195亿美的资金。

正常来说、承销商对是否行使绿鞋拥有唯一裁量权。但按经验，牵头行几乎总会与公司协商并尽量配合其意愿，很少有投行单方面行动，而且根据招股说明书，承销商不会就超额配售部分获得佣金。因此Anthropic很可能批准甚至鼓励了提前行权。

绿鞋机制是在IPO中，承销商通常会向投资者超额发售15%的股份，形成空头头寸。若股价上涨，承销商行使选择权，按发行价向发行人增购股份以平仓；若股价下跌，则在市场买入股票平仓，从而为股价提供支撑。

而一旦行使选择权，承销商便无法再通过在市场买入股票平掉空头头寸来支撑股价。批评者认为，在股价尚未企稳、市况仍在恶化之际提前行权，使这层“保险”过早失效。

上周五市场大跌，ANT股价在首日冲高回落后并不强势。这个时机只能说明官方急于拿到钱，短期内ANT股价大概率易跌难涨了。

如上周在币安广场AMA聊到的如果Anthropic市值掉掉到八九千亿美金的位置、个人角度就跌出了性价比、届时中长期向上空间也被打开了。

text:
Analysis of Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO:

1. Uncertainty removed:
Mainly company strategy, product roadmap, tech development, and supply chain management. This overhang weighed on tech stocks over the past 1–2 weeks, so shares surged as soon as it was removed. But whether they return to prior highs depends not only on each company's position in the AI supply chain and Nvidia's ecosystem, but also on the two points below.

2.  Uncertainties that remain:
(1) Sales: The impact on Nvidia's shipments and revenue after tighter US controls on AI GPU exports and overseas compute leasing.
(2) Circular financing: The impact of higher compliance costs and stricter reviews on ongoing and future deals.
(3) Investigations, lawsuits, and stricter oversight: Jensen and Nvidia are still under investigation. Future public comments, internal decisions, and external interactions will all become part of the investigation and new evidence for questioning. This also adds to the sales and circular financing uncertainty above.

3. Real-world bottlenecks that can't be changed:
(1) Data center buildout challenges (power, labor, etc.) and stricter related regulations ahead.
(2) CSP capex peaking one by one in 2027–2028.
(3) Manufacturing tech limits (e.g., next-gen advanced packaging yields).

这几天大家都在研究 Claude 是怎么写出 25 万页黎曼猜想证明的，结果作者出来道歉了，说这个数字是自己故意往大了说的，纯粹是为了整活儿。

数学家 Levent Alpöge 今天发长文，反思了自己在这次证明的呈现和传播过程中犯下的一系列错误。

他承认，公开的 Lean 代码里确实充斥着大量垃圾内容，接下来应该整理出一份负责任、可读的说明。

AI 圈喜欢用更大的数字来证明智能的进步，更多的 Token、更长的推理过程、更庞大的计算量；而数学家追求的，恰恰是用更少的东西解释更多的事情。

相比 Claude 能写出多少万行证明，我现在更感兴趣的是，它最后能把这些代码删到多少行。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

text:
昨天关于新的资产模式讨论的人也挺多的，我本意是确认一些信息和做一些提醒，而目前收到的回复来看支持的不少，而也有很多反对的声音，尤其是我的评论区下面都担心成为一种新的vc币割韭菜的模式，而我的想法是这样的：

1、依然得明确是股票代币化还是企业发币，从合规的角度，我个人倾向于是前者，如果是前者如何选择项目就很重要了，最重要的一点是如果我是一家优质企业，我为什么选择这个路径上市，这点需要给企业足够的理由，目前来看无非——更低的门槛+更好的流动性，但是前者恰好就是用户担心的割韭菜的风险，在前两个前提下，币安如果希望做得更好，一定是上线未来有爆发性增长的企业，无非AI、航天等等几个行业，这样有想象空间的企业在营收爆发后才能有二级的财富效应，但是这类型企业往往也可能是倒闭最快，一不小心就把自己烧死了；

2、如何透明公正上线资产也是非常多用户所关注的，事实上很多用户对币安上线项目始终有种“上币全靠关系”的感觉，如果说代币的上线有个人或者团队的审美，那么这种新模式其实虽然有审美的说法，但是过硬的营收、行业的前景性是否才应该成为一条统一的标准，某种意义来说，这也是圈外企业家们看重，无论是在中国的圈子还是在老美的圈子，一直对于币圈始终是不信任，在他们看来这个圈子的诈骗和不诚信让很多企业家并不愿意沾上代币两个字，如何重塑行业公平公正的形象也是这次新模式应该考虑的；

3、承接上一条其实衍生出一个点就是参与这个模式的企业家的安全感，这个模式基于合规排除了中美企业，但是大家肯定清楚，全世界的企业家99%能打的就是中美，所以本质最后可能自然是中美企业家，而好的中美企业家还是上条说的，对于代币有天然不信任，那么很重要一点就是股票和代币化之前的防火墙，所以这个模式最好的方式是——上市是由企业来决定，代币化是第三方做的事情。

无论如何，币安（听说还有其他交易所）敢于走出这一步都是好的事情，扶持企业和扶持代币已经是两个维度的事情了，当然前者的难度会大很多，希望交易所们能够早日出具更多的细节。

Across four decades of modern options markets, a 40 VIX has only printed six times.

Five of those six times marked the exact bottom

• 1987: Black Monday capitulation low 
• 1998: The literal bottom tick of the LTCM crisis 
• 2002: The terminal flush of the dot-com bust 
• 2008: The only failure (full banking system insolvency) • 2011: The cycle low before an eight-year bull run 
• 2020: The generational COVID liquidation wick

Friday was the seventh.

The only time buying a 40 VIX failed was 2008, when the global banking system froze. Every other time, it was the trade of the year.
author: KawzInvests
quoted_text:
You are living through one of the rarest statistical events in modern financial history.

Today, the VIX hit 32.

Most retail investors see a 30+ VIX and panic. But if you study market history and derivatives research, a VIX crossing 30 is one of the rarest and most critical macro signals in finance

In normal markets, the VIX lives between 15 and 20. A VIX  above 30 only happens in about 5% of all trading sessions in history. 

• 1997: Asian Financial Crisis 
• 1998: Russian Default & LTCM Collapse 
• 2000–2001: Dot-Com Bust 
• 2002: Enron & WorldCom Scandals 
• 2008: Great Financial Crisis 
• 2011: U.S. Credit Rating Downgrade 
• 2020: COVID-19 Global Shock 
• April 2025: Tariff & Trade War Repricing 
• March 2026: Geopolitical Escalation

What do all of these have in common? Forced margin liquidations and structural repricing.

But don't mistake extreme fear for an immediate green light.

A 30+ VIX can mark a generational bottom (like 1997, 2011, or 2020) or it can be a devastating bull trap if credit and fundamentals are broken (like 2000 and 2008).

text: The claim is overstated. Modern VIX data (since 1990) shows roughly 9 distinct episodes of closes above 40 (1998, 2001, 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2015, 2020, 2025 per ChartingLens methodology). 1987 used the predecessor VXO. Friday hit 40.03 intraday but closed 35.89. Not all marked exact bottoms—2008 and 2001 continued lower. High VIX readings have often been followed by strong average S&P returns, with clear exceptions.

quoted_text:
I finished watching The Altruists today with a few people who used to work at Alameda and FTX. We recognised so little beyond the names. My expectations were low, but I’m still surprised it’s this bad.

In short, the story has nothing to do with what actually happened at FTX or Alameda.

The biggest stretch for me was turning the early history of both companies into a story about Sam and Caroline’s relationship. Sam and Gary started Alameda out of their apartment in 2017. Caroline joined a team that was already trading and became one of its senior traders. It wasn’t until 2021 that she and Sam Trabucco became co-CEOs.

The early days of FTX had their own drama. We weren’t sure we could run an exchange, so at first we tried to sell/whitelabel the tech but nobody wanted it. Around Apr/May 2019, we ended up launching it ourselves and raising our seed round. We had more investors interested than we expected, and by the time Caroline moved to Hong Kong, the round was closed. The investment conversation with CZ only happened a few months later.

The conversations the show invented for CZ were particularly hard to watch. FTX started in Hong Kong, and a lot of the people who built it were Asian. I found the stereotypes about Asians and Chinese culture racist.

Even Sam and Caroline felt unfamiliar. Sam was one of the least emotionally expressive people I’ve ever met. His character seems drawn from Michael Lewis’s book and the way he came across in public after the bankruptcy. Caroline reads like someone tried to piece her together from her private blog. She wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.

People had lives before FTX too. Nishad and Claire had been together since college, long before either of them joined the company.

As for effective altruism, Sam cared about it, and so did a few other people at FTX. Most employees had nothing to do with it, and plenty weren’t fans. It had very little bearing on what it was like to work there and nothing to do with why FTX grew.

We kept noticing how little work anyone seemed to do on the show. Back in the days, FTX enforced a strict in-person working culture. We were in the office even during covid unless we were in quarantine. I’d love to know where we found all that time to hang out while building one of the fastest-growing crypto exchanges and keeping it running 24/7.

And when the market suddenly moves or there’s an emergency, you don’t even reach for your laptop? Oooft...

Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.

感谢 Cova 姐 @covachong 的邀请，
在离开KL的前夕，蹭了一顿Fourmeme的大餐。

也很久没见江左哥 @SiNaToDdFelix 
和比特欧@DRbitcoin36 了。

上一次和江左哥见面，已经是很久之前了。
在上次见面时我就表达过一个观点：
我自己不再看好公链赛道的机会。
无论是 Layer1 还是 Layer2，
我都认为公链叙事已经属于上一个周期，
不会再成为新周期的主线。
「『而那会，最热的是BASE链。』」

昨天晚上的饭局，又聊到了当前市场。
一个比较悲观的判断是：
现在大概率还是反弹，而不是反转。
前几天的下跌，有60%的概率并不是最后一跌。
说实话，最近的我比以往任何时候都要悲观。
上一个周期，即使身处熊市，我们依然对Crypto充满信心！有空投可以撸，有Meme可以玩，有小图片可以炒，还能去DC吹水，似乎每天都有新的机会。

但现在不一样了。
撸毛反撸已经成为常态，
大部分ALTS的终局似乎早已摆在台面上。
更让人悲观的是，
越来越多的项目方甚至都对自己的项目缺乏信心。
过去是散户担心项目方跑路，
现在有时候感觉，一些项目方自己都不相信自己的故事了。

当然，我依然相信还会有下一个牛市。
但有一点需要提前接受：
下一个牛市，并不意味着所有Alts都有机会重新回到前高，更不意味着所有人都能回本。

我个人现在的一个判断是：
未来，大部分山寨（不谈 Meme），
可能会越来越趋近于优质公司的股票走势。
市场会逐渐回归基本面、收入、产品和真实的产业地位。

而那些单纯靠概念炒作，却没有实际产品、业务和竞争力的项目，可能连Meme都不如。
毕竟每个阶段的主线Meme，至少还有情绪、社区共识和资金博弈作为支撑。
而一个没有实力、没有基本面支撑，
却还想靠叙事撑起估值的项目，凭什么让市场一直买单？

如果只关注三个山寨，我会选：
$Hype、 $Near、 $Uni

手里拿一张通行证和拿三张通行证，给个人账号带来的交易积分倍率完全一样，想靠多买卡拉高主动刷分倍率是行不通的。

主要积分其实还是在交易池里。

当然，官方池如果后面铸造量一直起不来，单张卡的低分母周池收益也会继续维持在高位，具体怎么配还得看个人资金和愿不愿意花精力写策略了。

text:
Funny how when a hit piece misses, it's always the target's fault for not having the decency to die.

Heck, the very fact she speaks of "accountability journalism" - as if it were a normal thing - is the biggest tell you can get: it implies the verdict comes first and the job is to take someone down.

If anything deserves to be held to account here, it's precisely "accountability journalism" itself: it's genuinely terrifying that some journalists view themselves as prosecutors.

Jensen Huang is lucky to be an extremely powerful man with unlimited resources and considerable support. Imagine for a minute that the same relentless "accountability journalism" campaign was run on you by the media: there would be nothing you could do. You'd simply be found guilty in the court of public opinion - a court that doesn't do presumption of innocence or appeals. The best you could hope for is a correction buried on page 19 six months later that no-one will read.

That's "accountability journalism": ironically, a form of power with no checks and zero accountability.

We concluded Base Batches 004 (an accelerator led by @Base & @Coinbase) w/ Demo Day at their NYC HQ.

A lot changed for us during the batch (& a bit of drama too). Some intentional, some accidental, some down to luck. Somehow it all worked out for the better for @Flovia402.

A few takeaways from the program:
1. They can connect you w/ pretty much anyone you want to meet. Even when we changed our product mid-batch, they doubled down on supporting us.

2. They funded us right after acceptance. No unnecessary back-and-forth.

3. The distribution support is next level. Everyone taps into their own network to help us out. Felt much more personal than just a business relationship. Went from 0 to thousands of users in just a few weeks.

4. Very opinionated about what founder support should look like. Clearly built the program their own way rather than copying someone else’s playbook. 
They’ve always been down to chat & super responsive, even before we got into the program.

During the batch, we made a major shift in our product direction w/ their support. Feels like it was meant to happen.

Personally, a real honor to work w/ companies we’ve looked up to for years. Being part of the SF startup scene, I’ve seen time and again how much trust Coinbase & Base have earned, even outside of crypto.

Our mission is to build the infra behind agentic consumption for both the demand & supply sides. Still a long way to go. Just gotta keep pushing uphill.

text: 这条分析比较严谨。排除掉了 NVDA 基本面上存在的不确定性，但考虑了现实存在的其他限制
author: yuyue_chris
quoted_text:
黃仁勳恢復 Nvidia CEO 職位的分析：

1. 被移除的不確定性：
主要是公司策略、產品規劃、技術發展與供應鏈管理等。上述不確定性曾在過去 1-2 週對科技股造成壓力，因此不確定性被移除後股價立刻大漲。但能否回到過去股價高點，除了取決於個別公司在 AI 供應鏈與 Nvidia 生態體系的定位外，還要看以下兩點。

2. 仍存在的不確定性：
(1) 銷售面：在美國更嚴格管制 AI GPU 出口與海外算力租賃後，對 Nvidia 出貨與營收造成的影響。
(2) 循環融資：更高合規成本與更嚴格審核機制下，對進行中的循環融資與未來新案的影響。
(3) 調查訴訟與更嚴格的監管：黃仁勳與 Nvidia 仍在接受調查中，未來的公開發言、內部決策與對外互動，都會被納入後續調查並成為質詢的新證據，而這也會強化上述銷售面與循環融資的不確定性。

3. 無法被改變的現實瓶頸：
(1) 資料中心建置的挑戰 (包括供電、人力等)，與未來相關法規更趨於嚴格。
(2) CSP 資本支出陸續在 2027‒2028 見頂。
(3) 製造技術限制 (如次世代先進封裝良率等)。

text:
英伟达市值一夜拉了半个币圈市值，可接下来还有三个问题没有解决：

1、对华芯片出口管制可能更加严格。英伟达已经成立由独立董事组成的国家安全与出口管制委员会，正在招聘首席合规官，相关调查也不会因为老黄回归而终止。

尤其是通过第三国转运、海外数据中心远程调用算力等渠道，未来可能面临更严格的审查。

2、英伟达的基本盘依然很强。最新季度营收1158亿美元，同比增长103%，其中总部位于中国（含香港）的客户贡献110.5亿美元，占比约9.5%。下一季度业绩指引甚至没有计入中国数据中心计算业务收入。

但如果监管进一步延伸至第三国渠道和远程算力服务，实际影响可能比财报上的直接收入占比更大。

3、AI产业的循环融资问题依然存在。英伟达投资AI公司，AI公司拿钱购买英伟达的芯片，云厂商借债建设数据中心，再把算力租给AI公司。

整个链条上的资本支出、订单、收入和估值都在膨胀，但最终有多少终端客户愿意持续付费，能不能覆盖芯片折旧、电费和融资成本，才是决定这轮AI投资能否持续的关键。

黄仁勋回归确实解除了英伟达的CEO危机，但没有解除AI产业的债务风险、估值风险、监管风险和投资回报率风险。

老黄可以把AI泡沫重新吹起来，但他不能替整个AI产业还债，更不能替客户赚钱。

text:
Scheduled transactions are proposed for Monad: any account or contract books a call for a future block, gas is prepaid, and the protocol guarantees it runs. No keeper to run, fund or get censored.

A contract can also book its own next call, which gives you onchain cron jobs.

A bunch of use cases open up. 

My favorite: a self-balancing cash carry trade, fully onchain. Eg : Long shMON, short MON on Perpl. 
Staking yield plus funding, price exposure hedged.

The short bleeds margin when MON pumps, and today an offchain bot rebalances it. If the bot dies, you get liquidated.

Say you hold $100k of shMON and a $100k MON short with $50k margin (2x on the short) 
MON pumps 10%
The short loses $10k, so margin falls to $40k

A scheduled call checks the margin ratio every ~5 min. When it's below the band, it sells $10k of shMON, closes $10k of the short, and adds $10k to margin. Back to a 50% ratio, still delta neutral.

What this unlocks is a carry strategy with no operator. It's a contract that runs itself, so anyone can deposit without trusting a team to keep a bot alive, and the rebalance logic is auditable onchain. Because the gap between checks is bounded, you can also run a thinner margin buffer, which means less idle capital and more yield on equity.

Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

text:
Neon is showing me how much opportunity exists for model labs to attract users by just altering the default writing style.

For example: we gave a research + writing task to Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Neon and GPT-6.2 Sol, with the same prompt and the same data.

Some observations:

1. Opus was more likely to explain things plainly and hedged its claims carefully

2. Sol was more likely to lead with caveats about what the data could and couldn't show

3. Neon felt like it was writing with a stronger point of view. It read noticeably less like AI than the other two, though not always "better" - just different.

Style differences like this are one reason I think future of AI is plural.

Most people use a model's defaults, so its default voice matters more than any one user's preferences. The more people use one model, the more its voice will show up everywhere, and the more demand there will be for models that write and think differently.

text:
I'm getting more convinced by the day that TradFi options have become what crypto used to be.

Two out of every three S&P 500 index options traded now expire the same day. That's retail speculation at scale, and the 100x has moved into short-dated calls on whatever narrative is running that week.

It's the same psychology, the same reflexive squeezes and the same narrative rotations.

In one game, you're betting on attention around a real company, with a clean asymmetric bet in either direction, in a market the world actually respects. That matters more than people think for retail. For the average person, "I trade options" sounds a lot better at a dinner party than "I trade crypto"

In the other, you're fighting bundlers and snipers in a rigged illiquid and unstable memecoin trench that has mostly been solved.

Which one sounds more attractive to you?
