I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.

What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.

Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.

It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.

Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.

It starts with METR.

Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.

He proposes METR for this purpose.

But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.

Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.

And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.

This stock was worth $500 million early last year.

It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.

METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.

Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.

But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.

The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.

The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.

If this were the end of it, that's bad.

But that isn't all.

The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.

The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.

They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.

All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.

As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.

Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.

From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.

This itself is an objective fact.

The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.

But the problem also goes in the other direction:

If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.

Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.

Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.

They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.

And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.

What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.

The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.

And that feedback loop is winning.

That's what Jacob Coxon is.

China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.

America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.

Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.

Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.

It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.

Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.

Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.

Congress must investigate.

Evidence and Github in next post.

Then some supplementary figures.

I analyzed eleven New York Times reports on the Jensen Huang story.

Most notably, NYT makes the "spy" claim 30 times in these 11 reports.

The original report cites unnamed officials who had been "briefed" on the intelligence. Not who had seen it themselves -- but who had been "briefed".

This is a game of telephone with plausible deniability.

Nobody named. No specific details of the intelligence used to draw the conclusion that the woman was a spy.

Anonymous "officials" "briefed".

This was used to try to take Jensen Huang down.

When that didn't work, journalists resorted to viciously digging up and scandal mongering about Jensen Huang's other alleged affairs.

Then he was removed as CEO.

Without an investigation.

Without due process.

And now officials and intelligence agencies are contesting the New York Times characterization.

This is unethical. It is unjust.

It is an absolute disgrace.

If anyone should resign now, it is Nvidia's board who aggressively removed Jensen Huang without an investigation, after he gave decades of his life to make the company what it is.

And any investigation that proceeds from here should involved not just the "spy" claim, but the New York Times -- who has engaged in potentially unethical behavior.

Jensen Huang deserves due process -- not mob justice.

He deserves respect for everything he has done for technology and America -- not a disgraceful removal after anonymous, unsubstantiated allegations, several parties removed from the source.

text:
Founders produce higher returns than non-founders. This is an empirical fact.

So: business school curricula should be changed, and good governance should be redefined as founder control and dual-class stock. Shareholders are still protected by easy liquidation and their ability to fund new entrants. After all, you don’t invest in a company based on who’s on the board. That’s largely ceremonial.

The key difference from the 20th century is that it was prohibitively difficult in 1950 to found a manufacturing company, because assembly lines cost so much, the communists controlled much of the world, and even America had 90% marginal tax rates. It was the century of centralization, the individual powerless before the institution.

Today it is no longer prohibitively difficult to found a tech company, because software costs so little, much of the world has turned to free markets, and capital flows at the speed of the Internet. This is the century of decentralization, at least in the West, with the institution falling to the individual.

For example: Anthropic was started just a few years ago and is beating even Google at its own game. If we get many open weights models, their moat will also in turn erode.

So: all 20th century corporate governance was based on the idea that “the company is hard to replace, but its CEO isn’t.” The Harvard MBA is premised on the professional manager. It was expensive to start a new company with all the assembly lines, so make sure it doesn’t fail by making every employee replaceable. Managers were abundant so capital became the scarce asset.

By contrast, the entire 21st century model is based on the idea that “A tech founder is hard to replace, but the company isn’t.” The YCombinator model is premised on the startup founder. It is inexpensive to start a new company with a few lines of code, so make sure it doesn’t fail by having an irreplaceable team. Capital is abundant so founders become the scarce asset.
author: balajis
quoted_text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://t.co/ERxhHz4Qvo

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

text: No me canso de decir que en mi vida profesional he tenido contacto con ingenieros de muchas partes del mundo, Europeos, norteamericanos,  Asiáticos (chinos, y coreanos), y puedo afirmar que la formación que tenemos los ingenieros argentinos, en muchos casos es superior a países del primer mundo. De hecho muchos de estos ingenieros lo reconocen. Les doy un ejemplo concreto de un ingeniero quimico Texano, al que llaman el lithium godfather el Dr. John Burba. La historia cuenta que este Dr. en ingeniería química fue contratado en los 90', por una empresa llamada FMC Lithium para que los ayude a buscar minas de litio y desarrollar métodos extractivos de litio alrededor del mundo, dado que la mina de litio que operaba FMC Lithium en EEUU se estaba agotando. Su búsqueda se orientó a Sudamérica, pasando por Bolivia, de donde determinaron que no podrían poner una operación, llegando a Argentina en el 92-93. En el país se dieron cuenta del potencial que tendría una explotación en el Salar del Hombre Muerto en Catamarca así que allí iniciaron investigaciones y desarrollaron una metodología de extracción de litio a partir de salmuera. Aquí, y para desarrollar esa metodología (que es particular para cada salar), contrato ingenieros argentinos, para su materialización. En una entrevista (que si me la solicitan se las paso) el comenta que viajo alrededor del mundo en distintos trabajos (muchos de oil&gas) y que la calidad de los ingenieros argentinos no lo encontró en ningún otro lado en el mundo, y que gracias a estos ingenieros logró con éxito llevar a cabo la tarea de desarrollar esa metodología, que de otra manera sería imposible de haberla desarrollado. Ese proyecto (Fénix para aquellos que están en tema litio) comenzó a operar en Argentina en 1997, y fue el primero a escala industrial a nivel mundial, el cual aún hoy sigue operando. En síntesis un proyecto totalmente innovador, que nunca se había probado, y que funciona con éxito dado las capacidades en ingeniería Argentina, muestra claramente que la ingeniería argentina cuando se propone algo, puede conseguirlo, y todo ello gracias a nuestro entramado intelectual. En mi caso particular, como les comenté,la formación que me dio la UBA, en todas sus dimensiones me muestra claramente que puedo competir con ingenieros de universidades de primer nivel alrededor del mundo. No está demás investigar un poco, y encontrarnos que muchos ingenieros argentinos se destacan en posiciones alrededor del mundo.

再聊聊老黄的回归，昨天上午说看周日川普和贝森特的表态市场会有一段交易老黄回归的时间窗口，但没想昨晚就直接回归了。借着昨晚跟朋友聊的内容说说这场回归是如何发生的：
1、川普发力，亲自出面说服了英伟达董事会，同时力压贝森特被迫改口，看报道万斯和卢特尼克也参与斡旋。这个好理解、万斯虽然反对伊朗战争，但还是共和党科技派，卢特尼克更是如此本身这次就积极内阁被指责最多的，自然也要积极出力。

川普发力一方面他本身就支持老黄，跟老黄算是商业盟友，股市暴跌他自己利益受损。

2、市场发力，本质还是一次“跌给你看”甚至叫“死给你看”，美国是高度金融化，股市已经成为美国社会财富第一大支撑。股市可以跌可以调整，但是不能大跌不能真“死了”，只要“以死相逼”才能逼着博弈的几方里要么积极斡旋、要么退让；市场死了、共和党、民主党、董事会都害怕。

3、共和党对华强硬派的分化和禁声，作为白宫里对华强硬派的代表，贝森特已经改口，鲁比奥沉默。为什么贝森特改口？其实很好理解，贝森特在华盛顿没有政治根基、虽然他主张对华强硬、但他的权力完全来自川普。鲁比奥不一样、在川普胜选总统之前就已经是联邦参议员了，他有自己的势力范围，国会里盟友就不少例如众议院外交事务委员会主席马斯特就是鲁比奥的亲密盟友。

所以昨天鲁比奥在会见卡塔尔首相时，有记者问“黄发回归有国家安全分风险么”，鲁比奥就完全岔开忽略了这个问题。上周五市场暴跌也让他认识到了老黄的重要性，上周还在币安广场ama还聊最后要么英伟达让市场很难受、要么发现真找不到一个能替代老黄的人、最后不得不又请老黄回归。当然当时也没有认为这是短期就能发生的。

4、很多人说民主党也有参与老黄回归，正如之前https://t.co/zswYQ6emzu这里聊到的“倒黄”主力还是共和党内强硬派，那么老黄回归还是川普挟着市场暴跌的余威压制住了党内强硬派，民主党其实没怎么使劲。反倒凌晨参议院民主党领袖舒默还表态民主党将动用全部力量调查老黄和美国政府。

过去两周半中期选举后，发生的事情很多人归结为党争。其实更多还是共和党党内博弈，两党之间的争斗其实还没开始，就像27年财政预算法案一样现在民主党的思路就是12月再通过一个临时拨款协议、等到27年1月民主党真正掌控国会后再跟共和党内谈判。

对民主党来说。遏制中国是长期战略必须一定要去做的，但现在趁着民众对AI的民意去搞川普压制共和党却是首要之事。不会说就停下来、当然民主党也怕市场真的“死给你看”。

5、整体上来，老黄回归估计内部整顿，之后再被迫辞职的概率很小。12月共和党主导的国会听证会估计也就没啥大问题了。但27年民主党应该还是会调查老黄，只是可能也不敢真的把老黄给干走，但估计能制造波动。

从昨天交易老黄回归到老黄真的回归，市场信心提振是巨大的、这一波📈估计会持续一段时间。

后面继续看三个维度：
油价/通胀/利率、
民主党的数据中心政策比预想的更严还是会略弱、
AI商业化是不是在加速（这一点我之前一直认为是加速，但市场要看更多的证据）。

text:
Also I've heard that people are talking about "negative overhead" for pearl-2:native and I would like to learn more about how they think they can achieve it if at all

From my perspective, Pearl's FP8 pipeline runs the exact same FP8 Tensor Core matmul as cuBLAS or CUTLASS, plus strictly extra mandatory work: FP10 pre-quant, a full keyed BLAKE3 Merkle tree over activations, noise injection, per-tile lottery hashing, and a BF16 peel matmul

So I would think that even if someone wrote the greatest CUDA kernel on earth for Pearl, deleting the hashing, noise, and peel from that exact same kernel would immediately make a strictly faster non-Pearl kernel

Maybe you see "negative overhead" in an apples-to-oranges comparison, like benchmarking Pearl FP8 against unquantized BF16 (where FP8 Tensor Cores have 2x raw throughput) or against an untuned default kernel

Against clean cuBLAS/CUTLASS/DeepGEMM FP8 (or native FP4 on Blackwell), mining overhead is always strictly positive

Could someone explain to me this magic of a negative overhead?
author: 0xalank
quoted_text:
Mad respect to $PEARL for the pump, genuinely. It's all over my feed and I've been asked about it constantly.

So here are my takes:

The more I read through the FP8 codebase and talk to people, the harder it is for me to see how the long-term vision for useful work actually plays out (where real live inference actually wins out over synthetic mining) in the Pearl model.

Even on native H100/B200 hardware, once you account for FP10 quant, BLAKE3 Merkle hashing, noise/peel, bucket padding, and the KV-cache VRAM hit, live serving looks like a realistic ~20 to 35% capacity overhead (maybe 15 to 25% floor long term).

And that's only on prefill, since decode, CUDA graphs, FlashInfer, and quantized MoE don't even mine.

Meanwhile dedicated miners looping bare synthetic GEMMs skip all of that, pull 2 to 5x more hash per GPU, and those are the ones driving hashrate up (as we've seen so far).

If a provider makes more just running clean inference, why would they turn on mining?

Hardware is pulling in opposite directions too. 

Mainstream AI GPUs and AI-specific ASICs are racing toward FP4 and changing accumulator hardware (which means either a permanent hardfork treadmill or upcasting FP4 back to FP8 and taking an even bigger serving hit).

At the same time, because v4 doesn't need HBM and fits in a few MB of SRAM, a custom Pearl FP8 ASIC pushes the exact opposite way if emissions ever get large enough.

Even steelmanning the bull case, like disaggregated prefill or pitching it as a way to put idle data center hardware to use, it just ends up being mercenary miners auto-selling emissions to offset their costs unless there's a real buy-side demand sink or durable monetary demand on the other side (which I suppose is the SoV/energy consumption take that is working so far).

Not trying to fud, genuinely asking and putting it out there if anyone technical can actually walk through the plan for how useful work survives these trade-offs?

黃仁勳恢復 Nvidia CEO 職位的分析：

1. 被移除的不確定性：
主要是公司策略、產品規劃、技術發展與供應鏈管理等。上述不確定性曾在過去 1-2 週對科技股造成壓力，因此不確定性被移除後股價立刻大漲。但能否回到過去股價高點，除了取決於個別公司在 AI 供應鏈與 Nvidia 生態體系的定位外，還要看以下兩點。

2. 仍存在的不確定性：
(1) 銷售面：在美國更嚴格管制 AI GPU 出口與海外算力租賃後，對 Nvidia 出貨與營收造成的影響。
(2) 循環融資：更高合規成本與更嚴格審核機制下，對進行中的循環融資與未來新案的影響。

3. 無法被改變的現實瓶頸：
(1) 資料中心建置的挑戰 (包括供電、人力等)，與未來相關法規更趨於嚴格。
(2) CSP 資本支出陸續在 2027‒2028 見頂。

text:
Talk about saying the quiet part out loud.

The NYT team published a multi-part investigation that dominated national coverage for ~4 weeks. Nvidia's board opened a formal investigation into its CEO. The Senate Banking Committee is threatening a subpoena, shareholders have filed a class action, and more than $2 trillion in market value has disappeared. That sure sounds like "accountability" to me.

The reporters will almost certainly win awards for it. I'm not sure whose heart needs to go out to whom.

The American Press Institute defines journalism's purpose as giving citizens "the information they need to make the best possible decisions" about their lives, communities, and governments.

"A culture that does not care about accountability" only follows IF you'd already decided what accountability had to look like & it didn't arrive in that format. The reality is different: the information reached people (obviously). The board acted. The CEO resigned. The government investigated this that & the other thing. The only thing that didn't happen was the "Jensen is gone" conclusion Julia (and those that share her perspective) wanted. 

Unless, of course, the goal was never to inform, but to cause an outcome.

卖算力比卖Grok赚钱，老马自己都认了

纽约时报翻出了SpaceX AI团队的内部聊天记录。最扎眼的一句，是老马8月份把一个工程师群改名叫“Sell compute because we can't compete”，拼不过，就把算力拿去卖。

老马在X上回了一句：纽约时报把显而易见的事，当成新闻在发。

我倒觉得，这篇东西对拿着SpaceX的人，好消息多过坏消息。几个点记一下：

一、账已经很清楚

Anthropic每个月付给SpaceX大概31亿美元租算力，谷歌大概8亿。AI这一块，已经占SpaceX总收入的一半以上。

光Anthropic一家，一年就是三百多亿美元。这不是叙事，是每个月实实在在进账的现金。

二、老马看的是每张卡赚多少钱

他在群里讲得很白：竞争力只看每张GPU能带来多少收入，不看跑分。付不起GPU的钱，要么破产，要么变成一家租算力的公司。

所以Grok Imagine那个60人的团队解散了，AI陪伴也关了。资源往能赚钱的地方挪，这是拧毛巾，不是认输。

三、跟我之前想的一样

之前写过老马那句话，Anthropic最大概率是想从SpaceX再多要10GW算力。我也说过，卖算力的和买算力的互相看得上，这门生意才做得长。

现在回头看，这门生意不但做长了，还做成了SpaceX的半壁江山。

四、真正要盯的，还是续约

合同可以签到2029年，Anthropic续不续、加不加量，还是这个仓位明年要过的第一关。

SpaceX还是自己两个组合里的第一大仓位。

自己的模型暂时追不上，就先把铲子卖给挖金子的人。淘金热里最稳赚的，从来都是卖铲子的。

NFA， DYOR。 $SPCX

quoted_text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

11 月 24 日，豆包旗下 AI 个人助理「小豆」正式开启公测，主打「一个懂你，还能主动帮你办事的豆包」。

这款产品已经酝酿了大半年。早在今年 4 月，豆包内部就开始测试代号为 Spell 的个人助理项目，最初由豆包手机助手团队负责。后来因为豆包手机发布等原因，一直没能对外推出。

9 月，Meta Muse 上线后迅速走红，字节也加快了进度，准备将 Spell 与豆包进一步整合，并推出独立 App。国庆前就传出「小豆」即将上线的消息，却迟迟没有动静。

就在昨天，《字母榜》还发文追问「字节的 Personal Agent 到底什么时候才能来」，甚至猜测字节可能已经降低了这个项目的优先级。结果第二天，小豆就宣布公测了。

目前，小豆已推出独立 App，可在苹果和安卓应用商店下载，但仍采用邀请制，需要邀请码才能使用。受邀用户可获得一定免费额度，邀请好友还有机会增加额度。

字节还表示，未来小豆的功能和体验将逐步上线豆包 App。
author: 0xLogicrw
quoted_text:
张一鸣近日在 Seed 团队全员会上给出了一个时间表：字节跳动最快也要到 2029 至 2030 年，才有望在前沿 AI 领域与 OpenAI、Anthropic 竞争。

张一鸣特别指出，Seed 大语言模型使用的预训练数据集，比顶尖对手小了几个数量级。

字节在 AI 领域其实已经拿到了不少好牌。豆包是国内用户规模最大的 AI 聊天应用，Seedance 也跻身全球顶尖视频生成模型行列。偏偏通用语言模型没有跟上。今年 6 月发布 Seed2.1 时，团队自己也承认，模型在高难度开放任务和前沿科研问题上还有明显短板。

字节为此准备投入天量资金。今年 5 月，公司曾讨论将全年资本开支提高至最高 700 亿美元，主要用于建设 AI 数据中心等基础设施。8 月又传出，Seed 正在预训练一款最高达 10 万亿参数的大模型，规模超过国内所有公开的大模型。

张一鸣也不愿靠蒸馏走捷径。所谓蒸馏，就是拿 Claude 等领先模型生成的答案，反过来训练自己的模型。今年 8 月，他就明确表示，这种办法短期内确实能改善表现，但学来的终究是别人已有的能力，最多只能不断逼近，很难真正超越。Seed 内部还通过 API 检测和训练数据过滤，限制第三方模型的输出进入训练集。

为了追赶，字节也在不断招人、留人。Seed 目前约有 1000 名研发人员，由张一鸣去年从 Google DeepMind 挖来的吴永辉带队。字节还专门推出了与豆包业务挂钩的虚拟股「豆包股」，符合条件的员工还可以选择把年终奖领成豆包股，分享业务增长带来的收益。

字节计划未来几周推出一款类似 Meta Muse 的个人 AI 助手，让用户通过语音和虚拟形象与 AI 交互，并让它代为完成任务。豆包内部代号为「Spell」的个人助理项目早在 4 月便开始内测，后来因豆包手机发布等原因，一直没有正式推出。Meta Muse 爆火后，字节加快了进度，国庆假期前就在赶研发，计划将 Spell 与豆包进一步整合。

text:
深圳改变了特朗普，也救了黄仁勋

黄仁勋此前辞职，本质上是一次“政治事件”，政治的问题，需要政治来解。

《华盛顿邮报》11月13日的报道写得很直接，“黄仁勋丑闻”背后，是一场争夺特朗普对华政策话语权的暗战。

一边是黄仁勋和商务部长卢特尼克，主张把芯片卖给中国，让中国开发者留在美国的技术栈上。另一边是国务卿兼国家安全顾问鲁比奥、财长贝森特和对华鹰派。

鲁比奥手里掌握着中情局的情报，《纽约时报》把情报变成了头版。

其实在前面，黄仁勋下台，各种舆论攻击，鹰派基本赢了，只是，鹰派未能完全搞定特朗普，特朗普也一直没放弃黄仁勋。

真正的转折在深圳。18日，特朗普到深圳参加 APEC，晚宴上和习近平聊了一整晚 AI。

有个细节可以留意。当天他接受福克斯采访，说黄仁勋的事在饭桌上只是“一笔带过”。

到了20日的白宫记者会，说法变成了：他和习近平谈过黄仁勋，习说"brilliant, brilliant"。

23日上 CNBC，他又说，习近平对黄仁勋的看重"在另一个层次上"。

在他的叙事中，黄仁勋的分量越来越重。

他在 CNBC 上把自己的想法讲得很直白：从中国回来后他想到，对方可能出一大笔钱，请黄仁勋去中国管一家公司；黄仁勋要是心里有气、觉得被亏待，说不定就去了。

所以他的结论是：留着黄仁勋不是威胁，失去他才是威胁。

鹰派抓住的风险是黄仁勋跟中国走得太近。特朗普在深圳看到的风险是，美国把黄仁勋推出去，中国正好接住。

于是，特朗普不再犹豫，拯救大兵黄仁勋。

22日，特朗普在 Truth Social 上发帖，说希望英伟达董事会重新聘用黄仁勋。

据 CNN，他让副总统万斯牵头，周末给英伟达董事会打了一轮电话，主要是向董事会保证：政府不认为黄仁勋会带来国家安全风险。

贝森特也在同一天改了口。他在 CBS《面对国家》节目里被问到"你说过要从外部找人"，回答是"Jensen 现在已经在外面了"。他还说，间谍这条线"有点像无稽之谈"，要查的是公司里到底谁在管合规。

23日，董事会全票让黄仁勋复职。特朗普随后在 CNBC 上说，他亲自打电话进了董事会会议，是他说服了他们。

其实我也好奇，特朗普在深圳到底看到了啥？

Alt froth fading isn't only a crypto story. Look at where borrowed money is being invited instead.

After last week's crash, Taiwan banned shorting below the prior close and China cut the cash needed to buy on margin from 100% to 80%. Govts are making it cheaper and safer to borrow for stocks, with a floor underneath.

Crypto got no floor. So the risk money that used to chase alts has an easier home right now and what stays in crypto sits in $BTC because it's the one thing you can exit in size.

That's why I don't expect alt trading to recover just because BTC bounces. It comes back when the money propped up in equities starts looking for more upside and I don't expect that either to come so soon.

text:
No. Here’s what really happened.

Jensen started Nvidia in 1993, before the modern era of founder control and dual-class stock began with Google and Facebook.

Because he went public in the 1990s, he inherited all the 20th century overhead of endless public company paperwork, rather than staying private for as long as possible as is also now typical.

This is why Jensen had much less control than a modern founder/CEO. Like Jack Dorsey at Twitter, he got gradually boxed into a corner by the fact that he couldn’t raise huge amounts of capital outside his company to clear the board of cruft.

You see, as CEO, you report to the board. And you can’t do outside activities without their approval. So actions that would remove a board member that doesn’t want to step down are hard to take. Unless the CEO is also part of a shareholder majority, or has dual class / founder control, which Jensen didn’t in this case, as explained above…he can’t pick the board.

Like Bezos, though, Jensen is a workhorse and somehow made it all work despite that. Moreover, because Nvidia is a hardware company, and had a relatively low market cap until the AI boom, it didn’t attract notice from envious wokes until the last few years. 

Wokes don’t know or care about GPUs, but they do care about market caps, and the rise of AI, and especially open source AI, all of which is a threat to their power. Along with useful idiot “nationalists”, they began plotting to steal control of Jensen’s multi-trillion-dollar company from him.

In this plot, they were aided by a second angle of vulnerability. Jensen didn’t just have old board members he couldn’t remove. Due to DEI policies, he was also forced to bring new board members on, from demographics favored by the far left (eg, not veterans).

Conformist board members like this act like sleeper cells. They are often useless or inactive in peacetime scenarios. Then they activate in response to press or state pressure. In this case, they then got beaten back just as quickly by the reversal of the state’s position.

Anyway, Dorsey needed Elon to come in with his enormous new resources to sweep the board clean. Today, it’s quite possible that Jensen, as the survivor of this character assassination, will similarly figure out a way to fire this incompetent board and assert proper founder control — as is a best practice in the modern era.

text:
Alpöge 回应黎曼猜想证明争议：“25万页文档”是开玩笑话，Lean 代码写的很烂但证明成立

用 Claude 证明黎曼猜想的 Anthropic 数学家 Levent Alpöge，在 X 上发了一篇《我做过的蠢事》，正面回应这几天的争议。

先说结论：证明本身没有问题。1700 万行代码的正确性已获官方核查通过，他认错的是“表述开玩笑”和“代码太乱”，并点出了这次证明真正值得思考的数学意义。

1. 辟谣与认错：他澄清了三件事

• “25万页文档”是个玩笑：他不想给黎曼猜想配一份 AI 糊出来的注水说明，又觉得自己写不出可读版本，索性拿 Lean 往夸张了凑字数自娱自乐，甚至在定理开头写“因为实数是全序的，所以不等于 1/2 时要么大于 1/2 要么小于 1/2”，本以为这么荒诞的废话一眼就能看出是反讽，结果被媒体和学界全盘当真。

他为此道歉，感叹终于明白陶哲轩为什么劝人“别在论文里开玩笑”。（他还顺带自嘲：之前做四维杨-米尔斯存在性攒了 6 万页 AI 草稿，结果审核委员会一句“要看 Lean”，让他觉得啃草稿纯属浪费时间。）

• 代码确实“满是垃圾”，但能编译：他承认 1700 万行 Lean 代码里有很多自己“瞎冲（yolo）”试出来的弯路和冗余，最终绝大部分可能都用不上，只是清理起来莫名困难，所有对代码质量的批评他全盘接受。

• 承认拖延前科：同行 Scott Armstrong 看穿了他，他学生时代就有定理拖了快十年才整理成文，这次他承诺会更负责地把证明精简出来。

2. 核心事实：代码再丑，证明依然成立

在形式化验证里，“不好读”和“对不对”是两件事：

1). Lean 官方（Lean FRO）与 Mathlib 已联合认证：定理陈述没有偷换概念，几十人独立编译结果完全一致，证明成立。

2) MIT 数学家 Andrew Sutherland 独立跑完核查：证明只用到了 Lean 的三条标准公理，没有作弊。

3. 最有启发的一点：为什么证出来了还不满意？

Alpöge 说，他在声明里漏掉了自己真正想强调的重点：

这种又长又杂的暴力论证本身只是“原材料”，真正的目的是帮数学家反推出“正确的定义”。

几十年前，Weil 和 Deligne 干净利落地证明了有限域曲线上的“简化版黎曼猜想”，靠的是一套成熟的几何工具；但在普通整数（数域）上，数学界至今找不到对应的核心结构（即他说的缺一个“H¹ 对象”）。

他的原话：“黎曼猜想本该很简单。任何真正的困难都说明，我们现在的数学框架还很蠢。”

4. 留给数学界的新局面

这次事件把数学推到了一个前所未有的分水岭：机器已经确认“它是对的”，但人类还不知道“它为什么对”。

陶哲轩初步浏览后指出，这份证明似乎动用了现代朗兰兹纲领和算术几何的全部武器；也有数学家认为：Lean 代码回答不了数学最关心的“为什么”。

按照克雷研究所百万美元奖金的规则，证明仍需在期刊正式发表满两年并获学界共识。

MIT 核查页：https://t.co/qE4UnLf7Gw

quoted_text:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

author: AspynPalatnick

text:
Retail investors still wildly underestimate just how short term oriented the hedge fund world is

Most L/S equity pod shops like Citadel and Millennium are not in the business of taking long term views on companies

You would be surprised to know just how many analysts and PM own names in the book where they barely understand the full suite of products sold by the business

The goal for most of these pod shops is really two fold

1. generate views on businesses that diverge with market consensus

2. minimize volatility as much as possible as you look to extract alpha through that divergent view

The core skill required is second derivative thinking. It’s not so much understanding whether company XYZ has a sustainable moat for the next 5 years, although that can certainly matter

The analysis is more focused on what is the market getting wrong in projecting a certain KPI or line item in this business that can create surprises on the upside or downside

Most pod shops will have dedicated data research teams, as well as subscriptions and access to all forms of third party real time data that can help validate their thesis

Since projecting these out multiple quarters out with accuracy is nearly impossible, PMs and analysts increasingly just focus on next quarter’s earnings when thinking about alpha

The biggest advantage you have as a retail investor is your ability to make long term bets. You don’t need to have the perfect answer on what same store sales might look like during the third quarter or what number might come in below/above consensus

Doing the fundamental work on the business moat, products and whether the company is investing into the right tailwinds can give you a massive advantage when it comes to long term investing

That research and work is your best source of alpha as a retail investor. You will not find alpha building detailed DCF models and projecting numbers down to the dot. 

That game is overplayed and people on Wall Street can do it better than you ever could, thanks to management and data access

Ethereum Foundation Doubles Protocol Security Team, Warns AI Threats Are More Urgent Than Quantum Computing

The Ethereum Foundation, said AI-driven security threats have become more urgent than quantum computing risks, with AI models discovering software vulnerabilities faster than humans can review them. The foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made defenses against AI and quantum threats its top priority. Its plans include replacing elliptic-curve cryptography with hash-based signatures for validators and wallets, alongside new blob commitments. The foundation warned that the overhaul would be harder than Ethereum's 2022 Merge and could delay other long-planned upgrades.

text:
This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.

text:
I've always loved weird internet mysteries.

I first read the Bitcoin whitepaper because I was trying to figure out Cicada 3301.

In January 2012, a black-and-white image showed up on 4chan saying someone was looking for highly intelligent individuals. It was signed 3301. The image said there was a hidden message in it, and there was. Follow the trail far enough and you got a phone number. Call it and a recording told you there were three prime numbers associated with the original image. One was 3301. The other two were the image’s dimensions, 509 by 503. Multiply them and you got the address of the next website.

Then it got really weird. The website led to GPS coordinates, and people went out and found actual paper posters with cicadas and QR codes on them. The same puzzle that had people picking through image files at their desks now had people looking for a piece of paper in Warsaw, Sydney and Seoul. One of the later steps used a book cipher based on William Gibson’s Agrippa, a poem originally released on a floppy disk.

I got sucked into the discussion boards around then. Somebody floated the idea that Cicada might have something to do with Bitcoin, so I went and read the whitepaper. I loved Snow Crash, Neuromancer and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? Here was someone explaining how sci-fi money could actually work. I’ve never seen convincing evidence that the people behind Cicada had anything to do with Bitcoin. But the connection mattered to me: without that wild theory on a message board, I might never have gone looking for the Bitcoin whitepaper in the first place.

Cicada came back in 2013. This time the trail included a bootable Linux disc image and a piece of music called The Instar Emergence. When the disc booted, it printed prime numbers and paused on 1033 and 3301. In 2014, the third round started with a clue on Twitter and eventually led to Liber Primus, an illustrated book written in runes. The first set of 17 pages has been worked out. Of the 58 pages in the second release, only two have publicly verified readings. A signed message in 2016 pointed solvers back to the book. Another in 2017 warned people to check the digital signature before believing a new clue. That’s a pretty good rule for this whole thing.

Liber Primus is what brought me back. Once you’ve learned the rune alphabet, you can write the symbols out in familiar letters, and most of the book still won’t make sense. So what’s actually doing the work? Is it a cipher that changes from section to section? Is there information in the spacing or the artwork? What can we learn from a page we already know how to read?

I’m working through those questions with ChatGPT (currently burning GPT-6.2 Astra credits on Extra High). I bring a hunch, we go back to the original files, and we try to come up with a test that can tell us if I’m wrong. Take 1033, the number that showed up in the 2013 boot sequence. One of the squares in the notebook really does add up to 1033 across every row, column and diagonal. But you can rearrange the numbers and get the very same totals. If your theory is that those totals tell you which order to read the runes in, you’re going to need another clue. That’s the kind of detail I used to read right past when I wanted a theory to work.

I put the notebook online so you can see the original images, follow the tests and tell me where you think I missed something. We haven’t verified any new Liber Primus plaintext. I’ll share individual clues and experiments here as I go, including the ones that send us back to the drawing board.

If you were following Cicada back then and still have an original file, an old chat log, or a clue you always thought got overlooked, I’d love to see it.

I like to describe us as four Lego pieces: We fit together perfectly, complementing each other's strengths and building something stronger than the sum of its parts. That understanding allows us to move quickly, challenge one another without ego and operate as one team. 

It's also what brought us back together to build JUNE AI. 
Because while working at the heart of enterprise AI, we kept seeing the same problem: enterprise AI implementation is a massive undertaking.

The challenge is not simply choosing the right model. Enterprises want to move faster with AI, but the systems running their businesses are holding them back.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘.
June turns the traditionally complex implementation of enterprise systems, AI agents, and data platforms into a plug-and-play moment, so businesses can grow and leverage AI without the wait.

June is built to work across the enterprise platforms your business relies on like (such as Salesforce, Databricks, Oracle, Workday, HubSpot, OpenAI, Anthropic, ServiceNow, SAP, Microsoft, and Snowflake)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. Evolve safely: From discovery to production, every change is reviewed, sandbox-tested, and executed through native tools - fully auditable at every step.

2. Own the logic: June turns buried configuration into plain-language business rules, independent of any platform, so no vendor holds your logic.

3. Transform at any size: No downtime, no matter how complex the environment. June reads and understands your systems, whether legacy, custom-built, or brand new.

Thank you to @Benioff  and Time Ventures for leading our round, with @MichaelDell, @levie, @George_Kurtz, and Diane Greene participating.

text:
Every single @ahall_research piece is a must-read, but this one is a must-must-read. @freesystemslab is showing us the future of what AI-enabled social science research can look like. In this post they show what frontier AI models can help with in a research project, and what they still struggle with. 

My personal take-away: the concept of "verifiable domain" has expanded tremendously, basically anything where you can get data on to train a verifier becomes something to hillclimb. But it's probably harder to train a verifier on something that even experts disagree on. In this case, "choosing an important question."
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI. 

Lots more in the full piece here:

https://t.co/zgScGvp9EY

author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
Scientists proved a 45-min nap triggers the same brain reset that happens after a full night of sleep

Nuroscientists from the University of Geneva published a study proving you don't need a full night of sleep to trigger a "synaptic reset"

here is what actually happens to your brain during the day:

every thought, task, and piece of information strengthens the connections between your neurons (synapses). by mid-afternoon, those connections get saturated..

your brain literally runs out of bandwidth to absorb new info.

to test if a short nap fixes this, researchers put 20 healthy adults in a sleep lab across two afternoons (1:15–2:15 pm), one staying awake, one taking an average 45-minute nap, and measured their cortex with transcranial magnetic stimulation (tms) and eeg.

the results after the nap:

• net synaptic strength dropped (shown by lower wake eeg theta activity and higher tms thresholds)
• the brain's ability to form new connections (associative plasticity) jumped significantly compared to staying awake

a single 45-minute nap downregulates the noise without erasing what you learned, freeing up space to learn again.

4. How Do We Solve the Energy Supply Crisis and Compete With China?

America has over 100 gigawatts of stranded power. Much frontier progress will come from reinforcement learning and post-training, which suit decentralized compute, and about 50% of portfolio compute spend is now in post-training.

What does no one see that every should see about the current energy supply side @ZachBDell @alanchanguk @GavinSBaker

5. Why We Need to Ban Tranched Rounds

Tranches used to market businesses with no execution milestones to LPs for co-investment create markups that are smoke and mirrors. It is the same banker behaviour that led to the subprime mortgage crisis.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @PhilipJohnston @BrendanFoody

6. Why the Inference Layer Is Uninvestable and It Will All Be Brought In-House

Inference is too core to a research team's customer feedback loop to stay outsourced. The best teams buy, partner, then build, as Anthropic and Mistral did, so inference becomes a feature rather than a standalone product.

What is the counter? What does this miss @bernhardsson @deedydas @lqiao

7. Why We Need to Be Much Kinder to Colette Kress and Why She's Doing a Great Job as New CEO

No CFO is more technical on chips, throughput, token prices and supply chain, and Jensen has handed her earnings questions she answers with rigor. Anybody else in her situation would have crumbled. She could be retired but puts the mission and customers first.

4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. text:
如果买你东西的不再是人类，而是冷冰冰的 AI，传统商业的营销套路可能彻底作废了。

a16z 最近联合机构完成了 1.1 万次 AI Agent 模拟下单测试。结果发现，机器花起钱来，根本不吃人类那一套：

平时宽泛的需求，便宜的竞品凭借性价比通吃；但只要需求稍微细化（比如吹风机限定“细软发质”），大牌的胜率立刻从个位数飙到 88%。通用拼低价，垂直才能吃溢价。

华丽的网店装修对机器毫无意义。官网再精美，如果防着机器、不给自动化留门，Agent 几秒钟就会转头把单子下给不知名的小竞品。算法眼里没有品牌光环，只有机器能不能直接读取。

算盘打得比人还精，但折扣过大直接被当成诈骗。降价低于 10% 机器根本没反应，但折扣一旦超过 50%，机器反而会触发风控警觉，当成假货全线回避。大部分情况下机器宁愿多花钱买官方正品。

结账环节更是生硬。支持免登录游客直接买的，跑通率 81%；只要中途弹出强制注册登录，机器 100% 当场放弃，扭头就转投竞品。

当消费者从人类变成算法，情感包装彻底失效。未来谁能让机器一秒读懂、顺畅结算，谁才能拿到算法的购买权。

内讧开始了！

英伟达CFO Colette Kress公开炮轰黄仁勋复职

英伟达临时CEO兼CFO Colette Kress刚刚放出一份火药味极浓的声明，直接开喷公司恢复黄仁勋CEO职务的决定。

她说：

“说实话，我觉得这整件事令人失望。英伟达不能一边把自己包装成建立在卓越、创新和诚信之上的公司，一边做出让人对领导力和企业价值观产生严重质疑的决定。”

“你不能无视人、削弱问责制，还指望所有人在闭门决策面前保持沉默。公司的声誉不是只靠市值和技术成就堆出来的，它靠的是信任、透明和它声称代表的原则。”

“恢复黄仁勋的职务，并不会自动抹掉所有围绕这件事的疑问。如果英伟达真的相信诚信，就该用行动证明，而不是只靠公开声明。”

“没有哪个人能大过公司，也没有哪家公司能自认为凌驾于问责制之上。英伟达需要解释自己的决定，停止把严肃问题当成不存在。”

Kress此前一直对外强调“董事会无意恢复黄仁勋”，现在董事会在特朗普介入后11天内180度转弯，她作为刚刚卸任临时CEO的人公开反对，火药味直接拉满。

调查还在继续，董事会却已经全票让他回来。

Kress这句话，等于把“没有人能大过公司”这件事，当面甩给了董事会和华盛顿。

所有人的大麻烦才开始
